title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
subtitle: Eleven things that have to be true before you move the first workload, learned from the waves where they weren't.
target_keyword: on premise to cloud migration" (SD 17, 320/mo, CPC $58.99)
banner_title: The landing zone checklist we run *before wave one*
body_oneline:
# The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave

Most failed migrations I have seen did not fail during the migration. They
failed about five weeks later, when someone asked a question nobody could
answer: *who gave that subscription permission to create a public load
balancer?*

The answer is almost always that the landing zone was built in parallel with the
first wave, by the same two people, under deadline. It worked well enough to get
workload one across. It did not survive workload forty.

So this is the checklist. Eleven things that have to be true before the first
production workload moves. None of them are exotic. The reason to write them
down is that under migration pressure, four or five always get deferred, and the
deferred ones are the ones that produce the five-week-later question.

## 1. Identity exists before compute exists

If your first VM lands before your identity model does, every later access
decision is a retrofit.

Concretely, before anything moves:

- Workload identities are federated to your existing IdP. No standalone cloud
  accounts with local credentials, not even for the pilot.
- Human access is role-assumption only, time-bounded, with no standing
  privileged access.
- Every role has a named owner. Not a team — a person.

The test: can you answer "which humans could have modified this resource
yesterday?" with a query rather than an investigation? If not, stop.

## 2. The account/subscription boundary is a blast radius decision

People choose account topology for billing clarity, then discover they chose
their blast radius too.

The rule we use: **one account per workload per environment**, not one account
per team. Teams reorganise; workloads have lifecycles. A workload-scoped
boundary means decommissioning is `delete account`, which is the only
decommissioning that ever actually happens.

```hcl
# Minimal shape — the point is that env is in the account identity,
# not a tag on shared infrastructure.
locals {
  accounts = {
    "payments-prod"    = { workload = "payments", env = "prod",    ou = "workloads/regulated" }
    "payments-nonprod" = { workload = "payments", env = "nonprod", ou = "workloads/regulated" }
    "catalog-prod"     = { workload = "catalog",  env = "prod",    ou = "workloads/standard" }
  }
}
```

Tags are for reporting. Accounts are for control. Do not try to use tags for
control; they are editable by the people you are controlling.

## 3. Guardrails are preventive, not detective

A detective control tells you someone created an unencrypted bucket. A
preventive control means they could not.

Both have a place, but the first wave needs preventive, because during a
migration your detective alerts go to a queue nobody is reading. Minimum set,
enforced at the organisation level so a workload account cannot opt out:

- No public object storage, by policy, with an explicit exception process that
  requires a second approver.
- Encryption at rest mandatory, with keys in your KMS, not the provider default.
- Region allowlist. This catches more mistakes than you would expect, and it is
  also your data-residency control.
- No IAM user creation. Federation only, as per item 1.

## 4. Network is designed for the steady state, not the migration

This is the one that bites hardest. Migration-period networking is temporary:
a big fat link back to the data centre, permissive routing, flat address space,
because you need everything to reach everything while it is half-moved.

Then the migration ends and that topology is production. Nobody unwinds it,
because unwinding it is a project with no feature in it.

Design the steady state first, then design the migration overlay as an
explicitly temporary thing with a removal ticket attached:

```
# Steady state: hub-spoke, spokes cannot route to each other
# Migration overlay: spoke -> on-prem via hub, TAGGED FOR REMOVAL
#
# The overlay routes carry an expiry tag. A weekly job opens a ticket
# for every overlay route older than its expiry. Crude, but it is the
# only thing that has ever actually got them removed.
```

Address space: allocate assuming three times the workloads you are migrating.
You will re-use this account structure for things that were never in the data
centre, and renumbering later is a genuine outage.

## 5. Cost attribution works on day one, not day ninety

If the first invoice arrives and you cannot split it by workload, you have lost
the ability to have a cost conversation for the rest of the programme. Finance
will ask "why is cloud expensive" and the only available answer will be a
shrug.

Mandatory tags, enforced preventively (you cannot create the resource without
them): `workload`, `env`, `owner`, `cost-centre`. Enforced, not requested — a
tagging policy without enforcement produces a tag coverage of about 60%, which
is the same as zero for attribution purposes.

This matters more than it sounds. Almost every "cloud is more expensive than
we thought" conversation is really an attribution failure, which is why
[cloud cost is an architecture problem](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem)
rather than a procurement one — you cannot fix a structure you cannot see.

## 6. Logging goes somewhere the workload account cannot delete

Audit logs in the account being audited is not an audit trail. Central logging
account, write-only from workload accounts, separate retention policy,
different access path.

The specific failure this prevents: an incident where you need to know what
happened, in an account where what happened included someone with broad
permissions.

## 7. There is a defined path to production, and it is the only one

Before the first wave, the deployment path exists and is used by the pilot
workload: source control → CI → artefact → environment promotion. No console
deploys to production. No exceptions for the migration.

The migration will generate enormous pressure to make exceptions, because
console-deploying one thing takes ten minutes and wiring it through the pipeline
takes two days. The two days are the point. Everything that goes in through the
console stays undocumented forever.

Short-lived credentials for the pipeline, federated via OIDC rather than stored
keys — I wrote up the mechanics of that separately, since it is the single
highest-value control you can add to a CI system.

## 8. Backup and restore are tested, in that order

Everyone configures backup. The checklist item is **restore**, performed once,
on the pilot workload, with the time recorded.

The recorded time is what you give the business when they ask about RTO. Not the
number from the provider documentation — your number, from your attempt, with
your data volume and your dependencies.

## 9. Observability exists before the thing you need to observe

Migrating a workload into an environment with no dashboards means your first
production incident is also your first attempt at instrumentation.

Baseline before wave one: infrastructure metrics, application logs with a
correlation ID that survives the service boundary, and one synthetic check per
workload that exercises a real user path. Not a health endpoint that returns
200 — a path that touches the database.

## 10. Somebody owns the landing zone as a product

Not a project. A product, with a backlog, a version, and a person whose job
includes it after the migration ends.

The alternative — landing zone as a project deliverable — produces an
environment that is correct on the day the project closes and drifts from that
day onward, with no mechanism to pull it back.

## 11. The first wave is deliberately boring

The pilot workload should be the one with the least business risk and the most
representative architecture. Those two usually conflict, and people resolve the
conflict by picking something trivially simple — a static site, an internal
tool with four users.

That teaches you nothing. A static site does not exercise identity, data
migration, cross-account networking or the restore path. Pick something dull but
*structurally complete*: a service with a database, an external dependency and a
scheduled job. Boring in business terms, complete in architectural terms.

---

## Running the checklist

We treat these as gates, not suggestions. The first wave does not start with
items outstanding, and the way that holds up under deadline pressure is that the
gate is reviewed by someone who is not responsible for the deadline.

Items 1-6 are the ones that are expensive to retrofit. 7-11 are expensive to
skip. If you only have time for six, take 1-6 and accept that you will be fixing
7-11 during the migration rather than before it.

Microsoft's
[Cloud Adoption Framework landing zone guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/landing-zone/)
covers the same ground in more depth and with Azure specifics; it is worth
reading even if you are on AWS, because the reasoning is portable and the
enforcement primitives map closely.

For how this fits into the wider sequence — assessment, wave planning,
the 7 Rs decision per application, and what to modernise during the move versus
after — Pixorama published
[the full step-by-step migration strategy](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud),
which is where this checklist sits as step two.

If you are running this with outside help rather than in-house, the thing to
test a partner on is whether they treat the landing zone as a product with an
owner or as a project deliverable. Their
[survey of DevOps consulting firms](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-devops-consulting-companies-india)
is a reasonable place to start a shortlist, and that question separates the
candidates faster than anything on their websites.

The thing I would most want to convince you of: the landing zone is not
preparation for the migration. It is the migration's only durable output. The
workloads were going to end up in the cloud either way. Whether they end up
somewhere governable is decided entirely in the weeks before the first one
moves.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
subtitle: We hit every milestone, moved every workload, and the bill went up 18%. The post-mortem took longer than the migration.
target_keyword: on premise to cloud migration" (SD 17, CPC $58.99, GSC pos 31)
banner_title: The cloud migration that *cost more* after we finished
body_oneline:
# The cloud migration that cost more after we finished

We finished a migration on time. Ninety-one workloads out of two data centres,
fourteen months, every wave inside its window. The programme closed, people were
thanked, and somebody made a slide with a green tick on it.

Four months later the monthly infrastructure bill was 18% higher than the
data-centre run rate it replaced.

Nobody had lied in the business case. The compute forecast was almost exactly
right — within 6%, which for a fourteen-month projection is good. The storage
forecast was fine. What we had done was model the cloud as a cheaper place to
run the same thing, which is the one assumption that guarantees this outcome.

I want to be specific about where the money went, because the generic version of
this story — "cloud cost optimisation is important" — is useless. The actual
causes were four, they were all architectural, and three of them were decided
before the first workload moved.

## 1. We paid for a hybrid period we told ourselves was temporary

The wave plan moved applications in order of business risk. Low-risk first,
critical last. Sensible, and it is what every methodology recommends.

It also meant that for eleven of the fourteen months, roughly a third of our
application dependencies ran across the boundary between the cloud and a data
centre. Every one of those calls was a charge. Reads that had been free on our
own switched network became metered egress.

The number was about $11,000 a month, averaged over the hybrid period. We had
budgeted zero, because at planning time nobody asked what the traffic between
wave 2 and wave 9 looked like.

The information was available. Flow logs existed. We had a dependency inventory.
What we did not have was anyone joining those two things and multiplying by a
price, which is an afternoon's work and would have changed the wave order.

The fix is not better forecasting. It is sequencing applications by *data
adjacency* rather than business risk, which is a different plan with a different
order and some uncomfortable conversations about moving a critical workload in
wave 3.

## 2. Lift and shift preserved the shape of a sizing decision made in 2017

About sixty of the ninety-one workloads were rehosted essentially as-is. That
was deliberate — a time-bound exit from a lease, and rehosting is the fastest
way out.

What it meant in practice: those VMs were sized for hardware bought in 2017 on a
three-year refresh cycle, which means they were sized for peak load plus a
growth margin plus a safety margin, because adding capacity meant a purchase
order and a six-week lead time.

That sizing logic is completely rational on owned hardware. The cost of
over-provisioning is a one-off capital inefficiency, and the cost of
under-provisioning is an outage you cannot fix quickly. Of course you oversize.

In the cloud that same logic is a recurring monthly charge for capacity you do
not use, and the under-provisioning risk it was protecting against no longer
exists, because you can resize in minutes.

We rehosted the machines *and the assumption*. Average CPU utilisation across
that estate, measured six months in, was 11%.

The honest version of the lift-and-shift decision is: this is a migration
strategy, not a cost strategy, and it defers the cost work rather than avoiding
it. We knew that. We said it in the steering committee. What we did not do was
put a date and an owner on the deferred work, so it did not happen.

## 3. Nobody could tell which team's spend was which

The first invoice was one number. By the third month people were asking why
cloud was expensive, and the only available answer was a breakdown by service
type — so much compute, so much storage, so much data transfer.

That is not an answer anyone can act on. "Compute is 40% of the bill" does not
tell a team that their batch job runs on an instance three sizes too large.

Tagging had been part of the landing zone design. It was a *policy* rather than
an *enforcement* — resources were supposed to carry owner and cost-centre tags.
Actual coverage, when we finally measured it, was 58%.

Fifty-eight percent coverage is functionally zero for attribution, because the
42% is not randomly distributed. It is concentrated in things created in a hurry
during cutover weekends, which is also where the oversized instances are.

We spent six weeks retro-tagging. Some resources we could not attribute at all
and had to trace through CloudTrail to find who created them. Two we switched
off to see who complained.

Making tags mandatory at creation — the resource simply cannot exist without
them — is a one-line policy change that would have saved all of it. It feels
bureaucratic in month one. It is the difference between having a cost
conversation and having an argument.

## 4. The architecture had a cost shape, and we had never looked at it

This is the one that actually mattered, and it is why the other three kept
coming back.

Six months post-migration we ran a cost-optimisation programme. Rightsizing,
reserved capacity, deleting orphaned volumes, scheduling non-production
environments off overnight. It worked: the bill came down 23% in a quarter.

Then it went back up over the following two quarters, to roughly where it had
been.

Because none of that touched the structure. The things we fixed were
consequences. The causes were a multi-AZ messaging cluster replicating across
zones on every write, a reporting service pulling full table extracts from
another service's database because there was no event stream, a batch pipeline
re-reading the same reference data forty times per run, and a chatty service
boundary in a request path that had been drawn around team ownership rather than
data locality.

Every one of those is a recurring cost generated by a design decision. Pricing
levers reduce the unit cost of running them. They do not stop you running them.

This is the part I would most want to transplant into the head of anyone about
to start: the cloud bill is a readout of your architecture. It is
[a finance costume](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem)
over a design problem, and a cost programme that only pulls pricing levers buys
exactly one good quarter.

## What we would do differently

Not "plan better". Four specific things, in the order they would happen:

**Join the flow logs to the wave plan, before the wave plan is approved.** Price
every cross-boundary dependency by the number of months it will span the
boundary. Resequence around the top five. This is an afternoon and it was worth
about $120,000 on this programme.

**Make the lift-and-shift deferral explicit, with a date.** "Rehost now,
rightsize within 90 days of each wave, owner named per workload." The deferral is
fine. The deferral without a date is how 11% utilisation survives for a year.

**Enforce tags preventively, not by policy.** Cannot create the resource without
`workload`, `env`, `owner`, `cost-centre`. Accept the friction in week one.

**Cost-review the architecture, not the invoice.** Once per quarter, pick the
three largest line items and ask what design decision produces them. Not "can we
get a discount on this" — "why does this exist". The answers are usually a
missing cache, a missing event stream, or a service boundary in the wrong place.

## The part that is genuinely hard

I do not want to make this sound like a process failure with a process fix.

The real difficulty is that the people who can see the cost shape of an
architecture are the architects, and they are fully occupied with the migration;
while the people who own the cost conversation are in finance, and they cannot
read an architecture. The gap between those two groups is where this money goes,
and no amount of dashboards closes it — dashboards give finance more detailed
numbers about things they still cannot act on.

What closed it for us, eventually, was putting one engineer in the monthly
finance review with a standing agenda item: here are the three largest cost
drivers, here is the design decision behind each, here is what changing it would
cost in engineering time. That meeting is where the batch pipeline got its
cache and the reporting service got its event stream.

It took us two years to set that meeting up. It should have existed in month
one, before the migration started, so that the hybrid-period egress forecast had
somewhere to be discussed.

---

If you are at the planning stage of one of these,
[we wrote the whole process up properly](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud)
— the assessment work, how to choose a strategy per application rather than per
programme, how to sequence waves, and what to modernise during the move versus
after. The part I would read twice is the assessment phase, because almost
everything in this post was knowable there and we did not look.

The migration itself was a success, for what it is worth. Ninety-one workloads,
on time, no major incident. We just measured it against the wrong thing.

# Issue 1: What we mean by "the software backbone"

This is a fortnightly letter about what engineering decisions cost. Not what
they cost in the business case — what they cost when the invoice arrives, or
when the migration is finished and the bill went up, or when the rewrite reaches
month fourteen.

I work at a firm that builds and modernises systems for mid-size and large
companies. That means I spend most of my time in the gap between what a plan
said and what happened, which turns out to be the most interesting place to
stand.

Over ten issues I want to make one argument from ten directions. Here it is, and
then I will tell you what I am not going to do.

## The claim

**Almost every expensive technology surprise is a structural decision showing up
late.**

Not a mistake. Not incompetence. A decision that was reasonable when it was
made, whose cost arrives in a different quarter, in a different currency, to a
different department — by which time nobody connects the two.

Three examples, each of which I will take properly in a later issue:

A company migrates to the cloud. Compute is forecast accurately. The bill goes
up, because for eleven months a third of their dependencies ran across the
boundary between two data centres and nobody priced the traffic. The structural
decision was the wave order, made at planning time by business risk. The cost
arrived as a line item called "data transfer" eight months later.

A team adds people to a legacy system to go faster. For two months output falls,
because the senior engineers who could have shipped are answering questions
instead. The structural decision was treating "backend engineer" as a fungible
unit. The cost arrived as a missed quarter.

A company fine-tunes a model so it will stop getting the return policy wrong. It
gets the policy wrong more confidently. The structural decision was confusing
knowledge with behaviour. The cost arrived as a customer complaint about an
answer that was stated very firmly.

In every case the information needed to avoid it was available at the time, and
in every case nobody was looking at it, because the question had been assigned
to a different function.

## Why "backbone"

The firm I work for uses the phrase "the software backbone of ambitious
enterprises", which is marketing language, and I want to rescue what is true in
it.

What is true: in most companies past a certain size, there is a set of systems
that everything else depends on, and almost nobody is responsible for their
shape. There are people responsible for features. People responsible for uptime.
People responsible for cost. Nobody responsible for whether the thing is
*coherent*.

So the shape drifts. Each individual decision is locally sensible. The sum is a
system where a reporting query locks tables during business hours, where two
services disagree about whether a discount applies to shipping, where the only
person who understands the billing logic is six months from retirement.

That incoherence is what eventually gets called "legacy", and by then the
conversation is about replacing it, which is usually the wrong conversation.

## What I am not going to do

**No predictions.** I do not know what AI will do to software engineering and
neither does anyone writing confidently about it.

**No tool reviews.** Which vector database, which framework, which cloud. These
decisions matter much less than the ones around them, and writing about them is
how a newsletter becomes an affiliate business.

**No case studies with the names changed and the numbers improved.** When I give
a figure, I will say where it came from and how many instances it is drawn from.
When it is three projects, I will say three projects. The ratios transfer; the
absolute numbers often do not.

**No selling.** I work for a company that does this for money, and I am not
going to pretend otherwise — the disclosure is at the bottom of every issue.
But this is not a funnel. If I have written something that only makes sense as a
lead magnet, I have failed at the brief I set myself, and you should tell me.

## What I would like from you

Disagreement, mostly. The claim above is falsifiable: if you have an expensive
technology surprise that was *not* a structural decision arriving late, I want
to hear it, because that is the most useful thing anyone could send me.

I will also take requests. If there is a decision you are facing that fits the
shape of this — a thing that looks cheap now and you suspect is not — reply and
I will think about it in public.

## The ten issues

Roughly, and I reserve the right to change my mind:

1. This one.
2. The four numbers that decide a migration.
3. Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first.
4. The modernisation decision tree I actually use.
5. Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they do not.
6. Retrieval is a product problem.
7. How to buy engineering capacity.
8. Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team.
9. Security that does not stop delivery.
10. How to run a vendor shortlist.

Two and three are the ones I have the most data on. Five is the one where I am
most likely to be wrong, and I will say so when I get there.

Next issue in a fortnight.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/), where I work on
cloud and platform engineering. Everything here is my own view and my own
reading of the projects I have been on. Where I use numbers from client work
they are anonymised and rounded, and I will tell you how many instances they
come from.*

# Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet

Every migration programme produces a wave plan in a spreadsheet. Wave 1, wave 2,
wave 3, with applications assigned to each and a date on top. And every
migration programme discovers somewhere around wave 3 that an application in
wave 5 is a synchronous dependency of an application in wave 2, so either wave 2
is not done or wave 5 just moved.

This is not a diligence failure. It is a representation failure. Dependencies
form a directed graph, and a spreadsheet cannot hold a graph — it can only hold
one flattening of it, chosen before you knew which flattening was feasible.

So: build the graph, compute the waves, regenerate when the graph changes.

## What you need from the CMDB

Less than you think. Three things:

```
applications:  id, name, criticality, owner, data_classification
dependencies:  source_app, target_app, kind (sync | async | batch | data)
constraints:   app_id, kind (freeze_window | licence | compliance | hardware_eol), detail
```

Your CMDB is wrong, by the way. Everyone's is. Expect 20-40% of dependencies to
be missing. The graph is still worth building, because a graph with known gaps
beats a spreadsheet with unknown ones — and the graph tells you *where* to spend
your discovery budget, which is the part that actually reduces risk.

Supplement from flow logs, which do not lie about what talks to what:

```python
# Netflow/VPC-flow-derived edges, intersected with CMDB-declared edges.
# The interesting set is the difference, not the union.
declared = set(cmdb_edges)
observed  = set(flow_edges)

undeclared = observed - declared   # these are your real risk
stale       = declared - observed  # these may be decommissioned, verify
```

Run that before you plan anything. The `undeclared` set is where wave 3 breaks.

## Dependency kinds are not equal

The single most useful modelling decision: edge weight by coupling type, because
they constrain the plan differently.

- **`sync`** — A calls B and waits. If they are separated across the WAN, A's
  latency budget absorbs the round trip. These must move together or you must
  accept the latency. Hard constraint.
- **`async`** — A queues to B. Tolerates separation well, as long as the queue
  is reachable from both sides. Soft constraint.
- **`batch`** — A reads B's extract nightly. Tolerates separation for a whole
  day. Nearly free.
- **`data`** — A and B share a database. These are not two applications for
  migration purposes; they are one unit. Collapse them.

Collapse `data` edges first. It usually shrinks the node count by 15-25% and
removes most of the apparent cycles.

```python
import networkx as nx

def build_graph(apps, deps):
    g = nx.DiGraph()
    for a in apps:
        g.add_node(a["id"], **a)
    for d in deps:
        g.add_edge(d["source_app"], d["target_app"], kind=d["kind"])
    return g

def collapse_shared_data(g):
    """Apps sharing a database migrate as one unit. Merge them into a
    single node so the wave algorithm cannot split them."""
    data_graph = nx.Graph()
    data_graph.add_nodes_from(g.nodes)
    data_graph.add_edges_from(
        (u, v) for u, v, k in g.edges(data="kind") if k == "data"
    )
    for group in nx.connected_components(data_graph):
        if len(group) > 1:
            keep, *rest = sorted(group)
            for other in rest:
                g = nx.contracted_nodes(g, keep, other, self_loops=False)
            g.nodes[keep]["merged_from"] = sorted(group)
    return g
```

`contracted_nodes` takes one pair at a time, so the group is folded pairwise
into its lowest-sorted member. Keeping `merged_from` on the surviving node
matters later: when the wave plan says "APP-0455 moves in wave 4", someone will
ask which seven things that actually means.

## Cycles are the real finding

Run a strongly-connected-components pass. Every SCC with more than one member is
a set of applications that mutually depend on each other and therefore *cannot
be ordered*. They move together, or you break the cycle first.

```python
def report_cycles(g):
    sccs = [c for c in nx.strongly_connected_components(g) if len(c) > 1]
    for c in sorted(sccs, key=len, reverse=True):
        print(f"cycle of {len(c)}: {sorted(c)}")
    return sccs
```

The first time you run this on a real estate, you will find one SCC with
somewhere between 8 and 40 members. That is your monolith, and it does not
matter that the architecture diagram shows it as separate applications.

This output is the single most valuable artefact of the whole exercise, because
it reframes the question. You are no longer asking "which wave does app X go
in?" You are asking "do we move these 23 things in one weekend, or do we spend
six weeks breaking three edges first?"

That is a
[legacy application modernization](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-application-modernization)
question rather than a migration question, and it is much better to meet it in
planning than in wave 3.

## Computing waves

With cycles collapsed, the graph is a DAG, and waves are a topological
generation walk — but inverted. Dependencies move *first*, so you want to layer
from the leaves of the dependency direction:

```python
def compute_waves(g, max_wave_size=12):
    """Wave N contains apps whose sync/data dependencies are all in waves < N."""
    hard = nx.DiGraph()
    hard.add_nodes_from(g.nodes)
    hard.add_edges_from(
        (u, v) for u, v, k in g.edges(data="kind") if k in ("sync", "data")
    )

    waves, placed = [], set()
    while len(placed) < hard.number_of_nodes():
        ready = [
            n for n in hard.nodes
            if n not in placed
            and all(dep in placed for dep in hard.successors(n))
        ]
        if not ready:
            raise ValueError("cycle remains — collapse SCCs first")

        # Deterministic, risk-ascending order within the wave
        ready.sort(key=lambda n: (
            g.nodes[n].get("criticality", 99),
            -hard.out_degree(n),
            n,
        ))
        wave = ready[:max_wave_size]
        waves.append(wave)
        placed.update(wave)
    return waves
```

Two details that matter more than the algorithm:

**`max_wave_size`** is a capacity constraint, not an architectural one. Set it
from how many applications your migration team can actually cut over in a
window. Twelve is a reasonable starting guess for a team of six with a weekend
window; measure after wave 1 and correct.

**Sorting by ascending criticality within a wave** means each wave starts with
its least critical members. If a wave runs out of time, you have deferred the
least important things, not whichever happened to be alphabetically last.

## Applying freeze windows and other constraints

The graph gives you a feasible order. Reality gives you a calendar: a retailer
cannot touch anything in November, a payroll system cannot move mid-month,
a licence expires in March, hardware goes EOL in June.

Do not encode these into the graph. Keep them as a separate filter applied to
the computed order, so that when the calendar changes you do not recompute
dependencies:

```python
def schedule(waves, constraints, calendar):
    """Assign dates to waves, deferring any wave whose members are
    frozen in the next available window."""
    plan, cursor = [], calendar.first_window()
    for wave in waves:
        while any(c.blocks(app, cursor) for app in wave for c in constraints):
            cursor = calendar.next_window(cursor)
        plan.append((cursor, wave))
        cursor = calendar.next_window(cursor)
    return plan
```

Hardware EOL deserves special handling, because it is the one constraint that
runs the other way: it is a *deadline*, not a blackout. An application on
hardware that dies in June must be in a wave before June, regardless of where
the topological order wants to put it. If the order says otherwise, you have
found a forced modernization: break the dependency, or accept a hybrid period
where that application runs in the cloud while its dependency is still on-prem.

Finding that in month one instead of month five is the entire return on building
this.

## Regenerate, don't maintain

The output is a plan, and plans are wrong. The value is not the first plan; it
is that the second one takes four minutes.

Put the graph build and wave computation in CI, triggered on changes to the
dependency source. Every run emits the wave plan, the cycle report, and a diff
against the last run. When a team discovers an undeclared dependency in week
seven — and they will — the question "what does this do to the plan?" is
answered by a commit rather than a workshop.

```
$ make wave-plan
  nodes: 247 (312 before data-collapse)
  cycles: 2 SCCs of size 23 and 4
  waves: 14 (max size 12)
  diff vs HEAD~1:
    APP-0912 moved wave 4 -> wave 7 (new sync dep on APP-0455)
    wave 9 now exceeds window capacity by 2
```

That diff is the artefact that makes the programme manageable. A spreadsheet
cannot produce it.

---

AWS's
[application portfolio assessment guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/application-portfolio-assessment-guide/introduction.html)
covers the data-collection side of this in more detail, including what to pull
from discovery tooling. It is worth pairing with this, because the graph is only
as good as the inventory feeding it.

For where wave planning sits in the overall sequence — assessment, landing zone,
the per-application 7 Rs decision, then waves, then optimisation — Pixorama put
[wave planning in context](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud)
in their full migration walkthrough. If you are evaluating partners to run the
programme, their list of
[cloud migration firms and how to read partner tiers](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-cloud-migration-companies-india)
is worth a look — a provider partner tier tells you about sales volume, not
about whether anyone there has built a dependency graph.

One closing opinion: the reason wave plans live in spreadsheets is that
spreadsheets are what the steering committee reads. Fine — generate the
spreadsheet *from* the graph. Just never let it become the source of truth,
because the moment someone edits a cell to make a date work, the graph and the
plan have diverged and only one of them knows about the dependency.

# Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture

There is a received wisdom about cloud migration that goes roughly: lift and
shift is what you do if you lack ambition. You will not get the benefits of the
cloud. You will move your problems rather than solve them. Do it properly —
refactor, go cloud-native, use managed services.

I have run migrations both ways and I think this wisdom is mostly wrong, or
rather, it is right about a thing that does not matter as much as it claims.

Here is the reframing I would offer: **rehosting is not an architectural choice
that happens to be fast. It is a scheduling choice that happens to have
architectural consequences.** Once you see it that way, the question stops being
"is lift and shift good" — a question with no answer — and becomes "what am I
buying with the time, and have I priced what I am deferring".

## The case against the received wisdom

The argument for refactoring during migration is that you are touching the
application anyway, so the marginal cost of improving it is low.

This is true for the code and false for everything else. Here is what actually
happens.

Migrating a workload as-is has a *bounded* set of unknowns. The application
behaves the same way; what changes is the infrastructure underneath it. When
something breaks, the cause is in a short list: networking, identity, storage
performance, a hardcoded hostname, a licence check pinned to a MAC address.
Painful, but enumerable.

Refactoring during migration has an *unbounded* set of unknowns, because now
both the infrastructure and the application have changed. When something breaks,
you do not know which half did it. And debugging that question — did the
behaviour change because we moved it or because we rewrote it — is where
migration schedules go to die. I have watched a two-week cutover become eleven
weeks over a single question of that shape.

There is a second problem, which is organisational. A refactor needs the people
who understand the application's business logic. A migration needs the people
who understand infrastructure. These are different people, and on a
sixty-workload programme you cannot have the first group available for all of
it. So the refactoring happens to whichever applications happen to be in the
wave when the domain expert is free, which is not a strategy.

## So what are you buying with the time?

This is the only question that matters, and it has real answers:

**An exit from a lease or a contract.** The most common and most legitimate. The
data centre contract ends in eleven months. A rehost fits in eleven months; a
refactor-everything programme does not. The alternative is not "a better
migration" — it is paying for a lease extension, which is a real number you can
compare against the cost of deferred modernisation.

**Hardware that is going to die.** Storage arrays out of support, a mainframe
with no spares, a database version the vendor stopped patching. The deadline is
set by physics and procurement, not by you.

**A data-centre event you want to stop fearing.** If you are one UPS failure
away from a bad week, getting out fast has a risk value that is hard to put on a
slide but is entirely real.

**Organisational attention.** This one is underrated. Migrations are funded by a
window of executive interest that does not last. A programme that delivers
something visible in six months can ask for another six. A programme that
delivers its first workload in month nine often does not get asked back.

Those are good reasons, and all four are about time. None of them is about
architecture.

## And what are you deferring?

The reason lift-and-shift gets a bad reputation is not that it is wrong. It is
that the deferred work is almost never scheduled, so "defer" silently becomes
"never", and two years later someone writes a blog post about how the cloud did
not deliver.

Be specific about the bill you are running up:

**Rightsizing.** Your VMs are sized for a procurement cycle, not for actual
load. Expect average utilisation somewhere between 8% and 20%. That is a
recurring overpayment starting the day the workload lands.

**Managed-service substitution.** A self-managed database on a VM costs you
patching, backup verification, failover testing and the engineer-hours to do all
three. Some of that is worth keeping. Most is not.

**Elasticity you cannot use.** A monolith that scales vertically cannot respond
to load by adding instances, so you pay for peak capacity continuously. This is
usually the largest single item and the hardest to fix.

**Resilience you now pay for differently.** On-prem redundancy was capital
already spent. In the cloud, multi-AZ is a recurring charge on every write that
crosses a zone. Keeping the on-prem resilience *pattern* in a cloud *pricing
model* is one of the quieter cost surprises.

Put numbers on those four, per workload, at planning time. Then the deferral is
a financing decision — we are paying X per month extra for Y months in exchange
for finishing Z months sooner — rather than an unexamined default.

## The decision rule I would actually use

Not per programme. Per application, which is the part most programmes get wrong
by choosing one strategy for everything.

**Rehost when:** the application works, the deadline is external, the business
logic is stable, and nobody on the team is frightened of it. Most applications
in most estates.

**Replatform** (same application, managed database or container runtime
underneath) **when:** the operational burden is the main cost and the
application does not care where its database lives. This is the highest
return-per-unit-risk option available and it is chronically under-used. Moving a
self-managed Postgres to a managed one is often a connection-string change and
eliminates a whole class of 3am work.

**Refactor when:** the application is actively blocking the business, *and* you
have the domain expert, *and* the cost shape is bad enough to justify it. Three
conditions, all required. Two out of three means wait.

**Replace** (buy something) **when:** the capability is not differentiating.
Payroll, expenses, CRM, ticketing. The fact that you built it in 2011 is not a
reason to keep it.

**Retire when:** you can find no user. Run this check properly — it is routine to
find 10-20% of an application estate has no meaningful traffic, and every one of
those is a workload you do not migrate, test, or pay for. Retiring is the only
strategy with a negative cost, and it is the one least likely to have an owner.

**Retain when:** the thing cannot move for a reason outside your control —
latency to a physical process, a regulatory constraint, a vendor licence that
forbids virtualisation. Say so explicitly and plan the hybrid rather than
discovering it.

The useful discipline is making this choice per application with a written
reason, which is what the 7 Rs framework is for — Pixorama has
[the 7 Rs broken down application by application](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud)
along with how to sequence the resulting mix, which is the harder half.

## The one thing I would not defer

If I were setting a single rule, it would be this: **lift and shift the
application, never the landing zone.**

Rehosting an application is a reversible, bounded compromise. Compromising on
identity, account structure, network topology, guardrails and cost attribution
is not. Those are the things everything else is built on top of, and retrofitting
them means touching every workload you already moved.

The migrations I have seen fail — genuinely fail, not just cost more than
planned — failed because the environment was built in parallel with the first
wave under deadline pressure, and it was never governable afterwards. The
applications were fine. They were fine in a place nobody could manage.

So: be as pragmatic as you like about the applications. Be inflexible about the
foundation. That asymmetry is, I think, the whole art of it.

## Where this leaves the received wisdom

"Lift and shift means you won't get cloud benefits" is true and incomplete. You
will not get cost or elasticity benefits. You will get out of the data centre,
on a deadline, with a bounded risk profile — and if that is what you needed, you
got what you paid for.

The failure mode is not choosing rehost. It is choosing rehost and then not
writing down what you deferred, because the deferred list is the entire second
half of the project and it has no champion once the migration programme closes
and everyone is thanked.

If the deferred work is genuinely a modernisation question rather than a
rightsizing one — if the answer involves changing what the application *is* —
then it is worth separating that out as its own decision rather than smuggling
it into a migration. The
[refactor, rebuild or replace](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace)
question has a different shape and a different cost curve, and migrations that
try to answer it mid-flight tend to answer it badly.

# Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration

Last issue I claimed that expensive technology surprises are structural
decisions showing up late. Migration is the cleanest example, so let me start
there.

I have reviewed a reasonable number of cloud migration business cases. They are
not bad documents. The compute forecast is usually within 10%, which for an
eighteen-month projection is respectable work.

They are also missing the same four numbers every time, and those four numbers
are what actually determine whether the programme comes in under its run-rate.

## Number one: cross-boundary gigabytes per wave-month

During a migration, some of your applications are in the cloud and some are
not. Every dependency that spans that boundary generates metered traffic that
was previously free, because it ran on a switch you already owned.

The number you want is: **for each dependency, the daily traffic volume
multiplied by the number of months its two endpoints will be on opposite sides of
the boundary.**

You can compute this. Flow logs tell you what talks to what and how much. The
wave plan tells you when each thing moves. Join them:

```
for each dependency (A -> B):
    gb_per_day     = flow_logs[A][B] / 30
    months_split   = abs(wave_of(A) - wave_of(B)) * months_per_wave
    cost           = gb_per_day * 30 * months_split * price_per_gb
```

On one programme I was close to, this came out at about $11,000 a month averaged
across an eleven-month hybrid period. Budgeted: zero. The information was
sitting in flow logs the whole time.

The reason nobody computes it is that it falls between two people. The
infrastructure team has the flow logs and does not own the business case. The
programme office owns the business case and has never seen a flow log.

What makes this number worth more than its own size: it is also a **resequencing
instruction**. A dependency carrying 80GB/day whose endpoints are six waves
apart is telling you to move those two applications together. Every time I have
seen this query run, it has changed the wave order.

## Number two: current utilisation of the machines you are about to copy

Not capacity. Utilisation. Average and p95 CPU and memory, over at least a
month, for every VM in scope.

The number is almost always lower than people expect — I have seen estates
average 8-20% — and the reason is structural and completely rational. On owned
hardware, you size for peak plus growth plus a safety margin, because adding
capacity means a purchase order and a six-week lead time. Over-provisioning
costs you a one-off capital inefficiency. Under-provisioning costs you an
outage you cannot fix quickly.

In the cloud, that same sizing logic is a recurring monthly charge for capacity
you do not use, protecting against a risk that no longer exists.

So if you rehost as-is, you are copying the machines *and the assumption*. The
number tells you how much that costs: the gap between what you are provisioning
and what you are using, priced monthly, from the day each wave lands.

I am not arguing against rehosting. It is frequently correct, and I will defend
it in a future issue. I am arguing that the deferral should have a number and a
date attached, because "we'll rightsize later" with no number and no owner
reliably becomes 11% utilisation a year later.

## Number three: tag coverage, measured not assumed

What percentage of your existing infrastructure can be attributed to a specific
business owner and cost centre, today, from metadata rather than from someone's
memory?

Measure it. Do not ask whether you have a tagging policy — everyone has a
tagging policy. Measure actual coverage.

In my experience the honest answer is somewhere between 50% and 70%, and the
missing portion is not randomly distributed. It is concentrated in things
created in a hurry, which is also where the oversized instances and the orphaned
volumes are.

Why this number decides the migration: at 60% coverage you cannot have a cost
conversation. The invoice arrives as one figure, finance asks why cloud is
expensive, and the only available answer is a breakdown by service type —
"compute is 40% of the bill" — which no team can act on.

The fix costs one policy change: make the tags mandatory at resource creation,
so the resource cannot exist without them. It feels bureaucratic in week one. It
is the difference between a cost conversation and an argument, and retro-tagging
later is six weeks of archaeology through audit logs.

## Number four: how long your engineering team takes to ship an infrastructure change

This is the one nobody thinks belongs in a migration business case, and I now
think it is the most predictive of the four.

Measure: from "we agree this change is needed" to "it is in production", for a
routine infrastructure change. Median, over the last ten.

If that number is two days, your migration will go roughly as planned, because
when you discover something — and you will discover something every week — you
can respond.

If it is six weeks, the migration will take much longer than the plan says,
regardless of how good the plan is. Every discovery becomes a six-week
decision, and discoveries are serial because each one changes what you look at
next.

This number is a property of your organisation, not your technology, and it is
the one you cannot buy your way out of. A migration programme with excellent
tooling and a six-week change cycle will be paced by the six weeks.

The useful consequence: if that number is bad, **fix it before the migration, not
during.** Six weeks spent on the deployment pipeline before wave one is
recovered several times over. I have watched a team do exactly this and it was
the highest-return decision of their programme, though it looked like a delay at
the time.

## What the four have in common

None of them are about the cloud.

Number one is about your dependency graph. Two is about a procurement cycle from
2017. Three is about governance discipline. Four is about your delivery
capability.

The cloud is where they become visible, because the cloud prices things that
were previously free or capital. That is the whole mechanism of the "cloud is
more expensive than we thought" conversation: not that the cloud is expensive,
but that it meters things your previous environment did not, and the meter is a
readout of structure you had never had to look at.

Which is last issue's claim, in a specific setting: the structural decisions were
made years ago. The migration just moved them somewhere with a price tag.

## If you are about to start one

Compute one, two and three this week. They are genuinely an afternoon each, and
between them they will tell you more about your migration's cost than another
month of planning.

Four takes longer because you have to look at your last ten changes honestly,
and the answer is often unwelcome.

Then put all four in the business case as explicit lines, including the ones that
make the saving look smaller. A business case that shows a modest saving and
survives contact with the invoice is worth considerably more than one that shows
a large saving and does not — not least because the second kind damages the
credibility of the next programme.

For the full sequence around all this — the assessment work, choosing a strategy
per application rather than per programme, how to build the landing zone before
wave one, and what to modernise during the move versus after — my colleagues
wrote
[the long version of this](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud)
with the steps laid out properly. The part I would read twice is the assessment
phase, because all four of these numbers belong there and it is the phase most
programmes compress.

A note if you are running this with a partner rather than in-house: ask which
of these four they will compute before the business case is signed. All four are
cheap, and a firm that has not offered them is quoting you a migration rather
than a result. My colleagues' notes on
[how to read a migration firm's partner tiers](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-cloud-migration-companies-india)
make a related point I had not thought about until I read it: a provider's
top-tier partner badge is a measure of committed spend routed through them,
which is not an incentive to make number two smaller.

Next issue: why cost-optimisation programmes get exactly one good quarter.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/), where I work on
cloud and platform engineering. Figures in this issue come from three migration
programmes, anonymised and rounded. The ratios transfer better than the absolute
numbers.*

# Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model

Every migration business case I have reviewed models compute accurately. Most
model storage adequately. Almost none model data movement, and data movement is
the line item that turns a 20% saving into a 15% increase.

The reason is structural. Compute cost is a function of things you chose
deliberately — instance sizes, counts, hours. Egress cost is a function of
something nobody chose: where the data happens to be relative to where the
compute happens to be, which in a migration is decided by wave sequencing rather
than by design.

Here is how to find it before the invoice does.

## Why it is invisible in planning

Pre-migration, all your traffic is on your own network. A service reading 200GB
a day from a database two racks away costs nothing marginal — the switch is a
capital asset, already paid for.

Post-migration, if that service is in the cloud and the database is still on
prem, the same 200GB a day is cross-boundary. At roughly $0.09/GB that is
$540/month for one dependency, and the uncomfortable part is that it is
*recurring for as long as the hybrid period lasts*, which is always longer than
planned.

Multiply across a mid-size estate during a 14-month migration and this is
routinely a six-figure line nobody budgeted.

Three distinct charges people conflate:

| Flow | Typical cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Internet egress | ~$0.05-0.12/GB | Tiered, falls with volume |
| Cross-region | ~$0.02/GB | Both directions in some services |
| Cross-AZ | ~$0.01/GB each way | **Both** directions — easy to double-count |
| Ingress | $0 | Which is why it feels free to move data in |
| NAT gateway processing | ~$0.045/GB | *On top of* egress, and often larger |

That last row is the one that surprises people. If your private-subnet workloads
reach the internet through a managed NAT gateway, you pay a processing fee per
gigabyte *plus* the egress. For high-volume flows the NAT fee can exceed the
egress fee. A VPC endpoint for the same service costs a fraction.

Cross-AZ is the quiet one. A three-AZ Kafka cluster with replication factor 3
pays cross-AZ on every replica write, in both directions, forever. That is an
architectural choice with a direct monthly number attached, and it is almost
never costed at design time.

## Finding it in your own traffic, before you migrate

You do not need a tool. You need flow logs and a dependency inventory, and you
need to join them.

```sql
-- Flow records, aggregated per application pair per day.
-- The question: for each candidate migration wave, how much traffic
-- crosses the boundary that the wave is about to create?
WITH flows AS (
  SELECT
    src.app_id              AS src_app,
    dst.app_id              AS dst_app,
    SUM(f.bytes) / 1e9      AS gb_per_day
  FROM flow_logs f
  JOIN asset_map src ON f.src_addr = src.ip
  JOIN asset_map dst ON f.dst_addr = dst.ip
  WHERE f.day >= CURRENT_DATE - 30
  GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT
  f.src_app,
  f.dst_app,
  ROUND(f.gb_per_day, 1)                       AS gb_per_day,
  w_src.wave                                   AS src_wave,
  w_dst.wave                                   AS dst_wave,
  -- Months of hybrid exposure for this edge
  GREATEST(w_src.wave, w_dst.wave) - LEAST(w_src.wave, w_dst.wave) AS waves_apart,
  ROUND(f.gb_per_day * 30 * 0.09, 0)           AS usd_per_month_if_split
FROM flows f
JOIN wave_plan w_src ON f.src_app = w_src.app_id
JOIN wave_plan w_dst ON f.dst_app = w_dst.app_id
WHERE w_src.wave <> w_dst.wave
  AND f.gb_per_day > 1
ORDER BY usd_per_month_if_split DESC;
```

The top twenty rows of that query are your egress forecast. They are also, more
usefully, a **resequencing instruction**: an edge carrying 80GB/day whose
endpoints are six waves apart is telling you to move those two applications
together.

This is the single highest-return query in migration planning and it takes an
afternoon. I have never run it on a real estate without finding at least one
pair that should obviously have been in the same wave.

## Data gravity is a design constraint, not a metaphor

"Data gravity" sounds like consultant-speak. It describes something concrete:
the larger a dataset, the more expensive it is to compute anywhere other than
where it lives, so compute migrates toward data rather than the reverse.

Practically, this means the sequencing rule is: **move the data first, or move
the data last, but never move the compute separately from the data it reads
heavily.**

The two workable patterns:

**Data first.** Replicate the datastore to the cloud, run it as a read replica
during transition, cut over writes when the dependent applications have moved.
Costs you an ingress period (free) and dual-running storage (cheap). Avoids
sustained egress entirely. This is almost always correct.

**Data last.** Keep the datastore on prem, move only applications whose read
volume is genuinely low. Requires the query above to prove "low" rather than
assume it.

The pattern that does not work, and is the default if you do not decide: move
applications in wave order and let the data follow whenever it is convenient.
That maximises the number of wave-months where a chatty edge spans the boundary.

## Instrument so attribution is possible

If you cannot attribute egress to a workload, you cannot have a conversation
about it — the bill arrives as one number and the discussion becomes "cloud is
expensive."

Minimum instrumentation, in place before wave one:

```hcl
# Every resource carries workload identity. Enforced by policy so the
# resource cannot be created without it — a tagging *request* gets you
# about 60% coverage, which is useless for attribution.
locals {
  required_tags = {
    workload    = var.workload
    env         = var.environment
    owner       = var.owner_email
    cost_centre = var.cost_centre
    data_class  = var.data_classification
  }
}

# VPC flow logs to the central logging account, with the fields you
# actually need for cost work.
resource "aws_flow_log" "workload" {
  log_destination      = var.central_flow_log_arn
  log_destination_type = "s3"
  traffic_type         = "ALL"
  vpc_id               = aws_vpc.workload.id

  # pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr matter: without them, traffic through an
  # intermediary is attributed to the intermediary, not the real endpoints.
  log_format = join(" ", [
    "$${version}", "$${account-id}", "$${vpc-id}", "$${subnet-id}",
    "$${srcaddr}", "$${dstaddr}", "$${srcport}", "$${dstport}",
    "$${protocol}", "$${bytes}", "$${packets}",
    "$${pkt-srcaddr}", "$${pkt-dstaddr}", "$${flow-direction}",
    "$${traffic-path}", "$${start}", "$${end}", "$${action}",
  ])
}
```

`pkt-srcaddr` and `pkt-dstaddr` versus `srcaddr`/`dstaddr` is the detail worth
knowing: with a NAT gateway or a transit gateway in the path, the plain fields
show the intermediary. You will attribute 40% of your egress to "the NAT
gateway", which is true and useless.

## The three fixes, in order of return

**1. VPC endpoints for provider services.** If workloads reach object storage,
queues, or secret stores over the internet via NAT, you are paying NAT
processing plus egress for traffic that never needed to leave the provider
network. Gateway endpoints for object storage are typically free. This is the
single cheapest fix available and it is frequently worth 20-30% of a NAT bill.

**2. Collapse chatty edges into one AZ or one service.** A cross-AZ call pattern
in a request path is paying twice per hop for availability you may not need at
that tier. Multi-AZ for the datastore, single-AZ for the stateless tier behind an
AZ-aware load balancer, is a legitimate design that many teams reject reflexively.

**3. Cache at the boundary, not at the service.** A read-through cache in the
cloud in front of an on-prem datastore converts sustained egress into a bounded
miss rate. During a hybrid period this is often the highest-leverage code change
available — one team I worked with cut a $4,100/month cross-boundary bill to
about $300 with a cache and a 15-minute TTL, because the data was reference data
that changed daily.

And one anti-fix: do not solve this with a reserved-capacity or committed-spend
discount. Commitments reduce the unit price of a structure you have not changed.
The structure is the problem — which is the whole argument in
[Pixorama wrote this up as an architecture problem wearing a finance costume](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem),
and it matches what I have seen every time: cost programmes that only touch
pricing get one good quarter and then revert.

## What to do on Monday

Run the flow-log join. Produce the top twenty cross-boundary edges with a dollar
figure. Take that list to whoever owns the wave plan and resequence around the
top five.

Then add egress as an explicit line in the business case, derived from that
query and the planned hybrid duration, rather than omitted. A business case that
shows a smaller saving and survives contact with the invoice is worth more than
one that shows a larger saving and does not.

Flexera's annual
[State of the Cloud report](https://info.flexera.com/CM-REPORT-State-of-the-Cloud)
survey has put managing cloud spend at or near the top of respondents' concerns
for years running, alongside consistently large self-reported waste. The waste is
not mostly idle instances. It is structural, and data movement is the largest
structural component nobody models.

For where this fits in sequencing — and why the assessment phase should include
the flow-log work rather than treating it as optimisation to do later —
Pixorama's
[migration strategy guide](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud)
puts it in step one, which is the right place for it. And if you are shortlisting
partners, their notes on
[reading cloud migration firms' partner tiers](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-cloud-migration-companies-india)
are a useful corrective: a top-tier badge measures committed spend through that
provider, which is close to the opposite of an incentive to reduce your bill.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
subtitle: The rewrite was approved, scoped and staffed. Cancelling it was the best engineering decision I have been part of.

body_oneline:
# We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work

The rewrite had a name, a budget, a two-year timeline and eleven people assigned
to it. It had a slide deck with a diagram of the target architecture, and the
diagram was genuinely good. I had helped make it.

We cancelled it in week five.

What we did instead was six months of work so unexciting that it was difficult
to report on. At the end of those six months, the system that was going to be
replaced was still there, still running the business, and nobody wanted to
replace it any more. Not because we had grown fond of it — because the things
that had made it intolerable were gone.

I have thought about this a lot since, because the decision was nearly the other
way, and the argument that changed it was not an engineering argument.

## What was actually wrong

The system was fourteen years old. Roughly 400,000 lines, a language two versions
out of support, a schema with 200 tables and some genuinely alarming design
decisions in it. Four people understood it; two of them were close to retirement.

Everyone agreed it had to go. When I asked people *why*, I got these answers:

1. Changes take too long. A small feature was six to eight weeks.
2. It breaks in production and we cannot tell why.
3. We cannot hire for it.
4. Deployments are a weekend event requiring four people.
5. It is going to fall over one day and we will not be able to fix it.

That list is what justified the rewrite. And looking at it now, the thing I
notice is that **not one of those five items is a statement about the
architecture.** They are all statements about the *experience of working on it*.

That distinction is what the week-five conversation turned on. Someone in a
review — not an engineer, our delivery lead — asked a question that I have
reused many times since: *if we fixed the five complaints without replacing the
system, would we still want to replace it?*

Nobody could say yes with a straight face.

## The six months

So we took the five complaints as the backlog. In order of how much they were
hurting:

### Deployments (6 weeks)

A weekend deployment needing four people meant we deployed monthly, which meant
every release carried a month of changes, which meant every failure was hard to
attribute, which meant we were cautious, which meant we deployed monthly.

We did not change the application. We automated the existing runbook. The
runbook was a 40-step Word document; it became a script, then a pipeline. Six
weeks, two engineers, no application code modified.

Deployment went from a staffed weekend to eleven minutes on a Tuesday.

This single change did more for the other four complaints than anything else we
did, which I did not expect. Feature lead time dropped before we had touched
anything that affects feature lead time, because the batch size collapsed.

### Observability (7 weeks)

"It breaks and we cannot tell why" was literally true: the application logged to
local files on each of six servers, with no correlation between them, and the
logs were rotated daily.

We added structured logging with a request ID threaded through the entry points,
shipped it centrally, and put up four dashboards and about a dozen alerts. We
did not instrument the whole system — we instrumented the eight code paths that
generated the most support tickets.

Mean time to diagnose went from "a day and a guess" to minutes for the common
cases. Two long-standing intermittent bugs were identified in the first
fortnight, because for the first time we could see them happen.

### The test harness (9 weeks)

This was the hardest part and the highest value. There were almost no tests. Any
change therefore required manual regression testing, which is where most of the
six-to-eight weeks went.

We did not try to retrofit unit tests across 400,000 lines; that is the project
that never finishes. We built a characterisation harness at the boundary: record
real requests and responses in production, replay them against a candidate
build, diff the outputs.

```
record (prod, 2 weeks of traffic) -> 140,000 request/response pairs
replay (candidate build)          -> diff
```

This is a crude technique and it was transformative. It does not tell you the
system is correct; it tells you the system has not *changed*, which is the actual
question when modifying a legacy system. Within a month, a change that had
required six weeks of manual regression could be validated in an afternoon.

It also found three places where the system's behaviour differed from its
documentation, which was educational for everyone who had been planning to
rewrite it from the documentation.

### Modularisation at the seams (10 weeks)

Only now did we touch the architecture, and only at the edges.

Two capabilities were genuinely separable and genuinely painful: a reporting
layer that locked tables during business hours, and a notification system that
nobody wanted to be near. We extracted both. New services, new code, clean
interfaces, with the characterisation harness proving the old behaviour was
preserved.

That is maybe 8% of the system by line count. It was most of the daily pain.

### Hiring (ongoing, mostly solved by the above)

"We cannot hire for it" turned out to be partly false. We could not hire people
excited about a system with no tests, no observability, and weekend deployments
— which is a different problem, and we had just fixed it. The language was a
smaller obstacle than the working conditions; competent engineers will learn an
unfashionable language for a well-run system, and will not join a badly-run one
for a fashionable one.

## What the rewrite would have actually cost

The two-year estimate was wrong in the way all rewrite estimates are wrong, and
I want to be precise about the mechanism rather than just asserting it.

The estimate was built from the *known* requirements — the documented behaviour,
the current feature set, the integrations we knew about. That part was probably
about right.

What it omitted:

**The undocumented behaviour.** Our characterisation harness found three
divergences in the eight code paths we instrumented. Extrapolated across the
system, there were hundreds of behaviours nobody had written down, each one load
-bearing for some customer, discoverable only by breaking it.

**The two-system period.** During a rewrite, both systems need maintenance.
Every feature request in those two years gets built twice or deferred. The
business does not stop for your migration, and the rewrite team's velocity
assumption generally pretends it does.

**The convergence problem.** The old system keeps changing while you rebuild it,
so the target keeps moving. Teams solve this by freezing the old system, which
the business overrules by month four.

My honest estimate is three and a half to four years, and a 40% chance of
abandonment somewhere in year two — at which point you have the original system
plus a half-finished replacement plus a demoralised team.

The six months of boring work cost roughly a tenth of the rewrite's first year
and delivered most of what people actually wanted.

## When the rewrite is right

I am not arguing rewrites are never correct. I have seen two that were, and they
had a common feature: **the requirements had changed, not just the code.**

If what the business needs is now materially different from what the system
does, then carefully preserving its existing behaviour is wasted effort — you are
spending money to keep something you want to get rid of. That is a genuine
rebuild case.

The rewrite that is usually wrong is the one where the requirements are stable
and the complaint is that the code is unpleasant. That is a maintainability
problem, and maintainability problems have cheaper solutions than replacement.

The question I would put to any rewrite proposal: *what will the new system do
that the old one does not?* If the answer is a list of qualities — it will be
testable, observable, modular, modern — those are properties you can add to the
system you have. If the answer is a list of capabilities the business needs and
cannot get, that is a rebuild.

Pixorama's framing of
[how to decide between the three](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace)
— refactor, rebuild or replace — is a more structured version of the same test,
and their broader piece on
[legacy application modernization](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-application-modernization)
covers the option space including buying a product, which in our case was
genuinely considered and rejected for one capability and accepted for another.

## The part that is hard to replicate

I will be honest about why this is difficult, because "just do the boring work"
is advice that ignores the real obstacle.

The rewrite was *easier to fund*. It had a narrative, a target architecture
diagram, a name, and an end state that sounded like progress. It was a thing you
could announce.

"We are going to spend six months automating the deployment, adding logging and
building a replay harness" is not an announcement. It has no end state. Nobody
gets promoted for it. The quarterly update is "deployment is faster now", which
is unglamorous next to "we are modernising the platform".

What made it possible for us was reframing the six months as **a precondition**
rather than an alternative. The pitch was not "do this instead of the rewrite".
It was: *we cannot safely rewrite this system until we can deploy it, observe it
and test it — so we are doing that first, and we will revisit the rewrite in six
months with much better information.*

That got funded. And six months later, with the information, nobody wanted it.

Which was, I think, always the likely outcome, and is a reasonable way to find
out.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
subtitle: Why cost-optimisation programmes get exactly one good quarter, and what the second quarter tells you.
