banner_title: Architecture debt shows up on the *finance dashboard*
body_oneline:
# Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first

Here is a pattern I have now seen four times, closely enough to be confident
about the mechanism.

A company's cloud bill is uncomfortable. Somebody runs a cost-optimisation
programme. Rightsizing, reserved capacity, deleting orphaned volumes, turning
non-production environments off overnight, negotiating a committed-spend
discount.

It works. The bill comes down 20-25% in a quarter. There is a slide.

Then over the following two or three quarters it climbs back to roughly where it
started, and the second cost-optimisation programme gets a worse reception than
the first.

## Why the second quarter undoes the first

Because the first programme fixed consequences, and the causes were untouched.

The things a cost programme typically fixes — oversized instances, idle
resources, un-discounted on-demand usage, dev environments running at 3am — are
all *symptoms of a structure that keeps producing them*. Delete the orphaned
volumes and the process that orphans volumes is still running. Rightsize the
instances and the deployment pattern that oversizes them is unchanged.

Meanwhile the actual cost drivers are things like:

- A messaging cluster replicating across availability zones on every write,
  paying cross-zone charges in both directions, forever.
- A reporting service pulling full table extracts from another service's
  database because there is no event stream, so the same data moves nightly at
  full volume.
- A batch pipeline re-reading the same reference dataset forty times in a single
  run, because each step was written independently and nobody owns the pipeline.
- A service boundary drawn around team ownership rather than data locality, so a
  request path crosses the network four times where it could cross once.

Every one of those is a recurring charge generated by a design decision. Pricing
levers reduce the *unit cost* of running them. They do not stop you running
them.

So the saving is real and bounded, and the growth underneath it continues. Hence
one good quarter.

## The finance dashboard as an architecture readout

What I find genuinely interesting about this is the direction of information
flow. The finance dashboard is often the **first** place architectural
incoherence becomes visible, and it shows up there before it shows up in any
engineering metric.

Think about why. A chatty service boundary does not necessarily make latency bad
enough to alert on. The nightly full-table extract completes within its window.
The over-replicated cluster is perfectly healthy. Nothing is broken. Every
dashboard an engineering team looks at is green.

But each of those is converting a design decision into a monthly charge, so the
bill grows in a shape that matches the architecture. The line item called "data
transfer" is a measurement of how much your services talk across boundaries.
The compute line is a measurement of your scaling model. These are
architectural facts, denominated in dollars.

Which means — and this is the part I want to land — **the cost report is
observability.** It is lagging, badly labelled, and aggregated by the wrong
dimensions, but it contains information about structure that no engineering
dashboard contains.

My colleagues made this argument at more length, calling cloud cost
[an architecture problem wearing a finance costume](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem),
which is a better phrase than any I have come up with and matches what I have
watched happen.

## The gap that makes this hard

I do not want to present this as a process failure with a process fix, because
the real obstacle is organisational and it is genuinely difficult.

The people who can read the cost shape of an architecture are architects and
senior engineers. They are fully occupied with delivery.

The people who own the cost conversation are in finance. They cannot read an
architecture, and no dashboard fixes that — giving finance a more detailed
breakdown of services they do not understand produces more precise confusion.

The gap between those two groups is where this money goes. And both groups are
behaving reasonably: finance is asking the right question in the only vocabulary
it has, and engineering is answering a different question because that is the
one it was asked.

What closed it on one programme I was part of — eventually, after about two years
of not closing it — was putting one engineer in the monthly finance review with a
standing agenda item. Three slides, every month:

1. The three largest cost drivers this month.
2. The design decision behind each.
3. What changing it would cost in engineering time.

That is it. No dashboard, no tooling, no FinOps platform. One engineer, three
slides, once a month.

That meeting is where the batch pipeline got its cache and the reporting service
got its event stream. Both had been obvious to engineers for over a year. Neither
had ever been prioritised, because they were invisible to the people doing the
prioritising — there was no feature in them, no incident driving them, and the
cost case had never been made in a room where it counted.

It should have existed in month one. I think it is probably the highest-leverage
meeting in any organisation spending meaningfully on cloud, and it costs an hour.

## The question that actually works

If you take one thing from this issue, take the reframing of the question.

The standard cost question is: **"can we reduce this line item?"** It leads to
pricing levers, because that is what it is asking about.

The better question is: **"why does this line item exist?"**

Applied to the four examples above, that question produces:

- *Why do we pay cross-zone transfer on every write?* Because the cluster is
  configured for an availability target nobody has validated against the
  business requirement. Maybe it is correct. Maybe it was a default.
- *Why does the reporting service read the whole table nightly?* Because there is
  no change stream. One is a week of work and removes the charge permanently.
- *Why does the pipeline read the reference data forty times?* Because nobody
  owns the pipeline end to end. A cache and an owner.
- *Why does this request cross the network four times?* Because the service
  boundaries follow the org chart from two reorganisations ago.

None of those answers is "we need a better discount". Three of the four are a
week or two of engineering with a permanent effect, which is a much better
return than a commitment discount that locks you into the current structure for
three years.

That last point deserves emphasis, because it is the trap: **a committed-spend
discount on a bad structure is worse than no discount.** You have reduced the
unit price and simultaneously made it harder to justify changing the thing,
because now you have committed capacity to fill.

## What I would do with one afternoon

Take last month's bill. Sort by cost, descending. Take the top five lines.

For each one, write a single sentence explaining which design decision produces
it. Not which service — which *decision*.

If you can write that sentence for all five, you are in better shape than most
organisations I have seen, and you have a prioritised architecture backlog with
dollar figures attached, which is the most fundable engineering artefact there
is.

If you cannot write it for three of them, that is the actual finding, and it is
usually an attribution problem rather than an understanding problem — which is
issue two's third number coming back round.

Next issue: the modernisation decision tree, and the rewrite I helped get
cancelled.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/), where I work on
cloud and platform engineering. The pattern described here is drawn from four
organisations; the three-slide meeting is from one of them.*

subtitle: The pattern is well known. The routing layer, the data problem and the exit criteria are where it actually goes wrong.

banner_title: The strangler fig, and *where it actually breaks*
body_oneline:
# The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite

Everyone knows the strangler fig pattern. Put a facade in front of the legacy
system, route one capability at a time to new code, repeat until the old thing
has no traffic, delete it.

The pattern is right. What nobody tells you is that roughly 70% of the work is
in three things the diagram does not show: where the routing decision lives, what
happens to the data, and how you decide you are finished. Get those wrong and
you end up in the failure mode that is genuinely worse than not starting — a
permanent two-system estate where every feature has to be built twice.

I have been through this four times. Here is what the diagram leaves out.

## The routing layer is a product, not a config file

The naive version: nginx with a growing list of path rules.

```nginx
# This works for about three months.
location /api/invoices { proxy_pass http://new-invoices; }
location /api/customers { proxy_pass http://legacy; }
location /api/orders    { proxy_pass http://legacy; }
```

It breaks the first time a migration is not clean along a path boundary — which
is the first time, because legacy systems are not organised by URL. You will
need to route on things like:

- **Tenant.** Migrate customer by customer, not endpoint by endpoint. Far lower
  risk, because a bug affects one tenant.
- **Percentage.** Ramp 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% on a single endpoint.
- **Request shape.** `GET /api/invoices` to the new service, `POST` still
  legacy, because reads are safe and writes are not.
- **A manual kill switch** that does not require a deploy.

That is four orthogonal dimensions, which means the routing decision is a
function, not a table:

```python
def route(request, flags):
    key = f"{request.method}:{request.route_pattern}"
    rule = flags.get(key)

    if rule is None or rule.disabled:
        return LEGACY

    if rule.tenant_allowlist and request.tenant_id in rule.tenant_allowlist:
        return NEW
    if rule.tenant_blocklist and request.tenant_id in rule.tenant_blocklist:
        return LEGACY

    # Stable per-tenant hash, so a tenant does not flap between
    # systems on consecutive requests. This matters enormously and
    # is the bug everyone ships first.
    if rule.percentage > 0:
        bucket = stable_hash(f"{key}:{request.tenant_id}") % 100
        if bucket < rule.percentage:
            return NEW

    return LEGACY
```

The stable hash is the detail I would underline. A naive `random() < 0.05`
means the same tenant hits the new service on one request and the legacy one on
the next. If the two have any state divergence at all — and they do — you get
intermittent, unreproducible bugs that cost a fortnight to diagnose.

Keep the flags in a store you can change without deploying, and make the kill
switch a single call that forces every rule to `LEGACY`. You will use it. The
first time you use it, the fact that it takes 20 seconds rather than a 40-minute
rollback deploy is the entire justification for building it.

## The data problem, which is the actual problem

Routing reads is easy. The hard question is what owns the data.

Three options, in increasing order of both difficulty and value:

### Option A: new service reads the legacy database

Fastest to ship. The new service is a read-model over the legacy schema.

```
[client] -> [router] -> [new-invoices] -> (reads) -> [legacy DB]
                     -> [legacy app]    -> (writes) -> [legacy DB]
```

Honest assessment: this is not modernization, it is a new UI. You have not
decoupled anything — the legacy schema is still the contract, and you cannot
delete the legacy system because it still owns writes. Useful as a first step to
build confidence. Dangerous if you stop here, because it *feels* like progress
and it is a dead end.

### Option B: dual write, legacy is source of truth

The new service writes to its own store and to the legacy one. Legacy stays
authoritative. Reads can come from either, and you compare them.

```python
def create_invoice(payload):
    legacy_result = legacy_client.create_invoice(payload)   # authoritative
    try:
        new_store.upsert(from_legacy(legacy_result))
    except Exception:
        # Never fail the request because the shadow write failed.
        metrics.increment("shadow_write.failure")
        log.exception("shadow write failed", invoice=legacy_result.id)
    return legacy_result
```

The point of this phase is not the writes — it is the **comparison**. Run the
new read path in shadow mode: serve the legacy answer, compute the new answer,
diff them, log the mismatches, serve nothing from the new path.

```python
def get_invoice(invoice_id):
    legacy = legacy_client.get_invoice(invoice_id)
    if flags.shadow_compare("get_invoice"):
        try:
            candidate = new_store.get(invoice_id)
            diff = compare(legacy, candidate, ignore=["updated_at"])
            if diff:
                metrics.increment("shadow.mismatch", tags=[f"fields:{len(diff)}"])
                log.warning("shadow mismatch", id=invoice_id, diff=diff)
        except Exception:
            metrics.increment("shadow.error")
    return legacy
```

Run this for weeks. The mismatch rate is your readiness metric, and it will be
appalling at first — in one case we started at 11% and spent five weeks getting
to 0.02%, and every one of those mismatches was a real behaviour in the legacy
system that nobody had documented. Rounding on partial refunds. A timezone
assumption in a date field. A status that could be `NULL` only for records
created before 2019.

**This is where the value of the whole exercise is.** The shadow comparison is
how you discover the actual specification. Skip it and you ship a new service
that is correct according to the requirements and wrong according to the
business.

### Option C: new service owns the data

Cut over writes. Legacy reads from the new service, or gets a feed, or is
decommissioned for that capability.

Only go here when the mismatch rate is near zero and stays there under a full
business cycle — which for most domains means a month-end, and for some means a
year-end.

## Exit criteria, decided in advance

Here is the failure mode that actually kills these programmes. Not technical
failure. Stalling.

You migrate the three easy capabilities, the ones with clean boundaries and low
risk. Momentum is great, the demo is impressive. Then you reach the capability
that touches everything — usually pricing, entitlements or whatever the
equivalent of "the billing engine" is in your domain. It is 40% of the monolith's
logic, it has no clean boundary, and the business case for migrating it is weak
because it works.

So it doesn't get migrated. And now you have two systems forever. Every feature
is built twice, every incident is diagnosed in two places, and the team that
owns the legacy system cannot be disbanded. The total cost of this steady state
is higher than either finishing or never starting.

Avoid it by writing down, before the first route is moved:

1. **The full capability inventory**, including the horrible one. If you cannot
   name an approach for the horrible one, you are not ready to start — you are
   planning to build a permanent hybrid and should decide that explicitly.
2. **A decommission date for the legacy system**, in the programme plan, with a
   named owner. Not "when migration completes". A date.
3. **A rule that the legacy system takes no new features** from day one.
   This is the one that gets violated, and every violation extends the
   endgame.
4. **The sequence ending with the hardest capability, not beginning with it** —
   but with the hardest one's approach designed first. Build confidence on easy
   wins, but design for the hard case, or your facade will not support it.

On point 4: if the horrible capability needs request-shape routing and
tenant-level data partitioning, build the facade with those from the start. A
routing layer designed for three clean path-based migrations will need to be
rebuilt for the fourth, and rebuilding the facade mid-programme is where
schedules die.

## When not to do this

Strangler fig is the right answer when the legacy system is large, works, and
carries business knowledge nobody has written down. It is the wrong answer when:

- **The system is small.** Under maybe 30k lines of comprehensible code, a
  rewrite with a shadow-compare period is cheaper than the facade.
- **You are replacing it with a commercial product.** Then the question is data
  migration and process change, not routing.
- **The business logic genuinely is obsolete.** If the requirements have changed
  such that you do not want the legacy behaviour, preserving it through careful
  shadow comparison is wasted effort. Rebuild.

That decision — whether this is a refactor, a rebuild or a replace — is upstream
of everything in this post, and getting it wrong means executing a pattern
beautifully in service of the wrong strategy. Pixorama's write-up on
[refactor, rebuild or replace](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace)
is a reasonable framework for making it, and they have
[the modernization options laid out](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-application-modernization)
with the trade-offs for each.

Martin Fowler's
[original write-up of the pattern](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/StranglerFigApplication.html)
remains the clearest statement of why it works, and is short.

One practical note on staffing this: the shadow-comparison phase needs people
who will sit with a 0.02% mismatch rate for five weeks rather than declare
victory at 2%. That is a temperament more than a skill set, and it is worth
testing for explicitly if you are bringing in a firm — Pixorama's
[comparison of custom software firms in India](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-software-development-companies-india)
is unusual in disclosing that they are one of the ten listed, which at least
tells you what you are reading.

---

The summary I would give a team starting this on Monday: the pattern is not the
hard part, and the new services are not the hard part. Build the routing layer as
a real product with a kill switch and stable per-tenant hashing. Spend
disproportionate time in shadow comparison, because that is where you learn what
the system actually does. And write the decommission date down before you start,
because the only version of this that fails is the one that never ends.

body_oneline:
# Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume

I have been close to four agent builds in the last eighteen months. Three of
them should not have been agents. One of them genuinely needed to be, and the
difference between those two categories turns out to be sharp, cheap to test
for, and almost never tested for.

The three that should not have been agents all shipped. They all work. They all
cost between four and nine times what the non-agent version would have cost, and
two of them are less reliable than a state machine would have been. That is the
expensive kind of success.

## The test

Here is the question I now ask first, before any discussion of frameworks,
models or tools:

**Can you draw the decision tree?**

Not "is it complicated". Not "does it have many branches". Just: if you sat down
with a domain expert and enough patience, could you enumerate the decision
points and what determines each one?

If yes, you have a workflow. Write the workflow. You may well want a model
*inside* it — for classification, extraction, summarisation, generation — but the
control flow belongs in code, where it is deterministic, testable, debuggable and
cheap.

If genuinely no — if the sequence of steps depends on what you discover while
doing it, in a way you cannot enumerate in advance — then you need something
that decides at runtime, and that is an agent.

That is the whole test. It takes an afternoon with a whiteboard and it would
have saved three projects a lot of money.

## The three that failed the test

### The invoice processor

Brief: "an agent that handles incoming supplier invoices."

What it actually needed to do: extract fields from a PDF, match the purchase
order, check the amount against tolerance, route exceptions to the right
approver, post to the ledger.

That is five steps in a fixed order. Every branch is enumerable: match found or
not, within tolerance or not, approver available or not. The *extraction* step
benefits enormously from a model — PDFs from 400 suppliers in 400 layouts is
exactly what models are good at. The *control flow* is a flowchart somebody in
accounts payable drew in 2019.

Built as an agent, it was non-deterministic in a domain where the auditors
require you to explain why a specific invoice was routed to a specific person.
"The model decided" is not an acceptable answer in a controls review, and we
spent six weeks building trace tooling to reconstruct decisions that a
`switch` statement would have made legible for free.

The right shape: deterministic pipeline, model called twice (extraction,
and a fuzzy supplier-name match), every branch in code.

### The onboarding assistant

Brief: "an agent that onboards new customers."

Reality: a sequence of document collections with conditional requirements based
on entity type and jurisdiction. Complicated — a decision table with about 90
rows. Not unknowable; the compliance team maintained that table in a
spreadsheet.

We built an agent that read the policy documents and reasoned about which
documents were required. It was right about 92% of the time.

The spreadsheet was right 100% of the time, because it *was* the policy.

This is the failure mode I find most painful: using a probabilistic system to
approximate a deterministic rule that already exists in written form. The agent
was doing lossy compression of a lookup table.

The right shape: the decision table, in code, generated from the compliance
team's spreadsheet. Model used for one thing — reading an uploaded document and
telling you whether it is the type of document it claims to be, which is a real
perception problem.

### The internal support bot

Brief: "an agent that answers employee IT questions and takes actions."

The answering part was a retrieval problem and worked well. The *taking actions*
part was where the agent framing caused damage: password resets, access
requests, software installs, each with an approval rule.

As an agent, it occasionally chained actions in ways nobody intended — granting
an access request as a step toward resolving a different ticket, which is
technically helpful and a security incident.

The right shape: retrieval for answering, and a fixed catalogue of actions each
gated by its own deterministic approval rule. The model proposes; code decides.

## The one that passed

A diagnostic assistant for a field-service operation. An engineer arrives at a
piece of industrial equipment that is not working. They describe symptoms. The
system helps them diagnose it.

Why this one genuinely needs an agent:

**The next step depends on what the previous step revealed, and the space is not
enumerable.** The equipment has thousands of failure modes, many in combination.
"Check the pressure reading" is the right next action only if the earlier
symptoms point there, and the number of symptom combinations is combinatorial
rather than listable.

**The information sources are heterogeneous and the right one is not known in
advance.** Manuals, past tickets, telemetry, parts inventory, an engineer's
free-text note from 2019. Which to consult depends on the hypothesis currently
being tested.

**The human is in the loop continuously.** The engineer is standing in front of
the machine, providing observations and overriding bad suggestions. The cost of
a wrong suggestion is low — the engineer says "no, that's not it" — and the cost
of a right suggestion is high.

**There is no existing decision tree, and the attempt to build one had already
failed.** They had tried, twice, with a rules engine. The tree was unmaintainable
within a year both times.

That is an agent. And notice the shape of it: **exploratory, human-supervised,
cheap-to-be-wrong, heterogeneous tools, genuinely unenumerable.** Those five
properties together are rare, and when they are all present the agent framing is
not just acceptable but clearly correct.

## Why the costume gets worn

I do not think people are being stupid. Three forces push toward agents:

**The demo is seductive and the hard part is invisible.** An agent that handles
one happy-path case takes an afternoon. The control plane that makes it safe —
budgets, loop detection, tool tiering, traces, evaluation — is roughly ten times
the loop itself, and none of it is visible in the demo.

**"Agent" is how the work gets funded.** A proposal to build a workflow with a
model in two steps competes for budget against a proposal to build an AI agent.
The second one wins, even when it is the same project described differently and
worse.

**The framework encourages it.** Agent frameworks make the loop trivial and the
deterministic alternative feel like a step backwards. If the easiest thing to
build is a loop, people build a loop.

## The hybrid that is usually right

The honest answer for most business problems is not agent-or-workflow. It is a
deterministic workflow with model calls at the perception and generation steps:

```
[intake] -> (model: extract)  -> [validate] -> [branch on rules]
                                                     |
                              +----------------------+
                              |                      |
                        [happy path]           [exception path]
                              |                      |
                      (model: draft reply)     [human review]
                              |                      |
                          [send]                 [resolve]
```

Everything in square brackets is code. Everything in parentheses is a model
call. The model does perception and language; the code does decisions.

This architecture is dull and it has properties that matter: every path is
testable, every decision is explainable to an auditor, the cost per transaction
is predictable, failures are attributable to a specific step, and you can change
the business rules without re-evaluating a prompt.

And when a genuine agent is needed, **put it inside one step of this
workflow**, not around the whole thing. The diagnostic assistant above is an
agent that lives inside a service-ticket workflow — the ticket lifecycle is
deterministic, the diagnosis step is agentic. That containment is what makes it
operable.

## What I would ask before approving one

1. **Draw the decision tree.** If it can be drawn, build it.
2. **Does a written rule already exist?** A policy document, a decision table, a
   runbook. If so, encode it; do not ask a model to infer it.
3. **What is the cost of a wrong action?** If it is high, the model proposes and
   code or a human decides. Always.
4. **Is a human in the loop continuously, or only at the end?** Continuous
   supervision makes agents much safer and much more likely to be the right
   choice.
5. **Who is on call for it?** An agent's failure modes are statistical. If there
   is no plan for traces, golden sets and regression gates, the project is not
   ready regardless of its architecture.

If you are at the stage of scoping this, Pixorama's survey of
[fifteen things companies are actually doing with agents right now](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases)
is a decent calibration exercise — what strikes me reading it is how narrow the
successful deployments are compared to how they get pitched internally. And
their walkthrough of
[how to build one](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-agent)
is a reasonable starting point once you have established that you should.

If you are buying this rather than building it, the five questions above are
the ones to put to an agency, and "draw me the decision tree for our use case"
is the single most informative thing you can ask in a sales meeting. A firm
that draws it has just told you the work is a workflow and quoted you for an
agent. Their guide to
[choosing an AI automation agency](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-ai-automation-agencies-in-the-usa-and-australia-for-2026-how-to-c)
covers the builder-versus-reseller distinction, which is the same distinction
from the buyer's side.

The claim I would defend: the most valuable thing you can do on an agent project
is spend one afternoon trying to draw the decision tree, specifically hoping to
succeed. Three times out of four you will, and you will have saved yourself a
year.

# Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use

A rewrite I had helped design got cancelled in week five. Eleven people, two
years, a target architecture diagram I was proud of.

What we did instead was six months of work so dull it was hard to report on, at
the end of which nobody wanted the rewrite any more. Not because we had grown
fond of the old system — because the things that made it intolerable were gone.

The question that cancelled it came from our delivery lead, not an engineer, and
I have used it on every modernisation conversation since:

> *If we fixed the complaints without replacing the system, would we still want
> to replace it?*

Nobody could say yes with a straight face.

Here is the tree that question sits inside. Five questions, in order. Order
matters — most of the value is in not reaching question five.

## Question 1: What are the actual complaints, stated as experiences?

Not "the architecture is bad". Not "it's legacy". Write down what people say
when they complain, in their words.

On ours, the list was:

1. Changes take six to eight weeks.
2. It breaks in production and we cannot tell why.
3. We cannot hire for it.
4. Deployments are a weekend event needing four people.
5. It will fall over one day and we will not be able to fix it.

Look at that list. **Not one item is a statement about the architecture.** They
are all statements about the experience of working on it.

That is the usual result, and it is the single most important thing this question
reveals. "Legacy" is overwhelmingly a description of working conditions, not of
design. And working conditions have much cheaper fixes than replacement.

If your list does contain genuine architectural statements — "we cannot add a
second currency because the schema assumes one", "we cannot serve customers in
another region because of a single-datacentre assumption" — those are real and
they move you down the tree. But check first, because the architectural framing
is the default vocabulary and it is usually imported.

## Question 2: Which complaints are fixable without replacement?

This is where most systems stop, and it is worth being systematic because the
answer is "more than you think".

Against our five:

**Deployments** → automate the existing runbook. Six weeks, two engineers, zero
application changes. Weekend event became eleven minutes on a Tuesday.

That one change improved three of the other four complaints, which I did not
predict. Feature lead time dropped before we touched anything that affects
feature lead time, because deploying monthly meant every release carried a
month of changes, which made every failure hard to attribute, which made us
cautious, which made us deploy monthly. Breaking that loop was worth more than
anything else we did.

**Observability** → structured logging with a request ID, shipped centrally,
dashboards and alerts on the eight code paths generating the most support
tickets. Seven weeks. Diagnosis went from a day and a guess to minutes.

**Testing** → this was the hard one. No tests, so every change needed manual
regression. We did not retrofit unit tests across 400,000 lines; that project
never finishes. We built a characterisation harness: record real production
traffic, replay it against a candidate build, diff the output.

It does not tell you the system is correct. It tells you the system has not
*changed*, which is the actual question when modifying something legacy. Nine
weeks, and it converted a six-week change into an afternoon's validation.

**Hiring** → turned out to be partly downstream of the above. We could not hire
people excited about a system with no tests, no observability and weekend
deployments. The unfashionable language was a smaller obstacle than the working
conditions. Competent engineers will learn an old language for a well-run
system and will not join a badly-run one for a fashionable one.

**Will fall over one day** → this is a resilience question, answerable with
backup verification, a tested restore and a documented failover, none of which
require replacement.

Four and a half of five complaints, fixed in six months, for roughly a tenth of
the rewrite's first year.

## Question 3: Have the requirements changed, or only the code's condition?

This is the actual dividing line, and I think it is the one question that
reliably separates a justified rebuild from an unjustified one.

**If the requirements are stable and the complaint is that the code is
unpleasant**, that is a maintainability problem. Maintainability problems have
cheaper solutions than replacement, which is questions one and two.

**If what the business now needs is materially different from what the system
does**, then carefully preserving its existing behaviour is wasted money. You
would be spending two years faithfully reproducing something you want to get rid
of.

That second case is a genuine rebuild, and I have seen two of them. Both
involved a business model change — in one case moving from one-off sales to
subscriptions, which touched every assumption in the data model and was not
reachable by refactoring.

The useful test: *what will the new system do that the old one does not?* If the
answer is a list of qualities — testable, observable, modular, modern — those are
properties you can add to what you have. If it is a list of capabilities the
business needs and cannot get, you have a rebuild.

## Question 4: Is this capability differentiating?

Before building anything, ask whether you should be building it.

Payroll, expenses, CRM, ticketing, document management, scheduling. The fact that
you built it in 2011 because nothing suitable existed is not a reason to rebuild
it in 2026, when the market has twenty options.

This question gets skipped because it is uncomfortable — it implies the last
fifteen years of work on that system was a detour — and because the people best
placed to evaluate the system are the people who built it.

Get someone else to answer it.

## Question 5: Only now, how?

If you have reached here, you have established that the complaints are not
fixable in place, the requirements have genuinely changed, and the capability is
differentiating.

Now the mechanics matter: incremental replacement behind a facade, parallel
build with a cutover, or capability-by-capability extraction. These have real
trade-offs and they are the subject of most writing about modernisation, which
is why I have left them last — the writing concentrates on question five and the
decisions are mostly made at questions two and three.

My colleagues have a structured version of this whole tree as
[refactor, rebuild or replace](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace),
which covers the question-five mechanics properly along with the trade-offs for
each path. It is the better reference if you have genuinely got to that point.

## Why the boring work is hard to choose

I want to be honest about the obstacle, because "just do the boring work" ignores
why people do not.

The rewrite was **easier to fund.** It had a name, a diagram, an end state, and a
narrative. It was a thing you could announce to a board.

"We are going to spend six months automating deployment, adding logging and
building a replay harness" is not an announcement. It has no end state. Nobody
is promoted for it. The quarterly update is "deployment is faster now", which
reads as maintenance next to "we are modernising the platform".

What made it fundable for us was reframing the six months as a **precondition**
rather than an alternative:

> *We cannot safely rewrite this system until we can deploy it, observe it and
> test it. So we are doing that first, and we will revisit the rewrite in six
> months with much better information.*

Nobody can argue with that. And six months later, with the information, the
rewrite was no longer attractive — which was, I suspect, always the likely
outcome, and is a perfectly respectable way to find out.

If you are facing one of these, that framing is the practical gift of this
issue. You do not have to win the argument against the rewrite. You only have to
establish that the rewrite should happen *after* the system is deployable,
observable and testable. Then let the six months make the argument for you.

If you want to buy the six months rather than staff it, be precise about what
you are buying, because "modernisation" as a service offering usually means
question five. The work in question two — deployment automation, structured
logging, a characterisation harness — is a
[DevOps consulting engagement](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-devops-consulting-companies-india)
and it is a different purchase with a different and much smaller price. Asking
for the second when a vendor is selling the first is the whole negotiation.

Next issue: where AI agents earn their keep, which is the one I am most likely
to be wrong about.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). The system in this
issue was about 400,000 lines and fourteen years old; the six-month programme and
its outcome are as described.*

# Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents

The RAG demo works. Two hundred documents, embeddings in a vector store, top-k
of 5, and the answers are good enough that someone says the word "production".

Then the corpus goes to 10,000 documents and quality falls off a cliff. Not
gracefully — the answers get confidently wrong, which is worse than getting
worse.

The instinct is to blame the vector store or reach for a bigger embedding model.
Usually neither is the problem. Three things break, in this order.

## Failure 1: your chunks lost their context

Here is the chunking everyone starts with:

```python
def chunk(text, size=1000, overlap=200):
    chunks, start = [], 0
    while start < len(text):
        chunks.append(text[start:start + size])
        start += size - overlap
    return chunks
```

At 200 documents this is fine, because the corpus is narrow enough that a
semantically vague chunk still retrieves against the right query. At 10,000 it
fails, and the reason is worth being precise about.

Consider a chunk from the middle of a policy document:

> "...this does not apply where the account has been dormant for more than 90
> days. In those cases the holder must re-verify before any withdrawal is
> processed. Exceptions require approval from the regional compliance lead..."

Embed that. What is it about? It has no subject. "This" refers to something
1,400 characters earlier, in a different chunk. The document title, the section,
the product it applies to — all absent.

At 200 documents, a query like *"what happens to dormant accounts"* retrieves it
anyway, because nothing else in the corpus mentions dormancy. At 10,000
documents there are 340 chunks mentioning dormancy across 60 products, and this
one has no signal to distinguish it from the other 339.

**The fix is to put the context into the chunk before embedding it.**

```python
def contextual_chunk(doc, chunk_text, section_path):
    """Prepend document and section context. The retrieval target is the
    enriched text; the text handed to the model can be either, but the
    enriched version usually reads better in the prompt too."""
    header = " > ".join(filter(None, [
        doc.title,
        doc.product,
        *section_path,
    ]))
    return f"[{header}]\n\n{chunk_text}"
```

So the chunk above becomes:

> "[Retail Savings Terms v4 > Personal Saver > Withdrawals > Dormancy]
>
> ...this does not apply where the account has been dormant for more than 90
> days..."

That single change has, in my experience, been worth more than every other
retrieval improvement combined. Anthropic published
[measurements on exactly this](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)
— generating a short context sentence per chunk with a cheap model and
prepending it, which is the same idea with a generation step instead of
structural metadata. Both work; structural metadata is free if you have it, and
you usually do.

**Chunk on structure, not character count.** Markdown headings, HTML sections,
PDF bookmarks, docx heading styles. A chunk that is one semantic unit retrieves
far better than a chunk that is exactly 1,000 characters ending mid-sentence:

```python
def structural_chunks(doc, max_chars=1500):
    for section in doc.sections():          # H1/H2/H3 tree
        body = section.text
        if len(body) <= max_chars:
            yield contextual_chunk(doc, body, section.path)
        else:
            # Only now fall back to splitting, and split on paragraph
            # boundaries within the section so context is preserved.
            for part in split_on_paragraphs(body, max_chars):
                yield contextual_chunk(doc, part, section.path)
```

## Failure 2: top-k is the wrong retrieval primitive at scale

`top_k=5` means "always return 5 things, regardless of whether any of them are
relevant." At 200 documents the 5 nearest neighbours are nearly always on-topic.
At 10,000 they include three things that are superficially similar and wrong.

And the model will use them. That is the confidently-wrong failure: the model
was handed irrelevant context and had no way to know it was irrelevant, so it
synthesised an answer from it.

Two changes:

**Retrieve wide, then rerank.** Vector similarity is a cheap approximation of
relevance. Use it as a filter, not a ranking.

```python
def retrieve(query, k_final=5):
    # Cast a much wider net than you intend to use
    candidates = vector_store.search(query, k=50)

    # Cross-encoder reranking: slower per item, dramatically more accurate,
    # because it sees query and document together rather than comparing
    # two independently-computed vectors.
    scored = reranker.score(query, [c.text for c in candidates])

    ranked = sorted(zip(candidates, scored), key=lambda x: -x[1])
    return [c for c, s in ranked[:k_final] if s > RELEVANCE_FLOOR]
```

Note the `RELEVANCE_FLOOR`. This is the part people skip, and it is the
difference between a system that says "I don't know" and one that invents an
answer. **Returning fewer than k results is a feature.** Returning zero and
telling the user you found nothing is a feature.

**Hybrid search, because embeddings are bad at exact tokens.** Dense vectors are
excellent at "documents about dormant accounts" and poor at "document reference
POL-4471-B" or "section 14.2(c)" or a product name the embedding model has never
seen. Run BM25 alongside and fuse:

```python
def hybrid_search(query, k=50):
    dense  = vector_store.search(query, k=k)
    sparse = bm25_index.search(query, k=k)
    return reciprocal_rank_fusion([dense, sparse], k=60)

def reciprocal_rank_fusion(result_lists, k=60):
    scores = {}
    for results in result_lists:
        for rank, item in enumerate(results, start=1):
            scores[item.id] = scores.get(item.id, 0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
```

RRF needs no score normalisation between the two systems, which is why it beats
weighted-sum fusion in practice — you do not have to tune a weight that drifts
every time you change embedding models.

## Failure 3: you have no way to know it broke

The thing that makes this failure mode expensive is not that it happens. It is
that nobody notices for six weeks, because the system produces fluent answers
throughout.

You need a golden set. Thirty to a hundred real questions with known-correct
source chunks, assembled from actual user queries, and run on every change:

```python
def evaluate(golden_set):
    """Retrieval metrics only. Deliberately not answer quality — if
    retrieval is wrong the answer cannot be right, and retrieval
    metrics are cheap, deterministic and debuggable."""
    recall_at_k, mrr = [], []
    for case in golden_set:
        retrieved = [c.id for c in retrieve(case.query, k_final=5)]
        hit = set(retrieved) & set(case.expected_chunk_ids)
        recall_at_k.append(1.0 if hit else 0.0)
        rank = next(
            (i for i, cid in enumerate(retrieved, 1)
             if cid in case.expected_chunk_ids),
            None,
        )
        mrr.append(1.0 / rank if rank else 0.0)

    return {
        "recall@5": sum(recall_at_k) / len(recall_at_k),
        "mrr@5":    sum(mrr) / len(mrr),
        "n":        len(golden_set),
    }
```

Gate deploys on this. A chunking change that improves one query class and
destroys another is invisible without it, and chunking changes do that
constantly.

The golden set is tedious to build and it is the highest-return two days of work
in the entire project. Build it from real queries — questions you invent are
systematically easier than questions users ask, because you unconsciously phrase
them using the corpus's own vocabulary.

## The order to fix things in

If quality has fallen apart at scale, in order:

1. **Add structural context to chunks.** Biggest single win, lowest effort.
2. **Chunk on document structure** rather than character windows.
3. **Retrieve 50, rerank to 5, with a relevance floor.** Second biggest win.
4. **Add BM25 and fuse with RRF.** Fixes the exact-token blind spot.
5. **Build the golden set.** Do this first if you have the time, because
   without it you cannot tell whether 1-4 helped.

Things that are usually *not* the problem, despite being where people start: the
vector database choice, the embedding model, the chunk size parameter, and the
LLM. Swapping a vector store rarely moves retrieval quality, because they are
all computing approximately the same nearest neighbours.

For the conceptual grounding — what retrieval is doing and why it beats
retraining for most business use cases — Pixorama has a readable explanation of
[what RAG actually is](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-rag-in-ai),
and if you are still at the stage of deciding your approach, their
[RAG vs fine-tuning](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning)
comparison frames the choice usefully: retrieval for knowledge that changes,
fine-tuning for behaviour that needs to change. If you are buying this work in
rather than building it, their round-up of
[AI development firms in India](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/top-ai-development-companies-india)
is a starting point — and the question I would put to any of them is how they
measure retrieval quality, because a firm with no answer has not built one of
these at scale.

The uncomfortable summary: RAG systems do not degrade gracefully with corpus
size, and the demo-to-production gap is almost entirely chunking and ranking. If
your 200-document prototype is good, you have learned that the plumbing works.
You have not yet learned anything about whether the retrieval does.

# RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question

It comes up in week one, every time. Someone has read that there are two
approaches to making a language model work on your data, and they want to know
which one the project is going to use, so it can go on the architecture slide.

The honest answer is "neither, probably, and certainly not yet", and the reason
is that the question assumes a problem shape that most projects do not have.

## What the two things actually do

Worth being precise, because the question is usually asked with a slightly wrong
model of both.

**Retrieval augments the model's *knowledge*.** At inference time you find
relevant documents and put them in the prompt. The model's behaviour does not
change; its available facts do. Knowledge updates the moment you update the
documents.

**Fine-tuning changes the model's *behaviour*.** You train on examples, and the
model learns a format, a tone, a task structure, a classification scheme. It is
poor at learning facts — you can teach a model that your return policy is 30
days and it will reproduce that with roughly the reliability of a half-remembered
fact, which is to say, not reliably enough for a policy.

So the actual distinction is **knowledge versus behaviour**, and framed that way
the question answers itself in most cases: if your problem is "the model does not
know our stuff", that is retrieval. If your problem is "the model does not do the
task in the right shape", that is fine-tuning. These are rarely the same problem
and they are not alternatives.

But that still is not the first question.

## The first question

**What does the correct output look like, and who decides?**

This sounds trivially simple and it is where projects fail. Not at the model
layer — at the specification layer.

A worked example. A client wanted an assistant that answered customer questions
about their products. Reasonable. We asked for fifty real questions with
correct answers.

It took eleven weeks to get them.

Not because anyone was slow. Because:

- Support, sales and the product team disagreed about correct answers to about a
  third of the questions.
- Several correct answers depended on the customer's contract, which meant the
  "correct answer" was a function, not a string.
- Four questions had answers that were correct but the legal team would not
  approve in writing.
- Six had no answer anywhere in the company; support staff improvised, and the
  improvisations were inconsistent and mostly fine.

By the time we had the fifty questions, the project had changed shape entirely.
About 40% of the value turned out to be in the *forcing function* — the company
now had agreed answers to its fifty most common questions, which it had not had
before, and which made the support team measurably better regardless of the AI.

And the technical approach had become obvious: retrieval over the newly-written
canonical answers, no fine-tuning, with contract-dependent questions routed to a
deterministic lookup because they were not a language problem at all.

We could not have chosen that architecture in week one. Nobody could have. The
information required to choose it did not exist.

## Why the question gets asked anyway

Three reasons, all structural rather than foolish:

**It is the only question with two named answers.** "RAG or fine-tuning" is
tractable. "What does correct look like" is an open-ended organisational
question that implicates several departments. People reach for the tractable one.

**It feels like an architecture decision, and architecture decisions are
supposed to come first.** But this is not architecture; it is implementation
detail. The architecture decision is what the system is for and what it is
allowed to do.

**Vendors ask it.** If you are evaluating platforms, they ask which approach you
need, because their product is better at one. That pushes the question earlier
than it belongs.

## The sequence I would actually follow

**1. Write down fifty real inputs and their correct outputs.** Real ones,
harvested from what users actually ask — not invented, because invented examples
are systematically easier and use your own internal vocabulary.

Expect this to be hard, slow and politically awkward. That difficulty is
information: it tells you the specification does not exist, and no model choice
compensates for that.

**2. Notice what the disagreements are about.** This is the highest-value output
of step one. Disagreements fall into categories:

- *We never decided* → you have a policy gap, and the AI project just found it
- *It depends on the customer* → deterministic lookup, not a language problem
- *Legal will not approve a written answer* → out of scope, route to a human
- *Genuinely ambiguous* → the system must be allowed to say so

Each category has a different solution and only one of them is a model problem.

**3. Now classify what remains.** With the fifty cases in hand, the technical
question is finally answerable:

- Outputs require facts from your corpus → retrieval
- Outputs require a consistent non-obvious structure or style → fine-tuning,
  possibly
- Outputs require multi-step work whose steps vary → an agent, maybe
- Outputs are a deterministic function of structured inputs → **not AI**. Write
  the function.

In my experience the split lands around: 60% retrieval, 25% not-AI-at-all, 10%
agent-shaped, 5% genuine fine-tuning candidates. The 25% is the surprising one
and it is pure profit — the cheapest, most reliable part of the system is the
part you did not build with a model.

**4. Build the evaluation before the system.** Your fifty cases are now a test
suite. This is the thing that makes every later decision empirical instead of
argumentative.

**5. Then pick retrieval or fine-tuning**, and discover that it was not a
difficult decision once steps one to four were done.

## When fine-tuning is genuinely right

To be fair to it, since I have been dismissive. Fine-tuning earns its place
when:

- You need a **consistent output format** that is awkward to prompt reliably — a
  specific JSON shape, a house style, a classification into forty categories
  with subtle boundaries.
- You have **thousands of examples** of the task being done correctly, as a
  natural by-product of existing work. Not examples you would have to create.
- **Latency or cost** matters enough that a smaller fine-tuned model beating a
  large prompted one is worth the training pipeline.
- The task is **narrow and stable**. Fine-tuning a model for something whose
  definition changes quarterly means retraining quarterly.

Classification and extraction at volume are the strongest cases. Question
answering over changing documents is the weakest, and is the thing people most
often propose fine-tuning for.

The trap worth naming: **fine-tuning does not fix hallucination.** It is
frequently proposed as a solution to it, on the theory that training on correct
facts produces correct facts. It does not; it produces a model that is more
confident in the vicinity of those facts, which is worse. Hallucination is
addressed by grounding the answer in retrieved text and by letting the system
decline to answer.

Pixorama's
[RAG vs fine-tuning in 2026](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning)
comparison is a fair treatment of the trade-off if you have reached step five
and genuinely need to choose. The thing I would add to any such comparison is
that the answer is "both, eventually, for different parts of the system" more
often than it is either one.

## The uncomfortable conclusion

The most useful AI projects I have been near spent their first month not doing AI.
They spent it establishing what correct means, which revealed that a quarter of
the scope was a deterministic rules problem, a quarter was an organisational
policy gap, and the remaining half was a well-specified retrieval problem.

The projects that started with the architecture question spent their first month
building a system and their next six discovering what it should have done.

And once you are into retrieval, the failure modes are entirely about corpus
quality, chunking and ranking rather than model choice — Pixorama's
[retrieval that survives contact with real users](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-that-survives-contact-with-users)
is about that second phase, which is where the actual engineering difficulty of
these systems lives.

So when someone asks in week one whether you are doing RAG or fine-tuning, the
useful reply is: *show me fifty questions and the answers you want.* The ensuing
eleven weeks are not a delay. They are the project.

# Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem

The RAG prototype works. Two hundred documents, embeddings in a vector store,
and the answers are good enough that somebody says "production".

At 10,000 documents it falls apart. Not gradually — the answers become
confidently wrong, which is worse than becoming vague.

The engineering fixes for this are real and I will summarise them. But the
reason I have titled this issue the way I have is that on the three RAG systems
I have worked on, **the binding constraint was never the retrieval
algorithm.** It was the corpus, and the corpus is a product decision.

## The technical half, briefly

Three things break, in order.

**Chunks lose their context.** The standard 1,000-character sliding window
produces chunks like:

> "...this does not apply where the account has been dormant for more than 90
> days. In those cases the holder must re-verify before any withdrawal..."

What is that about? "This" refers to something 1,400 characters earlier, in a
different chunk. No product name, no section, no document title. At 200
documents it retrieves anyway, because nothing else mentions dormancy. At 10,000
there are 340 chunks mentioning dormancy across 60 products and this one has
nothing to distinguish it.

The fix is to put the context *into* the chunk before embedding it — document
title, product, section path, prepended as a header. In my experience this one
change is worth more than every other retrieval improvement combined, and it is
an afternoon.

**Top-k is the wrong primitive.** `top_k=5` means "always return five things
whether or not any are relevant". At scale, three of the five are superficially
similar and wrong, and the model uses them, because it has no way to know they
are irrelevant. Retrieve fifty, rerank with a cross-encoder, cut at a relevance
floor. **Returning fewer than five is a feature. Returning none and saying so is
a feature.**

**Nobody notices it broke.** The system produces fluent answers throughout. You
need thirty to a hundred real questions with known-correct source documents, run
on every change, gating deploys.

That is the engineering, and it is genuinely most of what people need to hear.
My colleagues wrote up the production side of this as
[retrieval that survives contact with real users](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-that-survives-contact-with-users),
and if you are debugging a system right now that is the more immediately useful
read.

## The product half, which is the actual problem

Here is what happened on all three systems, and it took me until the third to
recognise the pattern.

We built retrieval over "the company's documentation". Quality was mediocre. We
improved chunking, added reranking, added hybrid search, built the golden set.
Quality got better. Still mediocre.

Then we looked at what we were retrieving *from*, properly, and found:

- **Four versions of the same policy**, three superseded, none marked as such.
  Retrieval was correctly finding the most semantically similar one, which was
  from 2021.
- **Documents that contradicted each other**, because two departments had
  written guidance independently and nobody had reconciled them. No retrieval
  system resolves that; it is not a retrieval question.
- **Answers that existed only in people's heads.** About 20% of the questions
  users asked had no answer anywhere in the corpus. Support staff improvised,
  and the improvisations were inconsistent and mostly fine.
- **Documents written for a different reader.** Internal process docs written
  for someone who already knows the product, retrieved to answer a question from
  someone who does not.

None of that is fixable by better retrieval. It is fixable by deciding what the
corpus is, which is a product and editorial decision about what your company
asserts to be true.

## The forcing function

On one of these, the most valuable thing the project produced was not the
system. It was the process of asking for fifty real questions with correct
answers.

It took eleven weeks to get them. Not because anyone was slow — because:

- Support, sales and product disagreed about correct answers to roughly a third.
- Several correct answers depended on the customer's contract, which meant the
  answer was a function, not a string.
- Four had answers the legal team would not approve in writing.
- Six had no answer anywhere in the company.

By the end, the company had agreed answers to its fifty most common questions,
which it had never had. The support team got measurably better *before* the AI
system shipped.

And the architecture had become obvious: retrieval over the newly-written
canonical answers; the contract-dependent questions routed to a deterministic
lookup because they were not a language problem; the legally-sensitive ones
escalated to a human by design.

We could not have chosen that architecture in week one. The information did not
exist.

## What this means for how you scope one

The implication I would draw, and it runs against how these projects are
usually planned:

**A RAG project is a content project with a retrieval system attached.**

The engineering is maybe a third of the work. The rest is deciding what your
company's canonical answers are, writing the ones that do not exist, retiring
the superseded versions, and reconciling the contradictions — and all of that
requires authority to decide what is true, which engineering does not have.

So the two questions I would ask before starting:

1. **Who can decide what the correct answer is?** If the answer is "it depends
   which department you ask", you have found the project's real first phase.
2. **Is anyone willing to retire documents?** A corpus that only grows will
   degrade indefinitely, because every superseded document competes with its
   replacement. This needs an owner and it is nobody's favourite job.

If both answers are unsatisfying, the retrieval work will produce a system that
faithfully surfaces your organisation's existing confusion. Which is, to be fair,
diagnostically useful — but it is not what was in the business case.

## The uncomfortable version

The most useful framing I have for this: **a retrieval system is a mirror.** It
will show you, with uncomfortable precision, that your documentation is four
years out of date, that two departments disagree, and that a fifth of what your
customers ask is answered by institutional memory rather than by anything
written down.

Teams respond to that by tuning the retrieval, because the retrieval is the part
they own. It does not help. You cannot rank your way out of a corpus that
contains three contradictory answers; whichever one you surface, you are wrong
two-thirds of the time, and the better your retrieval the more confidently you
are wrong.

The grounding for all this — what retrieval is actually doing, and why it beats
retraining for knowledge that changes — is explained more patiently than I have
managed here in
[a plain-English explanation of what RAG is doing](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-rag-in-ai),
which is a reasonable thing to send a non-technical stakeholder who is about to
sponsor one of these.

My one practical recommendation: before any engineering, spend two weeks getting
fifty real questions and their agreed answers. If that takes eleven weeks
instead, you have learned the most important thing about the project, and you
have learned it for the price of two weeks rather than two quarters.

Next issue: how to buy engineering capacity, and the four contract clauses that
took me two failures to work out.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Three RAG systems,
anonymised; the eleven-week figure is from one of them and I have rounded
nothing about it, because it is the detail I most want people to believe.*

# Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch

An agent is a loop: model decides, tool runs, result goes back, repeat until
done. Forty lines of code. The demo is genuinely impressive and takes an
afternoon.

Then you put it in front of real inputs and discover what the loop does when it
is confused. It does not stop. It retries the same failing tool eleven times. It
calls a paid API in a cycle. It decides that the way to resolve an ambiguous
instruction is to try every interpretation. One of ours, early on, spent $340 in
nineteen minutes re-reading the same document because a downstream parse error
made it believe each read had failed.

None of that is a model problem. It is a missing control plane. Here is the one
I would build on day one now, rather than day forty.

## The loop, unguarded

For reference, the thing we are hardening:

```python
def run_agent(task, tools, max_turns=20):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for _ in range(max_turns):
        response = model.complete(messages=messages, tools=tools)
        if not response.tool_calls:
            return response.text
        messages.append(response.as_message())
        for call in response.tool_calls:
            result = tools[call.name](**call.arguments)
            messages.append(tool_result(call.id, result))
    raise MaxTurnsExceeded()
```

`max_turns` is the only guard, and it is the wrong unit. Twenty turns can mean
two cheap calls or two hundred expensive ones, depending on how many tool calls
the model batches per turn.

## Budget in the units that actually hurt

Track three things, because they fail independently:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Budget:
    max_turns: int = 20
    max_tool_calls: int = 50
    max_cost_usd: float = 2.00
    max_wall_seconds: float = 300.0

    turns: int = 0
    tool_calls: int = 0
    cost_usd: float = 0.0
    started_at: float = field(default_factory=time.monotonic)

    def check(self):
        if self.turns >= self.max_turns:
            raise BudgetExceeded("turns", self.turns)
        if self.tool_calls >= self.max_tool_calls:
            raise BudgetExceeded("tool_calls", self.tool_calls)
        if self.cost_usd >= self.max_cost_usd:
            raise BudgetExceeded("cost", self.cost_usd)
        if time.monotonic() - self.started_at >= self.max_wall_seconds:
            raise BudgetExceeded("wall_clock", None)

    def remaining_note(self):
        """Told to the model, so it can prioritise rather than be
        cut off mid-thought."""
        return (
            f"Budget: {self.max_turns - self.turns} turns, "
            f"{self.max_tool_calls - self.tool_calls} tool calls, "
            f"${self.max_cost_usd - self.cost_usd:.2f} remaining."
        )
```

`remaining_note` is the non-obvious one and it changes behaviour a lot. An agent
that knows it has two turns left will summarise and conclude. An agent that is
killed at turn twenty produces nothing. Telling the model its budget converts a
hard failure into a degraded success.

**Per-tool budgets too**, because the aggregate does not catch the pathological
case:

```python
@dataclass
class ToolPolicy:
    max_calls: int = 10
    max_identical_calls: int = 2   # the one that saved us $340
    cost_per_call_usd: float = 0.0
    requires_approval: bool = False
```

`max_identical_calls` deserves its own paragraph. The single most common agent
pathology is calling the same tool with the same arguments repeatedly, because
the result did not change the model's situation and so the model's reasoning
arrives at the same next step. Hash the call:

```python
def call_signature(name, arguments):
    canonical = json.dumps(arguments, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256(f"{name}:{canonical}".encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
```

On the third identical call, do not execute it. Return a synthetic result that
tells the model what is happening:

```python
if seen[sig] > policy.max_identical_calls:
    return tool_result(
        call.id,
        "This exact call has already been made and returned the same result. "
        "Do not repeat it. Either use the result you already have, try a "
        "different approach, or report that you cannot complete the task.",
        is_error=True,
    )
```

Models respond to this well. It breaks the loop about 80% of the time without
aborting the task.

## The kill switch has to work from outside the process

A flag checked at the top of the loop is not a kill switch if the loop is
running in a worker you cannot reach. You need two levels.

**Level 1 — cooperative, checked every iteration:**

```python
def run_agent(task, tools, budget, control):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    while True:
        budget.check()
        if control.should_stop(run_id):      # external store, not in-process
            return halt(messages, reason=control.reason(run_id))
        ...
```

`control` reads from somewhere operationally reachable — Redis, a feature flag
service, a database row. The property that matters: an on-call engineer can stop
a running agent in under thirty seconds without a deploy and without finding the
right pod.

**Level 2 — a global circuit breaker**, because the thing you most often need to
stop is not one agent but all of them:

```python
class AgentCircuitBreaker:
    """Opens on error rate or spend rate across all runs. The failure
    we were protecting against: a provider returning malformed tool
    calls, which made every concurrent agent retry-loop at once."""

    def __init__(self, error_rate_threshold=0.25, spend_per_min_usd=10.0):
        self.error_rate_threshold = error_rate_threshold
        self.spend_per_min_usd = spend_per_min_usd

    def check(self):
        window = metrics.window(seconds=60)
        if window.error_rate > self.error_rate_threshold and window.count > 20:
            self.open("error_rate")
        if window.spend_usd > self.spend_per_min_usd:
            self.open("spend_rate")
        if self.is_open:
            raise CircuitOpen(self.reason)
```

Spend rate is the one to implement first. It is the failure that gets noticed by
finance rather than by monitoring, which is a bad way to find out.

## Classify tools by what they can destroy

Not all tools need the same treatment. Three tiers:

```python
TOOL_TIERS = {
    # Read-only. Cheap, idempotent, no approval.
    "search_documents":  Tier.READ,
    "get_customer":      Tier.READ,

    # Writes to systems we control and can undo.
    "create_draft":      Tier.REVERSIBLE,
    "update_ticket":     Tier.REVERSIBLE,

    # Outward-facing or irreversible. Never autonomous.
    "send_email":        Tier.IRREVERSIBLE,
    "issue_refund":      Tier.IRREVERSIBLE,
    "delete_record":     Tier.IRREVERSIBLE,
}
```

The rule we settled on: **`IRREVERSIBLE` tools are never called by the agent.**
The agent *proposes* them, the proposal goes to a human or to a deterministic
rule engine, and the action executes outside the loop.

This sounds like it defeats the purpose. It does not. In the deployments that
have actually worked, the agent's value was in the reasoning and the
assembly — reading six systems, working out what the situation is, drafting the
response. The final send is one click. Making that click a human's costs almost
nothing in throughput and removes the entire category of failure where an agent
emails four hundred customers.

If you do want autonomous irreversible actions, gate them on value:

```python
if tier is Tier.IRREVERSIBLE:
    if estimated_impact(call) > AUTONOMY_CEILING:
        return propose_for_approval(call)
    # Below the ceiling, act — and log loudly.
    audit.record(call, autonomous=True)
```

A refund under $50 can be autonomous. A refund over $5,000 cannot. That is a
business rule, written in code, outside the model.

## Traces, or you are debugging blind

Every run emits one trace, with a span per model call and per tool call, and the
attributes you need at 2am:

```python
with tracer.start_span("agent.run") as run_span:
    run_span.set_attributes({
        "agent.run_id": run_id,
        "agent.task_type": task_type,
        "agent.budget.max_cost_usd": budget.max_cost_usd,
    })
    ...
    with tracer.start_span("agent.tool_call") as span:
        span.set_attributes({
            "tool.name": call.name,
            "tool.tier": TOOL_TIERS[call.name].name,
            "tool.signature": sig,
            "tool.repeat_count": seen[sig],
            "tool.duration_ms": duration_ms,
            "tool.is_error": is_error,
        })
```

`tool.signature` and `tool.repeat_count` are what let you find loop pathologies
in aggregate rather than one anecdote at a time. Query for runs where any
signature repeated more than twice and you have a list of your prompt's
weaknesses, ranked by frequency.

The OpenTelemetry project has
[semantic conventions for GenAI spans](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/)
now; using them rather than inventing attribute names means your traces work in
whatever tooling you adopt later.

## What this adds up to

The loop is 40 lines. The control plane around it is maybe 400, and that ratio
is the honest shape of agent engineering. Budget in three units, per-tool call
limits with identical-call detection, an out-of-process kill switch, a spend-rate
circuit breaker, a tool tier model where irreversible actions are proposals, and
traces with call signatures.

None of it is clever. All of it is the difference between a demo and something
you can leave running.

If you are at the start of this, Pixorama's guide on
[how to build an AI agent](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-agent)
covers the loop and the tool-definition side in more detail than I have here,
and their survey of
[fifteen ways companies are using them right now](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases)
is a useful sanity check on scope — most of the deployments that work are
narrower than the ones people plan.

If you are considering an agency for this rather than building in-house, the
control plane above is the thing to interrogate them about. Most agency demos
show the loop; very few show a spend-rate circuit breaker or a tool tier model.
Pixorama's guide to
[choosing an AI automation agency](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-ai-automation-agencies-in-the-usa-and-australia-for-2026-how-to-c)
has a section on telling builders from resellers, and "show me your kill
switch" is the shortest version of that test I know.

The [Model Context Protocol spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) is also
worth reading before you design your tool layer, if only because standardising
on it means your tool definitions outlive your framework choice.
