# How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold

I have been in the room for maybe thirty of these, on both sides. The pitches
are remarkably similar, which is itself informative: they have converged on a
format that works on buyers, and that format is largely decoupled from whether
the agency is any good.

This is not a post about which agencies to hire. It is about the six questions
that produce different answers from good and bad agencies, and why the standard
pitch is constructed to avoid them.

## First, what the standard pitch contains

You will almost always get, in this order: a site audit with a number of
"errors" found, a list of keywords you are not ranking for with their search
volumes, a competitor comparison showing you behind, some case studies with
percentage increases, and a proposal with a monthly retainer and a list of
deliverables.

Every element of that is designed to establish that there is a problem and that
they have a process. None of it establishes that their process caused the
results in their case studies, which is the only thing you are actually buying.

So: six questions.

## 1. "What was this client's traffic before you started, in absolute numbers?"

Case studies are quoted in percentages. Percentages are chosen because they are
large.

"We grew organic traffic 340%" from 200 visits a month to 880 is a real
achievement on a tiny site and tells you almost nothing about what they could do
for a site with 40,000 visits. The mechanisms that take you from 200 to 880 —
fixing indexation, writing the first twenty pages, claiming the brand term — do
not exist on a mature site.

Ask for absolute before-and-after, the time period, and the starting domain
authority. A good agency gives you all three without flinching. An agency that
only has percentages is telling you their wins were on small sites, or that the
baseline was unflattering.

Follow-up worth asking: *what happened to that client's traffic in the twelve
months after the engagement ended?* The answer separates agencies who build
assets from agencies who rent you rankings.

## 2. "Which of those results would have happened anyway?"

This is the question that produces the most interesting silence.

Organic traffic grows for lots of reasons: the market grew, a competitor exited,
a Google update happened to favour the site's shape, seasonality, a PR event, a
product launch, the brand got better known through paid channels.

A good SEO agency has thought carefully about attribution, because they want
credit for the right things. They will talk about non-brand traffic separately
from brand, segment by landing page, and reference a baseline or a control.

An agency that has never considered the counterfactual is either not analytical
or is relying on you not asking. Both are disqualifying.

A specific probe: *do you report brand and non-brand organic separately?* If
they do not, their headline number includes people typing the company name,
which SEO did not cause.

## 3. "What will you do in month one that is not an audit?"

Audits are the agency's cheapest deliverable and your least valuable one. A
crawler produces an audit in twenty minutes; the consultant writes a summary.
Most of the "errors" are low-impact — missing alt text, meta descriptions a few
characters too long, a handful of redirect chains.

That work is not useless, but it is rarely why a site does not rank. It is
popular because it is schedulable, demonstrable, and requires no judgement.

The question tests whether they have a thesis about *your* site. A good answer
sounds like: "your category pages are competing with your blog posts for the
same terms, and the blog posts are winning, which is why the commercial pages do
not convert — we would fix that information architecture first." That is a
hypothesis with a mechanism.

A bad answer is a list of deliverables.

## 4. "How many links will you build, from where, and would you show me the last ten?"

Authority is usually the binding constraint — in my experience most sites that
are stuck are stuck on authority, not on-page work — so this is the most
important question and the one with the most evasive answers.

The honest spectrum:

- **"We do digital PR; links are earned and we cannot guarantee numbers."** This
  is the credible answer. It is also slow and expensive, and they should say so.
- **"We have relationships with publishers in your sector."** Plausible. Ask to
  see examples and check whether those sites have genuine audiences or exist to
  host paid placements.
- **"We'll build 40 links a month."** Nobody earns 40 editorial links a month.
  These are bought, from a network, and the risk sits with you.
- **"Links are not that important any more."** This is usually said by agencies
  that cannot build them.

Then ask for the last ten links they built for any client. Look at the pages
they are on. Does the page have other content? Does the site have real traffic?
Is your link one of nine outbound commercial links in a 600-word post about
nothing?

The reason this matters more than the rest combined: on-page work has a ceiling
set by your authority. If your domain has a few dozen referring domains and the
page-one incumbents have hundreds, no amount of content optimisation closes
that. An agency selling you content when your constraint is authority is
selling you the thing they can deliver rather than the thing you need.

## 5. "What would make you tell me to stop paying you?"

A real consultant has a view on when their work stops being worth it. Answers I
have heard and respected:

- "If your product pages do not convert, more traffic is a waste — fix that
  first."
- "Your category is dominated by three marketplaces; you will not outrank them,
  and you would do better on the long tail or on a different channel."
- "You have a six-week dev queue. SEO recommendations that cannot be implemented
  are not worth paying for."

That last one is the single most common real blocker and almost no agency raises
it in a pitch. SEO is largely a series of changes to a website; if your
engineering team cannot ship them, the retainer buys you a backlog.

An agency with no answer to this question has not located the boundary of their
own usefulness, which means they will keep invoicing past it.

## 6. "Who, specifically, will do the work?"

The person pitching is frequently not the person delivering. Normal, and fine if
disclosed.

Ask for the named individual, their experience, how many other accounts they
carry, and whether any of it is subcontracted. Then ask to speak to them before
signing.

Twelve accounts per strategist means roughly three hours a month on yours. That
can be fine for maintenance and is not enough to change anything. The arithmetic
is worth doing out loud: divide the retainer by a plausible blended rate and see
how many hours you are actually buying. The gap between that number and the
promised deliverables is the honest measure of the proposal.

## The pattern underneath all six

Each question asks the same thing in a different register: **is there a causal
story, and can you show me the mechanism?**

Good SEO is unglamorous and mostly consists of: making the site crawlable and
fast, organising information so that one page answers one intent, building
genuine authority slowly through work that is hard to fake, and removing
whatever is preventing the engineering team from shipping changes. Agencies that
do this are usually less impressive in a pitch than agencies that do not,
because their story has fewer numbers in it and more caveats.

The structural problem is that the pitch rewards confidence and the work rewards
patience, so the selection process is biased against the thing you want.

## A note on how the market looks from the inside

One more thing, since it is relevant to anyone reading agency comparison lists.

Search "best SEO agencies" plus any country and you will find dozens of listicle
pages, most of them published by agencies, directories, or content sites with no
assessment process. The ordering is frequently commercial. They cite each other.

That is not a reason to ignore them entirely — they are a reasonable way to
assemble a longlist of names you had not heard of. It is a reason not to treat
the ordering as a ranking. The useful move is to take the names and apply the
six questions, which is work the list has not done for you.

If you are shortlisting in Australia specifically, a survey of
[the Australian agency landscape](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-seo-agencies-australia)
is a reasonable place to collect names across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and
Perth before you start asking questions. And if what you actually need turns out
to be implementation capacity rather than strategy — which question 5 frequently
reveals —
[Australian web development firms](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/top-web-development-companies-australia)
may be the more useful shortlist, because an SEO retainer on top of a blocked
dev queue is money for recommendations nobody will implement.

That is, genuinely, the most common outcome I have seen: the company did not
need an SEO agency. It needed two engineering sprints and someone with authority
to decide what the category pages are for.

# Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't

I said in issue one that this was the topic where I am most likely to be wrong,
so let me be specific enough to be wrong usefully.

Four agent builds in the last eighteen months. Three should not have been
agents. One genuinely needed to be. All four shipped and all four work, which is
why this is a subtle argument rather than a horror story — the three that should
not have been agents cost between four and nine times what the alternative
would have cost, and two of them are less reliable than a state machine. That is
the expensive kind of success, and it is much harder to learn from than failure.

## The test, which takes an afternoon

Before any discussion of frameworks or models:

**Can you draw the decision tree?**

Not "is it complicated". Not "does it have a lot of branches". Just: if you sat
down with a domain expert and enough patience, could you enumerate the decision
points and what determines each one?

If yes, you have a workflow. Write the workflow. You may well want a model
*inside* it — for extraction, classification, summarisation, drafting — but the
control flow belongs in code, where it is deterministic, testable, cheap and
explainable.

If genuinely no — if the sequence depends on what you discover while doing it,
in a way you cannot enumerate in advance — you need something that decides at
runtime. That is an agent.

That is the whole test. An afternoon with a whiteboard, undertaken *hoping to
succeed*, would have saved three projects a lot of money.

## The three that failed it

**An invoice processor.** Brief: "an agent that handles supplier invoices."
Actual requirement: extract fields from a PDF, match the purchase order, check
against tolerance, route exceptions, post to the ledger. Five steps, fixed
order, every branch enumerable.

The extraction step benefits enormously from a model — 400 suppliers in 400
layouts is exactly what models are good at. The control flow is a flowchart
somebody in accounts payable drew in 2019.

As an agent it was non-deterministic in a domain where auditors require you to
explain why a specific invoice went to a specific approver. "The model decided"
does not survive a controls review, and we spent six weeks building trace
tooling to reconstruct decisions a `switch` statement would have made legible
for free.

**An onboarding assistant.** Document collection with conditional requirements
by entity type and jurisdiction. Complicated — about ninety rows of decision
table. Not unknowable: the compliance team maintained that table in a
spreadsheet.

We built an agent that read the policy documents and reasoned about which
documents were required. It was right about 92% of the time. The spreadsheet was
right 100% of the time, because it *was* the policy.

This is the failure mode I find hardest to forgive in myself: using a
probabilistic system to approximate a deterministic rule that already existed in
written form. We built lossy compression of a lookup table.

**An internal support bot.** The answering half was retrieval and worked well.
The taking-actions half was the problem: it occasionally chained actions in ways
nobody intended, granting an access request as a step toward resolving an
unrelated ticket. Technically helpful; also a security incident.

## The one that passed

A diagnostic assistant for field-service engineers. Someone arrives at
industrial equipment that is not working, describes symptoms, and the system
helps diagnose it.

Five properties made this genuinely agent-shaped:

1. **The next step depends on what the last step revealed**, and the symptom
   space is combinatorial rather than listable.
2. **The right information source is not known in advance** — manuals, past
   tickets, telemetry, parts inventory, an engineer's free-text note from 2019 —
   and which to consult depends on the hypothesis being tested.
3. **A human is in the loop continuously.** The engineer is standing in front of
   the machine, feeding in observations and rejecting bad suggestions.
4. **Being wrong is cheap.** The engineer says "no, that's not it." Being right
   is valuable.
5. **The decision tree had been attempted and had failed.** Twice, with a rules
   engine. Unmaintainable within a year both times.

That fifth property is the one I would weight most heavily, and it is the
cheapest to check. If nobody has tried to write the rules, the claim that the
rules cannot be written is unevidenced.

Those five together are rare. When all five hold, the agent framing is not just
acceptable but clearly right.

## Why the costume gets worn

Three forces, none of them stupidity:

**The demo is seductive and the hard part is invisible.** An agent that handles
one happy path takes an afternoon. The control plane that makes it safe —
budgets in cost and turns, loop detection, tool tiering, traces, evaluation
harness — is roughly ten times the loop, and none of it shows in the demo.

**"Agent" is how the work gets funded.** A proposal to build a workflow with two
model calls competes against a proposal to build an AI agent. The second wins,
even when it is the same project described worse.

**The framework encourages it.** If the easiest thing to build is a loop, people
build a loop.

## The shape that is usually right

For most business problems the answer is not agent-or-workflow. It is a
deterministic workflow with model calls at the perception and generation steps:

```
[intake] → (model: extract) → [validate] → [branch on rules]
                                                  │
                            ┌─────────────────────┴──────────────┐
                      [happy path]                       [exception path]
                            │                                   │
                  (model: draft reply)                   [human review]
                            │                                   │
                        [send]                              [resolve]
```

Square brackets are code. Parentheses are model calls. The model does perception
and language; code makes decisions.

This is dull and has the properties that matter: every path is testable, every
decision is explainable to an auditor, cost per transaction is predictable,
failures are attributable to a step, and you can change business rules without
re-evaluating a prompt.

And when an agent genuinely is needed, **put it inside one step of this
workflow** rather than around the whole thing. The diagnostic assistant is an
agent living inside a service-ticket workflow: the ticket lifecycle is
deterministic, the diagnosis step is agentic. That containment is what makes it
operable.

## The rule I would not bend

For anything irreversible or outward-facing — sending an email, issuing a
refund, granting access, deleting a record — **the agent proposes and code or a
human decides.** Always.

This sounds like it defeats the purpose and it does not. In every deployment I
have seen work, the value was in the reasoning and the assembly: reading six
systems, working out what the situation is, drafting the response. The final send
is one click. Making that click a human's costs almost nothing in throughput and
eliminates the entire category of failure where an agent emails four hundred
customers.

If you want autonomy on irreversible actions, gate it on value — a refund under
$50 can be autonomous, one over $5,000 cannot. That is a business rule, in code,
outside the model.

## Where I might be wrong

Two places, stated so they can be checked later.

**The test may be too conservative.** "Can you draw the decision tree" catches
cases where drawing it is *possible but uneconomic* — a tree with 4,000 branches
that would take a year to enumerate and a year to maintain. The onboarding case
had ninety rows, which is clearly worth writing. At what size does that flip? I
do not know, and I suspect the honest answer is that it depends on how fast the
rules change rather than on their count.

**Model capability may move the line.** My objections to the three failures are
largely about determinism and explainability, which are properties of the
architecture rather than the model's intelligence. Those objections should be
stable. But the reliability objection — 92% versus 100% — is a capability claim,
and capability claims age badly. If that gap closes, the onboarding case gets
closer to reasonable, though I would still want to know why you would prefer an
inferred policy to a written one.

For a wider view than my four, my colleagues catalogued
[fifteen use cases they have catalogued](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases)
across different industries, and what strikes me reading it is how much narrower
the successful deployments are than the way these projects get pitched
internally. The narrowest and most reliable category is the one that barely
looks like an agent at all —
[the receptionist-versus-answering-service comparison](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-answering-service-vs-human-receptionist)
is a good example of a bounded task with a clear fallback, which is why it
works.

Next issue: retrieval, and why the demo-to-production gap is almost entirely
chunking.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Four builds,
anonymised. If you have an agent deployment that passed my five-property test
and still failed, or failed it and worked anyway, please reply — that is the
most useful thing anyone could send me.*

# Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates

Here is the conversation that happens about four weeks after an agent ships.

> "Is it working?"
> "Users seem happy."
> "Should we change the prompt to handle the refund case better?"
> "Probably?"
> "Will that break anything else?"
> "...we'd find out."

That is not an engineering practice. And the reason teams end up there is that
agent evaluation looks like a research problem — benchmarks, LLM-as-judge,
accuracy percentages — when the production version is mostly a boring
observability problem with three artefacts.

## Why "accuracy" is the wrong top-line metric

An agent that answers 94% of questions correctly sounds good. It depends
entirely on the 6%.

Six percent wrong answers delivered confidently, in a customer-facing context,
is a worse product than 70% correct answers and 30% "I'll get a human." The
distribution of failure matters more than the rate, and a single accuracy number
deliberately hides it.

So the metrics that are worth putting on a dashboard:

| Metric | What it tells you | Target direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Task completion rate** | Did it finish without escalating? | Up, but not at the expense of the next row |
| **Confident-wrong rate** | Finished, answer was wrong | **Down, hard. This is the one that matters.** |
| **Appropriate escalation rate** | Didn't know, said so | Up — this is a success, not a failure |
| **Loop rate** | Repeated the same call ≥3× | Down; it is a prompt defect |
| **Cost per completed task** | Unit economics | Down, watch for it trading against quality |
| **p95 latency to resolution** | Usability | Down |

The second row is the expensive one to measure, because it needs ground truth.
The others come free from traces.

## Artefact 1: traces that answer questions at 2am

Every run emits one trace. Spans for the run, each model call, each tool call.
This is table stakes and most teams have some version of it; the attributes are
what make it useful.

```python
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer("agent")

def run_agent(task, tools, budget, ctx):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("agent.run") as run:
        run.set_attributes({
            "gen_ai.operation.name": "chat",
            "gen_ai.system": "anthropic",
            "agent.run_id": ctx.run_id,
            "agent.task_type": classify_task(task),   # <- critical
            "agent.tenant_id": ctx.tenant_id,
            "agent.entry_point": ctx.entry_point,
        })
        try:
            outcome = _loop(task, tools, budget, ctx)
            run.set_attributes({
                "agent.outcome": outcome.kind,          # completed|escalated|aborted
                "agent.turns": budget.turns,
                "agent.tool_calls": budget.tool_calls,
                "agent.cost_usd": budget.cost_usd,
                "agent.max_repeat_count": outcome.max_repeat,
            })
            return outcome
        except BudgetExceeded as e:
            run.set_attributes({"agent.outcome": "aborted", "agent.abort_reason": e.limit})
            raise
```

`agent.task_type` is the attribute that converts traces from anecdotes into
analysis. Without it, your dashboard says "87% completion" across a population
of wildly different tasks. With it, you discover completion is 97% for
`order_status` and 41% for `billing_dispute`, which is an actionable finding and
also the thing you would have found eventually by reading complaints.

Classify cheaply and deterministically — a keyword rule or a small classifier.
Do not use the agent itself to classify its own task type; you need this
attribute to be reliable when the agent is misbehaving.

The [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/)
define standard names for the model-call attributes (`gen_ai.*`). Use them for
anything they cover so your traces are portable across tooling, and namespace
your own under `agent.*`.

## Artefact 2: the golden set, built from production

Thirty to a hundred real tasks with known-correct outcomes. Not invented tasks —
invented ones are systematically easier, because you write them in the
vocabulary your system already handles.

Harvest from traces:

```python
def harvest_candidates(window_days=14, per_type=12):
    """Pull a stratified sample for human labelling. Deliberately
    oversamples failures, because that is where the information is."""
    buckets = {}
    for run in traces.query(window_days=window_days):
        key = (run["agent.task_type"], run["agent.outcome"])
        buckets.setdefault(key, []).append(run)

    sample = []
    for (task_type, outcome), runs in buckets.items():
        # 2:1 weighting toward non-completed outcomes
        n = per_type if outcome == "completed" else per_type * 2
        sample.extend(random.sample(runs, min(n, len(runs))))
    return sample
```

Then a human labels each: what *should* have happened. This is a day of
someone's time and there is no substitute for it. LLM-as-judge is useful for
scaling a rubric you have already validated against human labels; it is not
useful for establishing the rubric, because its failure modes correlate with the
agent's.

Store each case with the full input context, not just the question:

```python
@dataclass
class GoldenCase:
    id: str
    task_type: str
    input: dict                  # full context, incl. tenant state at the time
    expected_outcome: str        # completed | escalated
    expected_assertions: list    # see below
    notes: str                   # why a human judged it this way
```

**Assertions, not expected strings.** An agent's output is non-deterministic
prose; string-matching it produces a test suite that fails on paraphrase. Assert
on properties:

```python
expected_assertions = [
    Contains("refund"),                      # mentions the right concept
    MentionsAmount(142.50),                  # gets the number right
    NotContains("account number"),           # no PII leakage
    CalledTool("get_order"),                 # did the necessary lookup
    DidNotCallTool("issue_refund"),          # did NOT act autonomously
    ToolCallCountAtMost(6),                  # didn't flail
    Escalated(),                             # handed off appropriately
]
```

`CalledTool` / `DidNotCallTool` assertions are where most of the real value is.
Behavioural assertions on the trajectory are far more stable than assertions on
the final text, and they catch the failures you actually care about — an agent
that reaches the right answer by calling `issue_refund` twice is not a success.

## Artefact 3: the regression gate

Run the golden set on every prompt change, tool change, and model version
change. Block the deploy on regression.

```python
def evaluate(golden_set, agent_version):
    results = []
    for case in golden_set:
        trace = run_agent_isolated(case.input, record_trace=True)
        passed = [a for a in case.expected_assertions if a.check(trace)]
        results.append({
            "case_id": case.id,
            "task_type": case.task_type,
            "assertions_passed": len(passed),
            "assertions_total": len(case.expected_assertions),
            "hard_failures": [
                a for a in case.expected_assertions
                if a.is_hard and not a.check(trace)
            ],
            "cost_usd": trace.cost_usd,
            "tool_calls": trace.tool_call_count,
        })
    return summarise(results)
```

The gate has three conditions, and the second is the one teams forget:

```python
def gate(current, baseline):
    failures = []

    # 1. No hard-assertion failures, ever. PII leakage, autonomous
    #    irreversible actions, wrong monetary amounts.
    if current.hard_failures > 0:
        failures.append(f"{current.hard_failures} hard assertion failures")

    # 2. No per-task-type regression, even if the aggregate improved.
    #    This is the one that catches "fixed refunds, broke returns".
    for task_type, score in current.by_task_type.items():
        prior = baseline.by_task_type.get(task_type)
        if prior and score < prior - 0.05:
            failures.append(f"{task_type} regressed {prior:.2f} -> {score:.2f}")

    # 3. Cost did not balloon for equivalent quality.
    if current.mean_cost > baseline.mean_cost * 1.3:
        failures.append(f"cost +{(current.mean_cost/baseline.mean_cost - 1):.0%}")

    return failures
```

Condition 2 exists because prompt engineering is a zero-sum game more often than
anyone admits. You add an instruction to handle billing disputes better, the
model reweights, and order-status handling quietly degrades. The aggregate score
goes up. The per-type breakdown shows what you actually did.

I would go further: **treat the prompt as code under review**, with the eval
diff attached to the pull request:

```
$ make eval
  baseline: prompt@a3f9c21   current: prompt@HEAD
  
  task_type          baseline  current   delta
  order_status          0.97     0.91    -0.06  REGRESSION
  billing_dispute       0.41     0.78    +0.37
  refund_request        0.88     0.89    +0.01
  address_change        0.94     0.94     0.00
  ---
  aggregate             0.80     0.88    +0.08
  mean cost/task       $0.031   $0.047   +52%   WARN
  hard failures            0        0
  
  GATE: FAILED (order_status regression; cost +52%)
```

That output makes the trade-off explicit and arguable. "Aggregate +8%" would have
shipped it.

## Online: shadow mode, then ramp

Offline evals tell you about the distribution you sampled. Production has a
different one.

**Shadow mode** before anything user-facing: run the new version alongside the
current one, serve the current answer, record both, diff them. The disagreement
rate is your risk estimate, and inspecting fifty disagreements is the fastest
way to find out whether the new version is better or differently-wrong.

**Then ramp by task type, not by percentage.** 5% of all traffic exposes every
task type to the new version. 100% of `order_status` and 0% of everything else
limits the blast radius to the category you have the most evidence about, and it
is much easier to interpret.

Keep the kill switch reachable without a deploy. You will use it.

## The minimum viable version

If this is more than you can build this quarter, the order of return:

1. **Traces with `task_type` and `outcome`.** A day's work. Converts "users seem
   happy" into a number per category.
2. **Thirty golden cases with behavioural assertions.** Another day, mostly
   labelling. This is what makes change safe.
3. **The per-task-type regression gate.** An afternoon, once you have 1 and 2.

That is three days for a practice that holds up for years. Steps 1 and 2 in
either order; step 3 is worthless without both.

For a grounded view of which agent deployments are actually in production and
earning their keep — which is a useful corrective if your roadmap has eleven
agent initiatives on it — Pixorama's survey of
[where agents are actually being deployed](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases)
is a reasonable reality check. And if you are evaluating a vendor platform
rather than building, their buyer's guide on what
[survives real production traffic](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/conversational-ai-platform-buyers-guide)
asks most of the right questions, particularly about whether you can export
your own traces — which, if you cannot, means you cannot build any of this.

The same test applies to agencies. Pixorama's guide to
[choosing an AI automation agency](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-ai-automation-agencies-in-the-usa-and-australia-for-2026-how-to-c)
separates firms that build from firms that resell, and the cleanest version of
that question is this post's subject: ask what they measure, and whether you
get the traces. An agency that cannot show you a per-task-type breakdown of
their last deployment is describing a demo.

The one-line version: instrument `task_type`, label thirty real cases, gate on
per-type regression. Everything else in agent evaluation is refinement on top of
those three.

# Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly

We tried staff augmentation twice and got burned twice. The third time it worked
well enough that two of those engineers are still on the team four years later,
as employees.

Nothing changed about the model, the vendor quality, or our engineering practice
between attempt two and attempt three. What changed was four clauses in the
contract, and in retrospect both earlier failures were entirely predictable from
the documents we signed.

I am writing this because the standard post-mortem for a failed augmentation
engagement is "the contractors weren't good enough", and in both of our cases
that was false and also convenient.

## Failure one: we bought headcount instead of capability

The brief was "four backend engineers for six months." We got four backend
engineers. They were, on paper and in interview, fine.

What went wrong: we had a system with fourteen years of accumulated context, and
we had assumed that "backend engineer" was a fungible unit. The first eight
weeks were spent on onboarding, during which our two most senior people were
unavailable for anything else because they were answering questions.

So for two months we had *negative* capacity. Six engineers' worth of salary
producing less output than the two we started with. The engagement was six
months, which meant we got four months of productive work from four people,
minus two months of our seniors' time — call it a net gain of two or three
person-months for six person-months of cost.

Then the engagement ended and the context left with them.

**What I got wrong:** I was solving for a headcount gap when the actual
constraint was context. Adding people to a context-heavy system does not add
capacity in the short term; it subtracts it. This is the thing Brooks wrote down
fifty years ago and I had read and had not internalised.

## Failure two: nobody owned the output

Second attempt, smarter brief: two engineers, twelve months, one specific
subsystem.

Better. And it failed differently.

The vendor's engineers reported to a vendor delivery manager. Our team lead gave
them work. When priorities conflicted — and they did, constantly, because the
vendor was tracking against a statement of work and we were tracking against a
sprint — the engineers were put in an impossible position and resolved it by
following whoever asked most recently.

The subsystem got built. It worked. It also did not match how the rest of our
system was built, because the code review that would have caught that never
happened consistently — our engineers reviewed the vendor's PRs when they had
time, and when they did not, the vendor's own delivery manager approved them to
keep the SOW on schedule.

We spent four months after the engagement ended reworking it. That rework was
not in anyone's cost model.

**What I got wrong:** I treated the engagement as a delivery contract when I
needed it to be a capacity contract. A delivery contract makes the vendor
accountable for an outcome, which sounds good and means they control the
process. For work inside your own codebase, you want to control the process.

## The four clauses

Third attempt. Same model, same category of vendor. These four things were in
the contract.

### 1. Our definition of done, in the contract, by reference

> "Work is complete when it satisfies the Client's engineering standards as
> published at [internal URL], including code review approval by a Client
> engineer, test coverage thresholds, and documentation requirements. The
> Supplier's internal completion criteria do not apply."

The specific thing this prevents: a vendor marking work complete against their
own standard. The clause makes our review the gate, which means the vendor's
schedule pressure cannot route around it. It also means that when we tighten our
standards mid-engagement, that is not a change request.

### 2. Named individuals, with substitution control

> "The Supplier shall provide the individuals named in Schedule A. Substitution
> requires 30 days' written notice and Client approval. Any replacement shall be
> subject to Client technical assessment. The Supplier shall provide 4 weeks of
> overlap at no charge for any substitution initiated by the Supplier."

Rotation is the most expensive thing that happens in these engagements and the
default contract permits it freely. Every rotation resets the context cost.

The unpaid overlap is the clause that actually bites — it makes rotation
expensive for the vendor rather than for us, which aligns the incentive. We
invoked it once and the replacement was, unsurprisingly, more carefully chosen
than the first substitution they had proposed.

### 3. One reporting line, explicitly

> "Augmented personnel shall take technical direction solely from the Client
> engineering lead. The Supplier shall not assign, reprioritise or approve work
> for these individuals. The Supplier's account management role is limited to
> commercial and HR matters."

This is the clause that fixed failure two. It sounds aggressive and no vendor has
objected to it, because it is also simpler for them — they are selling capacity,
not managing a project.

It is also the clause that makes the engagement legally *look* more like
employment, which matters depending on jurisdiction. Get advice. In Australia,
the UK and parts of the US, direction-and-control is a key test for employment
classification, and the answer that works is usually about who sets hours, who
provides equipment, and whether there is an obligation to accept work — not
about who reviews the PR. But do not take my word for it.

### 4. An exit that transfers context, not just code

> "In the final 4 weeks of the engagement, Supplier personnel shall produce
> handover documentation covering architecture decisions, known defects,
> operational runbooks and open questions, and shall conduct walkthrough sessions
> with nominated Client engineers. 20% of the final invoice is contingent on
> Client acceptance of handover."

The withheld 20% is the part that makes this real. Handover is the first thing
dropped when the next engagement starts, because the engineers have already
moved on mentally and the vendor has nothing left to gain.

We have invoked this once, mildly — the documentation was thin, we asked for
more, we got it in a week.

## What augmentation is actually good for

Having now done it successfully, my view on the shape that works:

**Good:** a well-defined piece of work with a clear boundary, where you need
intense capacity for a bounded period and then none. A compliance deadline. A
platform migration. Building out a subsystem whose interface you control. Deep
specialist skills you need for eight weeks and cannot justify hiring — the
Postgres expert, the iOS build engineer, the person who actually understands
Kafka.

**Bad:** core product development on a long horizon. If the work is permanent,
hire. Augmentation's cost per unit of output is higher than employment once you
include context loss, and the whole advantage is the optionality — which you are
not using if the engagement keeps renewing.

**Worst:** augmentation as a hiring substitute because headcount is frozen but
contractor budget is not. This is extremely common and it is an accounting
arbitrage, not an engineering decision. You pay more, lose the context annually,
and the organisation never confronts the fact that it needs more engineers.

The framing I find most useful: augmentation buys you *time-boxed capacity with a
specific skill*, and the context transfer is the cost. If the work is long enough
that you will pay that cost more than twice, you wanted an employee. Pixorama's
breakdown of
[what staff augmentation is and when it beats hiring a project team](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-staff-augmentation)
makes the same distinction with the engagement-model comparison laid out, which
is worth reading before you write a brief — the choice between augmentation, a
managed project team, and hiring is usually made implicitly and should be made
explicitly.

## The thing I would tell myself in 2019

Both failures were visible in the contract before anyone wrote any code.

Attempt one's contract said "four backend engineers" with no mention of
onboarding, no ramp assumption, and no handover. The negative-capacity period was
fully predictable from that document.

Attempt two's contract had a statement of work with milestones and a vendor
delivery manager. The conflicting-priorities failure was the only possible
outcome of that structure.

So the lesson is not about vendor selection, which is where everyone looks. The
vendors were comparable; one of the two failures was with a well-regarded firm
that appears on most of
[the firms operating in this space](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/top-it-staff-augmentation-companies-usa).
The lesson is that the contract encodes the failure mode, and engineering leaders
mostly do not read it, because it arrives as a procurement document and looks
like someone else's job.

Read it. The four clauses above took an afternoon with our legal team and they
are the difference between the model working and not.

One practical note if you are sourcing offshore, which most people doing this
are: clause two matters considerably more in markets with high engineer
mobility, because substitution is more frequent and the vendor's cost of
replacing someone is lower. Pixorama's write-up on
[what to put in the contract when augmenting from India](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-staff-augmentation-companies-india)
goes into the sourcing side, and it is the one of these comparisons I have read
that leads with the contract rather than the vendor list.

# Issue 7: How to buy engineering capacity

I have been part of two failed staff augmentation engagements and one that
worked well enough that two of those engineers are now employees, four years on.

Nothing changed between attempt two and attempt three about the model, the
vendor quality, or our engineering practice. What changed was four clauses in
the contract.

I am writing this because the standard post-mortem for these is "the contractors
weren't good enough", and in both of our failures that was false and also
convenient.

## Failure one: we bought headcount when the constraint was context

Brief: four backend engineers, six months. We got four competent backend
engineers.

What went wrong: we had a system with fourteen years of undocumented context,
and we had assumed "backend engineer" was a fungible unit. The first eight weeks
were onboarding, during which our two most senior people were unavailable for
anything else because they were answering questions.

So for two months we had **negative capacity.** Six engineers' worth of cost
producing less than the two we started with.

Net across six months: maybe two or three person-months of gain for six
person-months of spend. Then the engagement ended and the context left.

This is Brooks, fifty years old, which I had read and had not internalised.
Adding people to a context-heavy system subtracts capacity before it adds any.

## Failure two: nobody owned the output

Smarter brief: two engineers, twelve months, one specific subsystem.

The vendor's engineers reported to a vendor delivery manager. Our team lead gave
them work. When priorities conflicted — constantly, because the vendor tracked a
statement of work and we tracked a sprint — the engineers were in an impossible
position and resolved it by following whoever asked most recently.

The subsystem got built and worked. It also did not match how the rest of our
system was built, because the code review that would have caught that happened
inconsistently: our engineers reviewed when they had time, and when they did not,
the vendor's delivery manager approved to keep the SOW on schedule.

Four months of rework afterwards, in nobody's cost model.

My mistake: I treated it as a delivery contract when I needed a capacity
contract. A delivery contract makes the vendor accountable for an outcome, which
sounds better and means **they** control the process. For work inside your own
codebase, you need to control the process.

## The four clauses

Third attempt, same model, comparable vendor.

### 1. Our definition of done, by reference

> *Work is complete when it satisfies the Client's engineering standards as
> published at [internal URL], including code review approval by a Client
> engineer, test coverage thresholds and documentation requirements. The
> Supplier's internal completion criteria do not apply.*

Prevents a vendor marking work complete against their own standard. Makes our
review the gate, so the vendor's schedule pressure cannot route around it. Also
means tightening our standards mid-engagement is not a change request.

### 2. Named individuals, with substitution control

> *The Supplier shall provide the individuals named in Schedule A. Substitution
> requires 30 days' written notice and Client approval. Any replacement shall be
> subject to Client technical assessment. The Supplier shall provide 4 weeks of
> overlap at no charge for any substitution initiated by the Supplier.*

Rotation is the most expensive thing that happens in these engagements and the
default contract permits it freely. Every rotation resets the context cost from
failure one.

The **unpaid overlap** is the clause that bites. It makes rotation expensive for
the vendor rather than for you, which aligns the incentive properly. We invoked
it once and the replacement was noticeably more carefully chosen than the first
substitution proposed.

### 3. One reporting line

> *Augmented personnel shall take technical direction solely from the Client
> engineering lead. The Supplier shall not assign, reprioritise or approve work
> for these individuals. The Supplier's account management role is limited to
> commercial and HR matters.*

This fixed failure two. It reads as aggressive and no vendor has objected,
because it is simpler for them — they are selling capacity, not managing a
project.

**One caution, and please take advice on it.** This clause makes the arrangement
look more like employment, and worker-classification tests in Australia, the UK
and much of the US weigh direction and control. In practice the tests turn more
on who sets hours, who provides equipment, and whether there is an obligation to
accept work than on who approves a pull request — but I am an engineer, not a
lawyer, and the consequences of getting this wrong land on your finance team.
Have someone qualified read it.

### 4. An exit that transfers context, not just code

> *In the final 4 weeks, Supplier personnel shall produce handover documentation
> covering architecture decisions, known defects, operational runbooks and open
> questions, and shall conduct walkthrough sessions with nominated Client
> engineers. 20% of the final invoice is contingent on Client acceptance of
> handover.*

The withheld 20% is what makes it real. Handover is the first thing dropped when
the next engagement starts, because the engineers have mentally moved on and the
vendor has nothing left to gain.

We invoked this once, mildly. Documentation was thin, we asked for more, we had
it in a week.

## What this model is actually for

Having now done it properly:

**Good:** a well-defined piece of work with a clear boundary, where you need
intense capacity for a bounded period and then none. A compliance deadline. A
platform migration. A subsystem whose interface you control. Deep specialist
skills for eight weeks that you cannot justify hiring — the Postgres expert, the
iOS build engineer, the person who genuinely understands Kafka.

**Bad:** core product development on a long horizon. If the work is permanent,
hire. Augmentation's cost per unit of output is higher than employment once you
count context loss, and the entire advantage is optionality — which you are not
using if the engagement keeps renewing.

**Worst:** augmentation as a hiring substitute because headcount is frozen but
contractor budget is not. Extremely common, and it is an accounting arbitrage
rather than an engineering decision. You pay more, lose the context annually, and
the organisation never confronts that it needs more engineers.

The framing that has served me: **augmentation buys time-boxed capacity with a
specific skill, and context transfer is the price.** If the work runs long enough
that you will pay that price more than twice, you wanted an employee.

My colleagues lay out that comparison — augmentation versus a managed project
team versus hiring — in their piece on
[when it beats hiring a project team](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-staff-augmentation),
and it is worth reading before writing a brief, because the choice between those
three is usually made implicitly and should be made on purpose.

If the gap you are filling is judgement rather than hands — nobody on the team
has designed a multi-tenant system or passed an enterprise security review —
that is a different purchase, and
[the fractional CTO version of this question](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-cto)
has its own failure modes, mostly about who owns the roadmap. I may do an issue
on that.

## The thing I would tell my 2019 self

Both failures were visible in the contract before anyone wrote code.

Attempt one's contract said "four backend engineers" with no ramp assumption, no
onboarding plan and no handover. The negative-capacity period was fully
predictable from that document.

Attempt two's had milestones and a vendor delivery manager. The
conflicting-priorities failure was the only available outcome of that structure.

So the lesson is not about vendor selection, which is where everyone looks and
where the comparison articles concentrate. The vendors were comparable — one
failure was with a well-regarded firm. The lesson is that **the contract encodes
the failure mode**, and engineering leaders mostly do not read it, because it
arrives as a procurement document and looks like someone else's job.

Read it. Four clauses, an afternoon with your legal team, and it is the
difference between the model working and not.

Next issue: shipping on two platforms, and why "one codebase" is the least
interesting part of cross-platform mobile.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Three engagements,
anonymised. The clause text above is paraphrased from contracts I have worked
under; it is illustrative and not legal drafting.*

body_oneline:
# Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC

Most "zero-trust programme" slide decks never reach production. Meanwhile the
single change with the best ratio of risk reduction to effort sits untouched in
every CI system: a static cloud access key, in a secret store, with broad
permissions and no expiry, usable by anyone who can trigger a workflow.

That key is the most valuable credential in most organisations. It outranks
individual engineer access because it is scoped to deploy, which means it can
modify production. And it is long-lived, so a single leak — a logged environment
variable, a compromised dependency, a fork PR with a misconfigured trigger — is
a persistent compromise rather than a time-boxed one.

OIDC federation removes it entirely. No key anywhere, credentials that live
fifteen minutes, and a trust policy that can be scoped to one repository on one
branch. This is a day's work and it is worth more than a quarter of policy
documents.

## What is actually happening

The CI provider becomes an identity provider. Instead of presenting a secret,
your workflow presents a signed JWT describing itself — this repo, this branch,
this workflow, this event type. Your cloud account verifies the signature
against the provider's public keys and, if the claims match a trust policy you
wrote, hands back temporary credentials.

```
[workflow] --(1) request JWT--> [CI provider OIDC endpoint]
[workflow] <-(2) signed JWT----
[workflow] --(3) AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity + JWT--> [STS]
                                                      |
                                      (4) verify sig against provider JWKS
                                      (5) match claims against trust policy
[workflow] <-(6) 15-minute credentials ---------------
```

Nothing is stored. There is no secret to leak, rotate, or inherit when someone
leaves.

## The trust policy is the whole security control

This is where the mistakes happen, so it is worth being slow here.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {
      "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
    },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":
          "repo:acme/payments-service:ref:refs/heads/main"
      }
    }
  }]
}
```

Three things about that `sub` claim:

**It is `StringEquals`, not `StringLike`.** The common catastrophic
misconfiguration is:

```json
"StringLike": { "...:sub": "repo:acme/*" }
```

which trusts every repository in the org, including the one a contractor has
write access to. Worse, I have seen:

```json
"StringLike": { "...:sub": "*" }
```

which trusts **every GitHub repository on the internet** to assume your
production deploy role. That is not a hypothetical; it has been found in real
accounts, because it is what you get when someone debugs a claims mismatch by
loosening the condition until it works.

**It pins the branch.** `ref:refs/heads/main` means a workflow on a feature
branch cannot assume this role. If you need deploys from tags, add a second
condition value for `ref:refs/tags/*` — explicitly, with `StringLike` scoped to
the tag namespace only.

**Pull requests need separate treatment.** The `pull_request` event produces
`sub` of `repo:acme/payments-service:pull_request`, which notably does **not**
identify the source branch. A PR from a fork can therefore satisfy a
`pull_request`-scoped trust policy. So: PR workflows get a read-only role, never
the deploy role. Non-negotiable.

Pin the environment instead when you want approval gates:

```json
"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":
  "repo:acme/payments-service:environment:production"
```

Combined with a protected environment that requires a reviewer, this means the
credential cannot be minted at all until a human approves — the control is in
identity, not in a pipeline step someone can reorder.

## The Terraform

```hcl
# One provider per CI system, per account.
resource "aws_iam_openid_connect_provider" "github" {
  url             = "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
  client_id_list  = ["sts.amazonaws.com"]
  # GitHub rotates these; AWS now validates against the library of
  # trusted CAs for this provider, but keeping it current is harmless.
  thumbprint_list = ["6938fd4d98bab03faadb97b34396831e3780aea1"]
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "deploy_trust" {
  statement {
    effect  = "Allow"
    actions = ["sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"]

    principals {
      type        = "Federated"
      identifiers = [aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github.arn]
    }

    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud"
      values   = ["sts.amazonaws.com"]
    }

    # Deliberately StringEquals with an explicit list.
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub"
      values = [
        "repo:${var.github_org}/${var.repo}:environment:production",
      ]
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_iam_role" "deploy" {
  name                 = "ci-deploy-${var.repo}"
  assume_role_policy   = data.aws_iam_policy_document.deploy_trust.json
  max_session_duration = 900          # 15 minutes. Deploys are not long.
  permissions_boundary = aws_iam_policy.ci_boundary.arn
}
```

Two details I would insist on:

**`max_session_duration = 900`.** The default is an hour. A deploy takes
minutes. Shortening the window costs nothing and bounds the damage from a
credential captured mid-run.

**A permissions boundary.** The deploy role's own policy says what it can do;
the boundary says what it can *never* do, regardless of future policy edits.
This is how you stop a well-meaning change from granting the CI role
`iam:*`:

```hcl
resource "aws_iam_policy" "ci_boundary" {
  name   = "ci-permissions-boundary"
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [
      { Effect = "Allow", Action = "*", Resource = "*" },
      {
        Effect = "Deny"
        Action = [
          "iam:CreateUser", "iam:CreateAccessKey",
          "iam:AttachUserPolicy", "iam:PutUserPolicy",
          "organizations:*", "account:*",
          "cloudtrail:StopLogging", "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail",
        ]
        Resource = "*"
      },
    ]
  })
}
```

`iam:CreateAccessKey` in that deny list is the important one. It is the
privilege-escalation path that converts a 15-minute federated credential back
into a permanent key — exactly the thing you just removed.

## The workflow

```yaml
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write      # required to request the JWT
  contents: read       # and nothing else

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production     # gates credential minting on approval
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-deploy-payments-service
          aws-region: ap-southeast-2
          role-duration-seconds: 900

      - run: ./deploy.sh
```

`permissions:` declared explicitly at the top is worth calling out. Without it
you inherit the repository default, which is frequently write-all. The
`id-token: write` permission is what allows the JWT request; everything else
should be the minimum the job needs.

## Migrating without a delivery freeze

The reason this does not get done is fear of breaking deploys. It does not have
to:

1. **Create the OIDC provider and roles alongside the existing keys.** Nothing
   changes yet.
2. **Switch one low-risk service's workflow** to the role. Keep its key in place
   as a rollback.
3. **Watch CloudTrail for both principals.** You want to see the role being used
   and the key going quiet.
4. **Deactivate the key — do not delete it.** Deactivation is instantly
   reversible; deletion is not. Leave it deactivated for a sprint.
5. **Repeat per service**, then delete the deactivated keys.
6. **Add the preventive control** so the problem cannot return:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Action": "iam:CreateAccessKey",
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringNotEquals": { "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/break-glass-admin" }
  }
}
```

Applied at the organisation level, that makes "add a CI access key" something
nobody can quietly do at 6pm under deadline. Which is the actual mechanism by
which these keys appear.

Step 3 is the one people skip and then regret. Watching both principals for a
few days is how you catch the scheduled job, in a workflow nobody remembered,
that still uses the key.

## Where this sits in a security programme

The argument I would make to anyone running a zero-trust initiative: this is the
work. Not the strategy document. An identity-based, short-lived,
narrowly-scoped, auditable credential replacing a permanent shared secret in the
highest-privilege system you own — in a day, with no delivery freeze.

That framing matters because security programmes typically fail by stopping
delivery, which is the argument in Pixorama's
[zero-trust without bringing delivery to a halt](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/zero-trust-without-stopping-delivery).
OIDC federation is the clearest example of the pattern: the secure version is
also the more convenient one, so it does not need enforcement.

If you are standing up a new cloud estate, make this part of the
[landing zone guardrails](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud)
from day one rather than retrofitting. Setting the `iam:CreateAccessKey` deny
before the first workload lands means you never accumulate the keys in the first
place.

GitHub's
[security hardening guide for OpenID Connect](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect)
documents the full claim set, including `job_workflow_ref`, which is worth using
if you want to pin trust to a specific reusable workflow rather than a branch.

GitLab, Bitbucket, CircleCI and Buildkite all support the same flow. The claim
names differ; the trust-policy reasoning is identical, as is the
`StringEquals`-not-`StringLike` rule.

If this is work you would outsource, it is a good interview question in both
directions — ask a prospective
[DevOps consulting firm](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-devops-consulting-companies-india)
how they handle CI credentials today. A firm still shipping static access keys
into client pipelines in 2026 has told you where their practice sits.

body_oneline:
# The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap

I have watched four fractional CTO arrangements. Two worked extremely well. Two
were expensive and ended awkwardly, and in both of those cases everyone involved
was competent and acting in good faith.

The difference was not the person. It was whether the company had decided, before
the engagement started, what the fractional CTO was allowed to decide — and
specifically whether they owned the technical roadmap or advised on it.

That sounds like a semantic distinction. It is the whole thing.

## The two failure modes

### The advisor with accountability

A company hires a fractional CTO two days a week. The brief is strategic
guidance: architecture, hiring, vendor selection, technical risk.

They are, implicitly, accountable for technical outcomes. They are also not
present when most decisions get made, because decisions happen in the three days
a week they are not there.

So they arrive on Tuesday to find that a choice has been made — a vendor
selected, a schema designed, a library adopted — and their options are to
accept it or to relitigate it. Accepting it repeatedly means they are not doing
the job. Relitigating it repeatedly makes them an obstacle, and the team learns
to route around them.

I watched this one end with the fractional CTO described as "not commercial
enough" and the engineering lead described as "not strategic enough", when the
actual problem was that two people had the same job and neither had been told.

### The decision-maker without context

The mirror image. A company gives the fractional CTO real authority — they own
technical decisions.

They make good decisions, judged on their merits. They also make them with
one-fifth of the context of a full-time person: they do not know that the
customer who drove the last architecture change is about to churn, that the
senior engineer is interviewing elsewhere, that the sales team has promised a
feature in a demo, or that the "temporary" integration is load-bearing for the
largest account.

Good decisions made on incomplete context look like bad decisions in retrospect,
and the person who made them is not there to adjust when the context surfaces.

## What the two successful ones had in common

Both drew an explicit line, in writing, before starting. Not a job description —
a decision-rights document. It looked roughly like this:

**Fractional CTO decides:**
- Architecture at the system-boundary level: what services exist, what owns what
  data, what the integration contracts are
- Build-versus-buy for anything over a threshold
- Technical hiring bar and the interview process
- Vendor selection for infrastructure and platform
- Security and compliance posture

**Engineering lead decides:**
- Everything inside a service boundary
- Sprint content and sequencing
- Libraries, patterns, tooling within the agreed architecture
- Day-to-day prioritisation and trade-offs

**Jointly, with the CEO breaking ties:**
- Roadmap sequencing against commercial commitments
- Anything that changes the hiring plan or the budget

The specific genius of that split, which I did not appreciate until I saw it
work, is that **it assigns decisions by how long they take to reverse, not by
how important they are.** The fractional CTO owns the decisions that are
expensive to undo and therefore benefit from experience and deliberation. The
full-time lead owns the decisions that need context and speed and are cheap to
revisit.

That maps naturally onto the actual constraint: the fractional person has
judgement but not presence. Give them the decisions where judgement dominates
and presence does not matter much. Two days a week is plenty of time to decide
what services exist. It is not enough to decide what the team does on Thursday.

## The diagnostic

If you are considering this, the question is not "should we hire a fractional
CTO". It is: **which of these three problems do you have?**

**Problem 1: nobody on the team has made these decisions before.** You have
capable engineers who have never designed a multi-tenant system, chosen between
managed services at scale, or built a security posture that passes enterprise
procurement. They will make these decisions anyway, by default, and some will be
expensive.

*This is the fractional CTO case.* Judgement is the scarce resource and it is
needed episodically. Two days a week is genuinely sufficient.

**Problem 2: you do not have enough engineers.** The decisions are fine; the
throughput is not.

*This is not the fractional CTO case*, and it is the most common mis-diagnosis.
A fractional CTO will not write your features, and hiring one when the
constraint is capacity produces a well-architected system that ships slowly.
What you want is
[augmenting the team you have](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-staff-augmentation)
or permanent hires, depending on whether the need is bounded.

**Problem 3: nobody is accountable for technical outcomes.** There is no
engineering leadership at all. Decisions are made by whoever cares most, which is
sometimes a product manager and sometimes the loudest engineer.

*This is also not the fractional CTO case*, or rather, it is a case where a
fractional CTO will fail. You cannot part-time your way into being the person
who holds a function together. A fractional person can provide judgement to an
existing structure; they cannot be the structure. Hire a full-time engineering
lead, even a less experienced one, and give them a fractional CTO to learn from.

That third configuration — a full-time lead with less experience plus a
fractional CTO with more — is, in my observation, the arrangement with the best
results and it is rarely what people set out to buy. It is cheaper than a
full-time experienced CTO, it develops someone internally, and it covers both
presence and judgement.

## The practical conditions

For the engagement to work, four things that are easy to get wrong:

**Fixed days, not flexible hours.** "Two days a week, whenever" means the
fractional CTO is never reliably available, so the team stops waiting for them.
Fixed days mean decisions can be scheduled.

**Attendance at the meeting where the roadmap is set.** Not a written update
afterwards. If they are not in that room, they are advising on a plan rather
than shaping it, and the first failure mode above is already in progress.

**A direct line to the CEO or founder.** The value of an experienced technologist
is largely in saying "that commercial commitment is not achievable" to the person
who made it. Routed through a layer, that message gets softened into
uselessness.

**An explicit end state.** Either the arrangement converts to full-time, or it
tapers as the internal lead grows into the role, or it ends at a milestone. An
open-ended fractional CTO engagement at month thirty is a sign that the company
has outsourced a permanent function, which costs more and builds nothing
internally.

On rates and the commercial shape — day rates, retainer versus equity, what the
market actually pays in the US versus Australia — Pixorama has
[rates in the US and Australia and when the role makes sense](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-cto)
written up with the numbers, which is useful because the published rates vary
enormously and the variance is mostly about scope rather than seniority.

## The uncomfortable bit

The reason this gets decided badly is that the decision-rights conversation is
awkward in a way that the hiring conversation is not.

Telling an incoming experienced technologist "you do not own sprint
prioritisation" feels like diminishing the role. Telling your existing
engineering lead "you do not own architecture any more" feels like a demotion.
Both conversations are easier to avoid, and avoiding them produces the
two-people-one-job failure.

Have them anyway, in week zero, with both people in the room. The version of
that conversation held in month seven, after an argument about a vendor choice,
is considerably worse.

The single question I would make anyone answer before signing: *when the
fractional CTO and the engineering lead disagree about an architecture decision,
who decides, and does everyone involved already know the answer?*

If the answer is "we'd work it out", the engagement has a predictable ending.

# Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery

I have watched three zero-trust programmes. Two produced documents. One produced
change.

The difference was not budget or executive support — the document-producing ones
had more of both. It was that the successful one started with changes where **the
secure version was also the more convenient version**, and therefore needed no
enforcement.

That is the whole thesis of this issue, and I want to make it concrete rather
than leave it as a slogan.

## Why security programmes stall

The standard shape: a maturity assessment, a target-state architecture, a
roadmap with workstreams, and a set of controls to be implemented across the
estate.

Every control in that roadmap makes someone's job harder. That is not a
criticism — it is the nature of a control. But it means every control has a
negotiation attached, and the negotiation is between a security team with
authority-on-paper and delivery teams with deadlines-in-practice.

Delivery wins those negotiations, mostly, and it wins them by attrition rather
than by argument. The control is agreed, scheduled, deprioritised, and raised
again next quarter. Two years later the maturity assessment is repeated and the
scores have barely moved.

The programmes that work invert the selection criterion. Instead of asking
*what is the highest-risk gap*, they ask **what is the highest-risk gap whose fix
makes life easier?** Those exist, there are more of them than people think, and
they build the credibility that the genuinely inconvenient controls later
require.

## The one I would do this quarter

Here is the specific example, and I think it is close to universal.

Somewhere in your CI system there is a static cloud access key. It has broad
permissions, because deploys need broad permissions. It does not expire. It is
usable by anyone who can trigger a workflow or read the secret store.

That key is plausibly the most valuable credential your organisation holds. It
outranks any individual engineer's access, because it is scoped to deploy —
which means it can modify production. And because it is long-lived, a single
exposure is a persistent compromise rather than a time-boxed one.

Every CI provider now supports OIDC federation, which removes it entirely. The
workflow presents a signed token describing itself — this repository, this
branch, this environment — your cloud account verifies it against the provider's
public keys, and if the claims match a policy you wrote, hands back credentials
that live fifteen minutes.

No key. Nothing to rotate. Nothing to inherit when someone leaves. Nothing to
leak.

**And it is less work than the thing it replaces.** No rotation schedule, no
secret to manage, no annual audit finding about key age, no "who has access to
this secret" question. The engineer whose life you were about to complicate
instead has one fewer thing to maintain.

That asymmetry is why this one actually ships. Nobody has to be persuaded,
because there is no trade-off to argue about.

## The two things to get right

I will keep this brief because the mechanics are well documented, but these two
mistakes are common enough to name.

**Scope the trust policy exactly.** The policy says which identities may assume
the role. The failure is loosening it until it works:

```
"sub": "repo:acme/payments:ref:refs/heads/main"   ← correct
"sub": "repo:acme/*"                               ← trusts every repo in the org
"sub": "*"                                         ← trusts every repo on GitHub
```

That third one is not hypothetical. It is what you get when someone debugs a
claims mismatch at 6pm by widening the condition until the error stops. Use exact
matching, not pattern matching, and review these policies specifically.

**Pull-request workflows get a read-only role.** The token for a pull-request
event does not identify the source branch, which means a PR from a fork can
satisfy a PR-scoped trust policy. Deploy roles are gated on the protected
environment, never on the PR event.

If you want the full mechanics — trust policy construction, permissions
boundaries, and migrating without a delivery freeze — my colleagues have the
argument and the implementation in
[zero-trust without bringing delivery to a halt](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/zero-trust-without-stopping-delivery).

## Migrating without a freeze

The reason this does not get done, despite being easy, is fear of breaking
deploys. It does not require a freeze:

1. Create the provider and roles **alongside** the existing keys. Nothing
   changes.
2. Switch one low-risk service. Keep its key in place as rollback.
3. **Watch the audit log for both principals** for a few days. This is the step
   people skip and regret — it is how you find the scheduled job in a workflow
   nobody remembered that still uses the key.
4. **Deactivate the key, do not delete it.** Deactivation is instantly
   reversible. Leave it deactivated for a sprint.
5. Repeat per service, then delete.
6. Add an organisation-level policy denying access-key creation, so the problem
   cannot return.

Step six is the one that makes it permanent. Without it, a key reappears within
a year, created in a hurry by someone solving a Friday problem — which is how
the original one got there.

## The general pattern

What makes the CI credential example work, generalised:

**The control removes a maintenance burden rather than adding one.** Short-lived
credentials remove rotation. A managed secret store removes the config file
nobody wants to own. Automated patching removes the quarterly scramble.

**The control is preventive rather than detective.** A policy that stops an
unencrypted bucket being created is better than an alert that one was created,
and it is also less work for everyone — no triage, no remediation ticket, no
exception register. Detective controls generate work indefinitely; preventive
ones generate work once.

**The control is enforced by infrastructure rather than by review.** Anything
that depends on someone remembering during code review will be missed under
deadline, and then the security team's role becomes catching omissions, which is
adversarial and does not scale.

If you order your roadmap by that pattern first, the inconvenient controls
afterwards land in a relationship where delivery teams have experienced security
work as something that helped them. That is worth more than any amount of
executive mandate.

## The best time to do this

Before the estate exists.

Everything above is a retrofit, and retrofits are where security programmes
spend their effort. If you are standing up a new cloud environment, the
organisation-level deny on access-key creation costs nothing on day one and
means you never accumulate the keys at all.

Same for encryption defaults, region allowlists, mandatory tags, and central
logging the workload account cannot delete. All trivial before the first
workload, all a programme afterwards.

This is the part that connects to issue two: the landing zone is not preparation
for a migration, it is the migration's only durable output. The workloads were
going to end up in the cloud anyway. Whether they end up somewhere governable is
decided in the weeks before the first one moves, and that is why these controls
belong
[built into the landing zone before the first workload lands](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud)
rather than added later.

I realise "do it at the start" is useless advice if you are not at the start.
So, for the much more common case: pick the one control whose fix removes work,
ship it, and use the credibility.

Next issue, the last one: how to run a vendor shortlist, which is the thing I
get asked about most and have the least systematic view of.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Three programmes,
anonymised. I am not a security specialist; this is the view from delivery, which
is a partial view and I would be glad to be corrected by someone whose job it
actually is.*
