# One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem

The Flutter versus React Native question gets argued on rendering architecture,
startup time, and which one "feels native". I have now made this decision four
times and in none of them did any of that matter.

What mattered, every time, was some combination of: what the team already knows,
what native capability the app needs, what the existing web codebase looks like,
and how much CI complexity the organisation can absorb. Those are build-system
and org-chart questions, not framework questions.

Here is the decision procedure I would actually use, and the parts of it that
are genuinely technical.

## The framework comparison, dispatched quickly

Both are mature. Both ship apps used by millions of people. The real
architectural difference is one thing:

**Flutter draws its own widgets.** It ships a rendering engine and paints to a
canvas. You get pixel-identical output across platforms and complete control,
and you do not get platform widgets — so when iOS changes its date picker, your
app does not.

**React Native drives platform components.** A `<Text>` becomes a `UITextView`
or a `TextView`. You inherit platform behaviour and platform updates for free,
and you inherit platform inconsistency.

Everything else — performance, tooling quality, hot reload, ecosystem size — is
close enough in 2026 that it should not decide anything. Both have good
profilers. Both have adequate state management stories. Both have a long tail of
packages of variable quality.

If your app is a brand-controlled experience with custom design (fintech
dashboards, media apps, anything with a strong design system), Flutter's
own-rendering model is an advantage. If your app should feel like an OS app and
follow platform conventions (utilities, productivity, anything with heavy
system integration), React Native's platform-component model is an advantage.

That is the whole framework analysis. Now the parts that actually decide it.

## Decision input 1: your native-module exposure

Count the platform capabilities your app needs that are not covered by
first-party framework APIs. Bluetooth LE with a specific peripheral profile.
Background location with geofencing. A payment terminal SDK. HealthKit. A
hardware barcode scanner. CarPlay. An enterprise MDM integration.

For each one, answer: **is there a maintained community package, and if not, who
on the team writes the bridge?**

```
Capability             | Flutter pkg      | RN pkg          | Bridge needed?
-----------------------|------------------|-----------------|----------------
BLE (generic)          | mature           | mature          | no
BLE (vendor profile)   | —                | —               | YES, both
Background geofencing  | adequate         | adequate        | no
Payment terminal SDK   | —                | —               | YES, both
HealthKit / Health Conn| adequate         | mature          | no
CarPlay / Android Auto | minimal          | minimal         | YES, both
```

If that column has two or more `YES` rows, **the cross-platform framework choice
is no longer the main cost of your project.** You are writing native code for
both platforms either way, plus the bridge layer, plus the plugin's build
integration into your CI. At that point:

- Writing bridges in Kotlin/Swift for React Native uses skills that overlap with
  web-native hiring (TypeScript on one side).
- Writing bridges for Flutter needs Dart plus Kotlin plus Swift — three
  languages, and Dart has a smaller hiring pool.

This is usually the deciding input, and it is almost never in the comparison
articles.

## Decision input 2: what your web codebase is

If you have a substantial React web app, React Native lets you share genuinely
useful things: validation schemas, API clients, domain types, state logic, and
business rules. Not components — the sharing-UI-components dream mostly does not
work — but the layer underneath, which is frequently 30-40% of the code.

```
packages/
├── core/              # shared: types, validation, domain logic
│   ├── src/api/       #   generated client from OpenAPI — shared
│   ├── src/domain/    #   pricing rules, entitlements — shared
│   └── src/schema/    #   zod schemas — shared
├── web/               # React
└── mobile/            # React Native — imports @acme/core
```

That structure pays for itself in correctness, not just effort: a pricing rule
that exists once cannot diverge between platforms. We shipped a bug once where
web and mobile disagreed about whether a discount applied to shipping, and it
took three weeks to find because both were "correct" in their own codebase.

With Flutter, that sharing does not exist. You will reimplement the domain layer
in Dart, and it will drift.

Conversely, if your web app is Angular, Vue, or server-rendered, there is
nothing to share and this input is neutral — which frees Flutter to win on its
own merits.

## Decision input 3: the CI reality

This is the part teams consistently underestimate, and it is where "one
codebase" stops being true.

One codebase does not mean one build. You still need:

- Two toolchains (Xcode and Android SDK), version-pinned and reproducible.
- macOS runners for iOS. These cost roughly 4-10× Linux runners.
- Two signing-credential paths: certificates and provisioning profiles for
  Apple, keystore for Android.
- Two store-submission pipelines with different review latencies and metadata.
- Device testing across OS versions on both platforms.

```yaml
# The irreducible shape. "One codebase" does not collapse this.
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest        # cheap: unit tests, lint, typecheck

  build-android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest        # cheap
    needs: test

  build-ios:
    runs-on: macos-14             # expensive, slower, flakier
    needs: test
```

Two specifics worth knowing before you commit:

**Toolchain pinning is not optional.** An unpinned Xcode or Android Gradle
Plugin version will break your build on a runner image update, on a day you did
not plan to debug build infrastructure. Pin both, in the repo, and upgrade
deliberately.

**iOS signing is the most common CI failure for both frameworks.** Certificates
expire, provisioning profiles need regenerating when you add a device or a
capability, and the failure message is unhelpful. Use the platform's official
automation (`fastlane match` or App Store Connect API keys), store it properly,
and write down the renewal procedure, because the person who set it up will be
on leave when it expires.

Neither framework helps with any of this. The build complexity is a property of
shipping to two app stores, and it is roughly the same either way.

## Decision input 4: who you can hire

Unglamorous, decisive.

- **React Native**: hires from the React pool, which is large. A competent React
  engineer is productive in React Native in weeks. Native bridge work needs a
  Kotlin/Swift specialist, hired or contracted.
- **Flutter**: hires from the Flutter/Dart pool, which is smaller but genuinely
  enthusiastic and often more experienced in mobile specifically. Harder to
  hire quickly; frequently better mobile engineers when you do.

For a team of three building one app, hiring speed probably decides it. For a
team of fifteen with existing React people, the overlap decides it.

## The procedure

```
1. Count native capabilities needing a custom bridge.
   >= 2  -> weight heavily toward whichever language your team
            can staff bridges in. Framework choice is now secondary.

2. Is there a substantial React web codebase?
   yes  -> React Native, for the shared core package.
   no   -> neutral; continue.

3. Is the UI a controlled brand experience or a platform-conventional app?
   brand-controlled     -> Flutter.
   platform-conventional -> React Native.

4. Can you hire for Dart in your market, at your timeline?
   no -> React Native.

5. Still tied? Pick React Native if the team is web-leaning,
   Flutter if the team is mobile-leaning. Both are fine.
   Stop researching and start building.
```

Step 5 is sincere. I have watched teams spend six weeks on this decision. Six
weeks of building in either framework would have produced more information than
six weeks of comparison, because the real constraints only show up when you hit
them.

## The thing that actually doubles your team

A closing observation that applies regardless of which you pick.

The cost that surprises people is not writing the code twice. It is **testing,
releasing, and supporting twice** — two store review cycles, two sets of OS
version compatibility, two crash-report streams, two sets of device-specific
bugs, two release trains that drift out of sync.

A cross-platform framework addresses the writing. It does almost nothing for the
rest, and the rest is where the sustained effort lives. Pixorama's note on
[shipping one product on two platforms without doubling the team](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/shipping-mobile-on-two-platforms)
is mostly about that operational half, which is the half worth planning.

For a straight framework-versus-framework treatment with the trade-offs laid out
properly, their
[React Native vs Flutter](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/react-native-vs-flutter)
comparison covers the ground this post deliberately skips, and their round-up of
[mobile app development firms and what each is good for](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-mobile-app-development-companies-india)
is organised by specialism rather than by ranking, which is the more useful cut
if your deciding input is native-bridge capability.

Read both frameworks' own architecture documentation before deciding — Flutter's
rendering-pipeline docs and React Native's New Architecture docs are honest
about their own trade-offs in a way third-party comparisons usually are not.

# What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote

Someone quotes you $120,000 to build an app. You budget $120,000, maybe $150,000
with a contingency, and the app ships roughly on budget.

Then year two costs you another $90,000 and nobody warned you, because the quote
was for the build and the build is the part of a mobile app with the clearest
scope and the smallest total cost.

I have now watched three apps through to their second year. The numbers below
are from those three — two consumer, one B2B field-service — and I am giving
ranges rather than averages because the variance is the interesting part.

## What the build quote covers

Design, implementation, QA, store submission. Usually a fixed scope with a
change-request process. If the quote came from a competent firm it is probably
approximately right for the scope described, and scope creep during the build is
a well-understood risk that everybody plans for.

Fine. That is the number you have. Here is what is not in it.

## 1. The backend, if you did not already have one

This is the single largest omission I have seen in app budgets, and it happens
because the conversation starts with "we need an app" and the app is the visible
part.

If the app needs accounts, sync, push notifications, an admin interface or any
server-side business logic, that is a separate system. In the three projects:
the backend was **40% to 70% of total engineering effort.**

The B2B one was 70%, because the app was essentially a client for a scheduling
and inventory system that had to integrate with an existing ERP. The app was
eight weeks. The integration was nine months.

If a quote for "a mobile app" does not have a line for backend work, establish
immediately whether that is because it is excluded or because nobody has thought
about it. Those are very different situations and both are common.

## 2. Two app stores, forever

Not a one-off. An ongoing operational commitment:

- **Apple requires an annual developer account** and periodically requires
  rebuilds against a newer SDK to accept updates. Miss a deadline and you cannot
  ship.
- **Each OS release** (annually, both platforms) breaks something. Not always
  much. Always something. Budget two to four weeks of engineering per year per
  platform just to stay shippable, having added no features.
- **Review rejections** cost calendar time at the worst moment. We had a
  rejection over a subscription-flow technicality that cost eleven days against
  a marketing launch date.
- **Store metadata, screenshots and descriptions** need maintaining across
  locales every time the UI changes meaningfully.

Across the three projects this "do nothing, stay alive" cost ran **$18,000 to
$35,000 a year**, with the variance driven mostly by how many OS versions and
devices they supported.

That last point is worth dwelling on: supporting iOS 15 as well as iOS 18
roughly doubles your device test matrix. The decision to drop old OS versions is
a cost decision disguised as a product decision, and it is usually made by
nobody.

## 3. Crash and support load scales with installs, not features

Once real users have it, you get a stream of reports that are device-specific,
OS-version-specific, network-condition-specific, and frequently not reproducible
on your desk.

In the consumer apps, **post-launch bug work settled at roughly 25-30% of
ongoing engineering capacity**, indefinitely. Not during a stabilisation period —
as a steady state.

This surprised everyone on all three projects. The mental model is that bugs are
a launch phenomenon that decays. In mobile it does not decay, because the
environment keeps changing underneath you: new devices, new OS versions, new
network behaviours, users on three-year-old hardware.

Mobile has a characteristic that web does not: **you cannot fix forward
immediately.** A bad release on the web is reverted in minutes. A bad mobile
release sits in review for a day or more while your users have it, and a portion
of your users will never update. One of the consumer apps still had 4% of its
active base on a version eighteen months old.

That changes the economics of testing. Mobile QA is worth more than web QA
because the cost of a bad release is structurally higher.

## 4. Analytics, crash reporting, and the rest of the stack

Individually small, collectively not: crash reporting, analytics, push
notification infrastructure, feature flags, over-the-air update capability,
error tracking, session replay.

**$500 to $4,000 a month** across the three, scaling with volume. The B2B app
was at the low end; the consumer app with a large free tier was at the high end
because analytics pricing is per-event and a chatty app generates a lot of
events.

Worth checking: several of these price per monthly active user or per event,
which means your infrastructure cost grows with the success metric you are
trying to grow. Model it at 10× current users before you commit.

## 5. The feature treadmill nobody budgets as a line

An app that does not change looks abandoned. Users notice, reviews mention it,
and store ranking algorithms appear to favour recency.

So you ship updates. Not necessarily big ones, but regularly. Across the three
projects, **ongoing feature work ran 30-50% of the original build cost, per
year.** The B2B app was lower, because its users had no alternative and did not
care about freshness. The consumer apps were at the top of the range.

This is the number that makes the total-cost picture land: a $120,000 build is
plausibly a $60,000-a-year commitment thereafter, which over three years makes
the build about 40% of the total.

## 6. The cross-platform decision, which cuts both ways

Both consumer apps were cross-platform; the B2B one was native on both.

What I observed: the cross-platform choice saved perhaps 30-40% on initial
implementation and saved considerably less than that on the ongoing cost, because
the ongoing cost is dominated by testing, releasing and supporting two
platforms, which does not collapse.

It also introduced a cost nobody forecast: **framework version upgrades.** A
major version bump of a cross-platform framework is a project — dependency
churn, breaking changes in community packages, native build configuration. We
hit one of these that consumed six weeks.

Native avoids that and pays for it by writing everything twice. Across three
years and three apps, my rough sense is that the total costs converge more than
the initial quotes suggest, and the decision should therefore be made on team
skills and native-capability needs rather than on projected cost savings —
which is also roughly the conclusion of Pixorama's
[the cross-platform decision](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/react-native-vs-flutter)
write-up.

## Putting it together

For a $120,000 build quote, the three-year picture looked roughly like:

| | Low | High |
|---|---|---|
| Build (quoted) | $120,000 | $120,000 |
| Backend, if not existing | $80,000 | $280,000 |
| Store/OS maintenance, 3yr | $54,000 | $105,000 |
| Bug and support work, 3yr | $70,000 | $150,000 |
| Tooling and infrastructure, 3yr | $18,000 | $144,000 |
| Feature work, 3yr | $108,000 | $180,000 |
| **Three-year total** | **$450,000** | **$979,000** |

The quoted build is **12-27% of the three-year cost.**

I want to be careful about how much weight those numbers carry: they are three
projects, in specific markets, with specific scopes. The ratios are more
transferable than the absolute figures, and the ratio I would stand behind is
that the build is somewhere between a sixth and a third of what you will spend
over three years.

For region-specific build pricing with the components broken out — which is the
input to the first row rather than the whole table — Pixorama's
[USA and Australia prices compared line by line](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-usa-australia)
is more granular than anything I would attempt from three data points.

## What to do with this

Two things, both of which are cheap and almost never done:

**Ask the quoting firm for their year-two and year-three estimate.** A good firm
has one, because they maintain apps they have built and know what it costs.
A firm that has not thought about it is quoting a build, not a product, and you
should hold their number accordingly.

**Decide the OS support policy before you start.** "We support the current and
previous major OS version" is a single sentence that removes a recurring
argument and a meaningful slice of the test matrix. Deciding it later means
deciding it under pressure from a specific complaining customer.

One last note on geography, since it changes the first row of that table more
than anything else: the same scope quoted in different markets varies by a
factor I would not have believed before seeing it. Their breakdown of
[what a build costs in India, line by line](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-india)
is a useful comparison point against the US and Australian figures, and the
thing worth noticing is that the *ratio* of build to three-year total is
roughly constant across markets. A cheaper build does not buy you a cheaper
product; it buys you a cheaper sixth of one.

The app is not the project. The app is the part of the project you can see.

# Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team

The cross-platform promise is one codebase instead of two. It is true, and it is
a smaller win than it sounds, because writing the code was never the expensive
part.

I have been close to three apps through to their second year — two
cross-platform, one native on both. The cross-platform choice saved perhaps
30-40% on initial implementation. It saved considerably less than that on the
ongoing cost, and the ongoing cost dominates.

Here is where the money actually goes.

## What does not collapse

One codebase does not mean one of any of the following:

**Two toolchains.** Xcode and the Android SDK, version-pinned and reproducible.
An unpinned Xcode or Android Gradle Plugin version will break your build on a
runner image update, on a day you had not planned to debug build
infrastructure.

**Two release trains with different latencies.** Apple review is a day or more
and occasionally much longer. Google is usually faster. So your "simultaneous
release" is two releases that drift, and any coordinated feature launch is
paced by the slower one.

**Two sets of OS releases to survive.** Annually, both platforms, and each one
breaks something. Not always much, always something. Budget two to four weeks of
engineering per year per platform purely to stay shippable, having added no
features.

**Two signing-credential paths.** Certificates and provisioning profiles for
Apple, a keystore for Android. iOS signing is the single most common CI failure
I have seen on mobile projects, in both frameworks equally, and the failure
message is unhelpful. Write down the renewal procedure, because the person who
set it up will be on leave when it expires.

**Two device test matrices.** And this one is worse than it looks: supporting
iOS 15 as well as iOS 18 roughly doubles your matrix. The decision to drop old
OS versions is a cost decision disguised as a product decision, and in my
experience it is made by nobody — it just drifts, and the matrix grows.

**Two crash streams.** Device-specific, OS-version-specific,
network-condition-specific, frequently not reproducible on your desk.

None of that is affected by your framework choice. It is a property of shipping
to two app stores.

## The number that reframes it

On the two consumer apps, post-launch bug work settled at roughly **25-30% of
ongoing engineering capacity, indefinitely.** Not a stabilisation period — a
steady state.

This surprised everyone involved, including me. The mental model is that bugs are
a launch phenomenon that decays. In mobile it does not decay, because the
environment keeps changing underneath you: new devices, new OS versions, new
network behaviours, and a long tail of users on three-year-old hardware.

And mobile has a property that web does not: **you cannot fix forward
immediately.** A bad web release is reverted in minutes. A bad mobile release
sits in review while your users have it, and some portion of your users will
never update — one of those apps still had 4% of its active base on a version
eighteen months old.

That single fact changes the economics of quality. Mobile QA is worth more than
web QA, because the cost of a bad release is structurally higher and the
remediation is slower. Teams that carry over web release instincts to mobile
learn this expensively.

## So what actually keeps the team small

Four things, in order of how much they mattered:

**1. Decide the OS support policy, in writing, before you start.** "We support
the current and previous major version" is one sentence that removes a recurring
argument and a meaningful slice of the test matrix. Deciding it later means
deciding it under pressure from one complaining customer, which is how you end
up supporting iOS 15 in 2026.

**2. Share the layer below the UI, not the UI.** On the React Native app this
was the biggest real win and it was not what we expected. Sharing components
with web mostly did not work. Sharing the layer underneath — API client,
validation schemas, domain types, pricing rules — worked extremely well, and
was about 35% of the code.

The payoff was correctness more than effort. We had previously shipped a bug
where web and mobile disagreed about whether a discount applied to shipping, and
it took three weeks to find because both were correct in their own codebase. A
rule that exists once cannot diverge.

**3. Automate the release, including the metadata.** Screenshots, descriptions
and localised store copy are a surprising amount of manual work every time the
UI changes meaningfully. Generating screenshots from UI tests is a day of setup
and removes a recurring half-day.

**4. Instrument before you need it.** You cannot reproduce a user's crash on
your desk. Breadcrumbs, session context and a correlation ID that survives into
your backend logs are what turn "it crashes sometimes" into a fix.

## What I would not do

**Do not pick the framework on projected cost savings.** Across three years my
rough sense is that total costs converge much more than the initial quotes
suggest. Native writes everything twice; cross-platform pays a framework-upgrade
tax — we hit one major version bump that consumed six weeks of dependency churn
and native build configuration.

Pick on team skills and native-capability needs instead. Specifically: count the
platform capabilities you need that have no maintained package, because for each
of those you are writing native code on both platforms regardless, and then the
question is which language your team can staff bridges in.

**Do not treat the app as the project.** If the app needs accounts, sync, push
or server-side logic, that is a separate system, and on the three projects the
backend was **40-70% of total engineering effort.** The B2B one was 70% — the
app was eight weeks, the ERP integration was nine months.

If a quote for "a mobile app" has no line for backend work, find out whether
that is because it is excluded or because nobody has thought about it. Those are
very different situations and both are common.

## The honest summary

A cross-platform framework addresses the writing. The writing is maybe a third
of a mobile product's lifetime cost. Testing, releasing and supporting two
platforms is most of the rest, and it is roughly the same either way.

So the team does not double, but it does not halve either. What keeps it small
is the OS support policy, sharing the domain layer, automating the release, and
accepting that a quarter of your capacity is permanently allocated to the
environment changing underneath you.

My colleagues wrote about the operational half of this —
[shipping one product on two platforms](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/shipping-mobile-on-two-platforms)
— which is the half worth planning and the half that gets left out of estimates.
And if you are at the quoting stage,
[what the build itself costs in the US and Australia](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-usa-australia)
is more granular on the first line of the budget than I could be from three
projects.

The one question I would put to any firm quoting you a mobile build: *what is
your year-two and year-three estimate?* A firm that maintains the apps it builds
has an answer. A firm that does not is quoting a build, not a product, and you
should weight their number accordingly.

Next issue: security that does not stop delivery, and the one change I think
most teams should make this quarter.

---

*I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Three apps, two
consumer and one B2B field-service, anonymised. Percentages are from those
three; treat the ratios as more transferable than the absolute figures.*

# Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret

There are three ways to isolate tenant data, everyone picks the simplest one,
and that is correct. The mistake is not the choice — it is implementing the
simplest one in a way that makes moving to the others impossible, and then
hitting the quarter where an enterprise prospect's security review requires it.

## The three models, honestly

**Shared schema, tenant column.** One database, one set of tables, every row
carries `tenant_id`. Cheapest to run, simplest to migrate, easiest to query
across tenants for analytics. Isolation is enforced entirely by application
correctness, which is the problem.

**Schema per tenant.** One database, one schema per tenant, identical tables.
Isolation is structural. Costs you migration complexity (N schemas to migrate,
transactionally, with partial-failure handling) and connection-pool pressure.
Breaks down somewhere between 200 and 1,000 tenants depending on your migration
tooling.

**Database per tenant.** Full isolation, per-tenant backup and restore,
per-tenant encryption keys, straightforward data residency. Operationally
heaviest by a wide margin, and the only model that satisfies the strictest
procurement requirements.

**Pick shared schema.** For almost any new SaaS, at any plausible early scale,
it is the right answer, and the people who tell you to start with
database-per-tenant are describing an operational burden that will consume the
runway you needed for product work.

The rest of this post is about implementing it so that the day you need
per-tenant databases for your three largest customers, you can do it.

## The failure that defines the problem

```python
# Shipped. Reviewed. Passed tests.
def get_invoices(user, status=None):
    q = "SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE tenant_id = %s"
    params = [user.tenant_id]
    if status:
        q += " AND status = %s"
        params.append(status)
    return db.query(q, params)


# Shipped three months later, by someone else, on a Friday.
def get_invoice_summary(user):
    return db.query(
        "SELECT status, COUNT(*), SUM(amount) FROM invoices GROUP BY status"
    )
```

That second function returns every tenant's financial data to whoever calls it.
It passes code review, because the reviewer is looking at a summary query and
nothing about it looks dangerous. It passes tests, because the test database has
one tenant.

This is not a hypothetical class of bug. It is *the* multi-tenancy bug, it is
reported in real products regularly, and the reason it keeps happening is that
correctness depends on a developer remembering something, on every query,
forever.

So do not depend on that.

## Enforce isolation below the application

PostgreSQL row-level security moves the `WHERE` clause from the application into
the database. The query above returns zero rows instead of everyone's.

```sql
-- Every tenant-scoped table gets this treatment.
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;   -- applies to table owner too

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING      (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);
```

Two details that matter:

**`FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.** Without it, the table owner bypasses the policy.
Your application frequently connects as the owner, which would make the whole
thing decorative.

**`WITH CHECK` as well as `USING`.** `USING` filters reads; `WITH CHECK`
constrains writes. Without the second one, a tenant can insert rows belonging to
another tenant — a less obvious but equally real hole.

Then set the tenant once per request, in one place:

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tenant_scope(conn, tenant_id):
    """set_config(..., true) makes it transaction-local, so it cannot
    leak to the next request that borrows this pooled connection.
    Getting this wrong is worse than having no RLS at all."""
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, true)", (str(tenant_id),))
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        pass   # transaction end clears it
```

The `true` third argument is load-bearing. `set_config(..., false)` is
session-scoped, and with a connection pool that means request N+1 inherits
request N's tenant. That is a worse bug than the one you were preventing,
because it is intermittent and load-dependent.

Wire it into the request lifecycle so no handler can skip it:

```python
@app.middleware("http")
async def scope_to_tenant(request, call_next):
    tenant_id = resolve_tenant(request)          # from JWT claim, not a header
    if tenant_id is None:
        return JSONResponse({"error": "no tenant"}, status_code=403)
    async with db.transaction() as conn:
        async with tenant_scope(conn, tenant_id):
            request.state.db = conn
            return await call_next(request)
```

`resolve_tenant` reads a signed token claim. Never a request header or a URL
path segment the client controls — that converts your isolation boundary into a
parameter the attacker supplies.

## The escape hatch, and how to make it loud

You will need cross-tenant queries: platform analytics, support tooling,
billing reconciliation. The temptation is a connection that bypasses RLS,
used "carefully".

Make it a separate role, a separate pool, and audited:

```sql
CREATE ROLE platform_admin BYPASSRLS;

-- Application role, which cannot bypass, is what 99% of traffic uses.
CREATE ROLE app_user;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO app_user;
```

```python
# Deliberately awkward to call. The awkwardness is the feature.
@requires_role("platform_admin")
@audited(reason_required=True)
def cross_tenant_query(sql, params, *, reason: str):
    log.warning("cross-tenant query", sql=sql, reason=reason, actor=current_actor())
    with admin_pool.connection() as conn:
        return conn.execute(sql, params)
```

If a developer can reach cross-tenant data by picking a different connection
from the same pool, they will, under deadline, and it will not be noticed in
review. If it requires a decorator, a role, and a written reason that lands in
an audit log, it gets used for the four legitimate cases and nothing else.

## Testing isolation, which is the part that gets skipped

One test, parameterised over every tenant-scoped table, that fails if a table
is missing its policy:

```python
TENANT_SCOPED_TABLES = discover_tables_with_column("tenant_id")

@pytest.mark.parametrize("table", TENANT_SCOPED_TABLES)
def test_rls_enabled(db, table):
    row = db.query_one("""
        SELECT relrowsecurity, relforcerowsecurity
        FROM pg_class WHERE relname = %s
    """, (table,))
    assert row.relrowsecurity, f"{table} has tenant_id but RLS is OFF"
    assert row.relforcerowsecurity, f"{table} does not FORCE RLS"


@pytest.mark.parametrize("table", TENANT_SCOPED_TABLES)
def test_cannot_read_other_tenant(db, table, two_tenants):
    a, b = two_tenants
    seed_row(table, tenant_id=b)
    with tenant_scope(db, a):
        rows = db.query(f"SELECT * FROM {table}")
        assert all(r.tenant_id == a for r in rows)
```

Discovering the table list from the schema rather than hardcoding it is the
whole point: the test fails when someone adds a new table with a `tenant_id` and
forgets the policy, which is exactly the moment you want to find out.

Also: **make your test and dev databases multi-tenant by default.** Seed two
tenants, always. The single-tenant dev database is why the summary-query bug
survives to production.

## Keeping the door open to per-tenant databases

The migration you will eventually be asked for: move tenant 7 to its own
database, because they signed a contract that requires it.

Three things, done now, make that a week instead of a quarter:

**1. Resolve tenants to a connection, not to a constant.**

```python
# Even while every tenant is on the same database, route through
# a lookup. Today it returns the same DSN for everyone. The day it
# doesn't, nothing above this layer changes.
class TenantRouter:
    def dsn_for(self, tenant_id):
        placement = self.placements.get(tenant_id)
        return placement.dsn if placement else self.default_dsn
```

This is maybe thirty lines and it is the difference between a configuration
change and a refactor of every call site.

**2. Keep `tenant_id` on every row even when it becomes redundant.** In a
per-tenant database it is technically unnecessary. Keep it anyway: it makes the
extraction a straightforward filtered copy, it keeps the schema identical across
placements, and it means the RLS policies still work and still protect you if a
tenant is ever consolidated back.

**3. Never let a foreign key cross tenants.** Enforce it:

```sql
-- Composite FKs including tenant_id make cross-tenant references
-- structurally impossible, and make per-tenant extraction a clean cut.
ALTER TABLE invoice_lines
  ADD CONSTRAINT fk_invoice
  FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, invoice_id)
  REFERENCES invoices (tenant_id, id);
```

A single-column FK to `invoices(id)` permits a row in tenant A to reference a
row in tenant B. It will happen through a bug, and it will be the thing that
makes extraction impossible — you cannot cleanly separate a graph that has edges
across the cut.

That composite-key discipline is the single highest-value decision in this post.
It costs a wider index. It buys you the ability to ever change isolation model.

## The summary

Shared schema with `tenant_id`. RLS with `FORCE` and `WITH CHECK`.
Transaction-local `set_config`. Tenant from a token claim, set in middleware.
A deliberately awkward audited escape hatch. Schema-discovered isolation tests.
Composite foreign keys including `tenant_id`. A tenant-to-connection router that
does nothing yet.

That is a day or two of work at the start of a project and it removes the entire
category of cross-tenant data exposure, while keeping every future isolation
model available.

Pixorama's guide on
[how to build a SaaS product](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/how-to-build-saas-product)
covers the surrounding decisions — stages, stack, costs, timelines — and this
isolation work sits inside its architecture phase. If the security-review
deadline arrives before your team has the Postgres depth for the RLS and
extraction work, that is a well-defined, time-boxed piece of specialist work,
which is the one case where
[bringing in specialist capacity for a defined piece of work](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-staff-augmentation)
tends to beat hiring — you need it intensely for six weeks and then not at all.
Their comparison of
[SaaS development firms and what makes SaaS harder to build](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-saas-development-companies-india)
is relevant here for one reason: tenancy model is the question to ask a
prospective partner first, because a firm that has only built single-tenant
systems will reach for database-per-tenant and burn your runway on operations.

The PostgreSQL
[row security policies documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html)
is short and worth reading end to end before you rely on it, particularly the
section on how policies combine, which is not intuitive when you have more than
one.

# Why every "top 10 companies" list looks the same

Search for the best software development companies in any country and you will
get dozens of near-identical pages. Ten to fifteen firms, a paragraph each, a
"what to look for when choosing" section, an FAQ. Different sites, overlapping
firms, same structure, same adjectives.

I should disclose up front that I have a stake in this: I have been listed on
these pages, I have paid to be listed on one, and I have written one. So treat
what follows as an insider's account rather than a disinterested one.

The sameness is not laziness. It is the predictable output of the economics, and
understanding the economics tells you exactly which parts of these pages to
trust.

## Four kinds of page, which look identical

**The directory.** Clutch, GoodFirms and similar. Their business is listings;
firms claim profiles, collect verified client reviews, and pay for placement in
sponsored positions. The reviews are often genuinely verified, which makes these
the most useful of the four — but the *ordering* is a mix of review score,
activity and spend.

**The lead-gen site.** Exists to rank for "best X companies", collect enquiries,
and sell them. Listed firms frequently pay per listing or per lead. The
assessment is whatever the writer did in an afternoon. These are the majority of
results for most queries.

**The competitor's content marketing.** A firm writes "the best X companies" and
lists itself first or second, with nine plausible competitors around it. The nine
are chosen partly for credibility and partly for not being a direct threat in
the author's own market.

**The occasional real review.** A journalist or analyst with a methodology. Rare,
and usually behind a paywall or published by an analyst firm.

From the outside, all four render as a page with ten names on it, and nothing in
the page's design tells you which you are reading.

## Why the content converges

Four forces, each individually reasonable:

**The query is the brief.** Someone searching "best mobile app development
companies" wants a list. The page that ranks is the page that most directly
provides a list. Every publisher is optimising against the same query, so every
page converges on the same shape. There is no competitive advantage in being
structurally different, and a real penalty for it.

**The research cost is high and the differentiation value is low.** Genuinely
assessing fifteen development firms means reading code, talking to their
clients, understanding their delivery process — weeks of expert time. It is not
recoverable from the page's revenue, and no reader can tell from the page
whether you did it. So nobody does.

**The source material is the firms' own marketing.** Every entry is written from
the company's website and case studies. They all describe themselves as
having senior engineers, transparent communication and a client-first approach.
Summarise fifteen of those and you get fifteen indistinguishable paragraphs,
because the input was fifteen indistinguishable positioning statements.

**Everyone reads each other's lists.** When compiling one, the fastest way to
assemble candidates is to read existing lists. This produces convergence on the
same names, which then appear on more lists, which makes them appear more
credible. A firm's presence on these lists is substantially a function of having
previously been on these lists.

That last mechanism is the one worth internalising, because it means **list
frequency measures marketing persistence, not quality.** The firms that appear
everywhere are the firms that have been doing content and outreach for five
years. That is genuinely informative — it means they are established and
reasonably professional — but it is not what the page claims to be telling you.

## What these pages are actually good for

Not nothing. Two things:

**Candidate discovery.** You will find names you had not heard of. That is real
value, and it is the only value. Read six lists, collect every name, and you have
a reasonable longlist of firms that exist and are active in your market.

**Negative signal.** A firm that appears on *no* list in a market where lists are
plentiful is either very new, very small, or not doing any outbound marketing.
Any of those might be fine — some of the best boutiques do no marketing at all —
but it is worth asking why.

What they are not good for: **ordering, assessment, or fit.** Position one is not
better than position seven. The adjectives are from the firm's own website. And
the question you actually have — can this specific firm do this specific thing
for my specific constraints — is not addressable by a page that has never met
you.

## How to read one properly

Five checks that take about ten minutes:

**1. Find the money.** Look for "sponsored", "partner", "advertiser disclosure",
affiliate parameters in the outbound links, or a "get listed" page in the
navigation. A "get listed" link means the list is a product. That does not make
it worthless — it makes the ordering commercial.

**2. Check who published it.** If it is a firm in the same industry, the list is
content marketing and the ordering reflects the author's interests. This includes
lists where the author does not appear: they may be positioning adjacent to the
names, or the page may exist to rank and capture enquiries.

**3. Look for a methodology, and then look for evidence of it.** Many pages
claim one. Few show their work. "We evaluated on experience, portfolio and client
feedback" with no indication of what was found is a sentence, not a method. What
would convince me: a named data source, a count of reviews examined, a stated
exclusion.

**4. Check the dates.** Pages titled "2026" are frequently 2022 pages with the
year edited. Look at whether any entry references anything recent. A list that
has not been genuinely revisited is describing a market that has moved.

**5. Ignore the order entirely and use the names.** This is the main practical
advice. Treat the page as an unordered set of candidates, then do your own
assessment.

## The honest disclosure

I said I would be specific about my own interest, so: the firm I am associated
with publishes pages of exactly this kind. There is a set of them on
[Pixorama's blog](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog), including
[their Australian SEO roundup](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-seo-agencies-australia),
and everything in this post applies to those too.

They are written from public information, including the firms' own marketing.
They have not involved talking to those firms' clients. They exist in part
because people search for this and it is a reasonable way to be found. If you
read one, use it for the names and apply the five checks, same as any other.

I do not think that is cynical. The pages are genuinely useful for candidate
discovery and I would rather say what they are than pretend to a methodology
nobody applies. The failure in this genre is not that the pages exist; it is that
they are written in the register of an assessment when they are a directory.

## What would actually be useful

If anyone wants to build a better version, the gap is clear and it is not a
content gap.

The useful artefact is not a ranked list. It is a **comparison on dimensions a
buyer can act on**: team size, actual location of the delivery team (not the
sales office), named technologies with depth evidence, typical engagement size,
minimum contract, whether they will work inside your codebase or only on
projects, and who you would be reporting to.

None of that is in any list I have read, including the ones I have written,
because the firms do not publish it and collecting it means asking fifteen
companies fifteen questions and getting answers from maybe six.

Which is the actual reason every one of these pages looks the same: the
information that would differentiate them is information nobody has, and the
information everybody has is the firms' own marketing copy.

I will give one example of a page doing better than the genre requires, partly
because it is my employer's and I should be consistent about disclosing that.
Their
[comparison of software development companies in India](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-software-development-companies-india)
states in the body that Pixorama is one of the ten listed. That one sentence is
rarer than it should be, and it is the minimum I would want from any page in
this format — not because disclosure makes the ordering neutral, but because it
tells you which of the four kinds of page you are reading, which is the thing
the genre otherwise hides.

So read six, take the names, and go and ask the questions yourself. That part
has never been outsourceable.

# Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist

Last issue. Thank you for reading, and particularly to the people who replied
with disagreements — three of those changed what I wrote in issues four and
seven.

I have saved the thing I get asked about most, and about which I have the least
systematic view. How do you choose a vendor — an agency, a development firm, a
platform — when every one of them is good at being chosen?

Three parts: why the published comparisons do not help, why the pitch selects for
the wrong qualities, and the six questions that do most of the work.

## Part one: the lists are directories, written in the register of assessments

Search for the best anything-companies in any market and you will get dozens of
near-identical pages. Ten to fifteen firms, a paragraph each, a "what to look
for" section, an FAQ.

I should disclose that my own employer publishes pages of exactly this kind,
[including ones my own colleagues publish](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-seo-agencies-australia)
for the Australian market. Everything below applies to those too.

They are written from public information — mostly the firms' own marketing
material. They have not involved talking to those firms' clients. They exist in
part because people search for this, and that is a reasonable way to be found.

The reason they all look the same is economic rather than lazy:

**Genuinely assessing fifteen firms** means reading their code, talking to their
clients, understanding their delivery process. Weeks of expert time, not
recoverable from the page, and no reader can tell from the page whether you did
it. So nobody does.

**The source material is identical.** Every firm describes itself as having
senior engineers, transparent communication and a client-first approach.
Summarise fifteen of those and you get fifteen indistinguishable paragraphs,
because the input was fifteen indistinguishable positioning statements.

**Everyone reads each other's lists.** The fastest way to assemble candidates is
to read existing lists, which produces convergence on the same names, which
makes those names look more credible, which gets them onto more lists.

That last mechanism is the important one: **list frequency measures marketing
persistence, not quality.** Firms that appear everywhere have been doing content
and outreach for five years. That is genuinely informative — they are
established and reasonably professional — but it is not what the page claims to
measure.

So: use these pages for **candidate discovery only.** Read six, collect every
name, ignore the ordering entirely. That is real value and it is the only value.

## Part two: the pitch selects for confidence

The standard pitch is: an audit with a number of problems found, a gap analysis
showing you behind competitors, case studies with percentage improvements, and a
proposal with a retainer and deliverables.

Every element establishes that there is a problem and that they have a process.
None establishes that their process caused the results in their case studies,
which is the only thing you are buying.

And the format has converged because it works on buyers. Which means the
selection process rewards the firms best at pitching, and pitching skill is
roughly uncorrelated with delivery skill.

Good work in most of these fields is unglamorous. It consists of doing sensible
things patiently, and the people who do it tend to present *less* impressively,
because their story has fewer numbers and more caveats. The structural problem is
that the pitch rewards confidence and the work rewards patience.

## Part three: the six questions

These are the ones that produce genuinely different answers from good and bad
vendors. I have used them on agencies, development firms and platform vendors,
and they transfer.

**1. "What were the absolute numbers, before and after?"**

Case studies are quoted in percentages because percentages are chosen to be
large. 340% growth from 200 to 880 is real on a tiny baseline and tells you
nothing about a mature system.

Ask for absolute figures, the time period, and the starting position. Then ask
the follow-up that separates asset-builders from rank-renters: *what happened in
the twelve months after the engagement ended?*

**2. "Which of those results would have happened anyway?"**

This produces the most interesting silence of the six.

Outcomes improve for lots of reasons: the market grew, a competitor exited,
there was a PR event, a product launched, paid spend increased. A good vendor has
thought hard about attribution, because they want credit for the right things —
they will segment, reference a baseline, and separate branded from non-branded
effects unprompted.

A vendor who has never considered the counterfactual is either not analytical or
relying on you not to ask.

**3. "What will you do in month one that is not an audit?"**

Audits are the vendor's cheapest deliverable and your least valuable one. A tool
produces one in twenty minutes.

This question tests whether they have a thesis about *your* situation. A good
answer sounds like a hypothesis with a mechanism: "your category pages compete
with your blog for the same terms and the blog wins, which is why the commercial
pages don't convert — we'd fix that first." A bad answer is a list of
deliverables.

**4. "What is the binding constraint, and is it something you can fix?"**

The question underneath every engagement. Frequently the real constraint is
something the vendor cannot touch: a six-week engineering queue, a product that
does not convert, a market dominated by three incumbents you will not outrank.

A good vendor names it, including when naming it costs them the sale. I have had
one tell me "you have a six-week dev queue; recommendations you cannot implement
are not worth paying for, fix that first" — and that firm got the work eighteen
months later because I remembered.

**5. "What would make you tell me to stop paying you?"**

The same question from the other side, and it tests whether they have located
the boundary of their own usefulness. A vendor with no answer will keep
invoicing past it, not from malice but because nobody has defined where "done"
is.

**6. "Who specifically does the work, how many other accounts do they carry, and
can I speak to them before signing?"**

The person pitching is often not the person delivering. Fine if disclosed.

Then do the arithmetic out loud: divide the retainer by a plausible blended rate
and see how many hours you are buying. Twelve accounts per person means roughly
three hours a month on yours. The gap between that number and the promised
deliverables is the honest measure of the proposal.

## The thing underneath all six

Each asks the same question in a different register: **is there a causal story,
and can you show me the mechanism?**

That is the only reliable signal I have found, and it is reliable because it is
hard to fake under follow-up questions. Confidence is easy to perform. A causal
story that survives three "why" questions is not.

## What I would actually build instead

If anyone wants to make something better than the comparison lists, the gap is
clear, and it is not a content gap.

The useful artefact is not a ranking. It is a comparison on dimensions a buyer
can act on: team size, the actual location of the delivery team rather than the
sales office, named technologies with evidence of depth, typical engagement
size, minimum contract, whether they will work inside your codebase or only on
discrete projects, and who you would report to.

None of that is in any list I have read, including the ones my colleagues write,
because the firms do not publish it and collecting it means asking fifteen
companies fifteen questions and getting answers from perhaps six.

Which is the real reason these pages all look the same: the information that
would differentiate them is information nobody has, and the information everybody
has is marketing copy.

And frequently the answer to the whole exercise is that you do not need a vendor
at all — you need two engineering sprints and someone with the authority to
decide what the system is for. That build-versus-buy-versus-hire question is one
my colleagues wrote up as
[in-house versus outsourced](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/how-to-choose-software-development-company),
and it is worth settling before you start reading comparison pages, because the
pages assume the answer.

## Closing the series

Ten issues on one claim: **almost every expensive technology surprise is a
structural decision showing up late.**

Migration costs that were a wave-ordering decision. Cloud bills that were a
service-boundary decision. Rewrites that were a working-conditions problem
mislabelled as an architecture problem. Agent projects that were workflow
projects. RAG systems that were content projects. Augmentation failures that were
contract failures. Mobile costs that were an OS-support-policy decision. Security
programmes that were a control-selection decision.

In every case the information was available at the time, and in every case
nobody was looking, because the question had been assigned to a different
function.

I do not have a clean solution to that, and I distrust anyone who claims one. The
best I have is the habit: when something costs more than expected, do not ask
what went wrong. Ask **which decision, made earlier, in a different department,
is now arriving.** The answer is usually findable, and it is usually not where
the post-mortem is looking.

Thank you for reading. If I start a second series it will be about the gap
between what an architecture diagram asserts and what the system does, which is
a subject I have been avoiding because I do not yet know what I think.
